dem.text: Whether the people we elect have to face the voters who hired them, or can keep their jobs by pleasing a narrower crowd.

eco.q: Who does our country work for?
eco.text: How much of what working households produce and spend comes back to them as security, and how much collects at the top.

opening.kicker: A systems atlas of American democracy and the economy
paras: You feel it at the kitchen table first. Rent climbs faster than pay. The people we elect often seem to hear someone else before they hear us. This atlas traces how that happens, one documented connection at a time.

The map below follows the story across five areas, read from left to right. Concentrated wealth and market power decide who gets heard in politics. Officials in safe seats have less reason to listen to anyone else, and the checks inside government weaken when few of them face a real race. Policy then tilts toward insiders. Along the bottom, the return line carries that tilt back into wealth at the top, and the circle turns again.
Every loop in the atlas also shows where a reform can interrupt it, and every link carries a grade for how strong its evidence is.
opening.return: Policy that favors insiders adds to wealth at the top.

parts.story: Some forces push on the system from outside it. New technology, global trade, foreign interference and shocks like wars and pandemics all shift the ground under the five areas. The atlas takes them as given and tracks how the system responds to them, and who comes out ahead.
parts.text: Conditions the model treats as given, such as technology and geography.

parts.chapter: Who holds the money and the market
parts.story: This is where the story starts: who owns what. When a small share of households holds most of the wealth and a few firms control a market, workers have less room to bargain and families have less cushion when prices rise. Housing is part of it too. Scarce homes push rents up and add to what owners already hold. These conditions decide who has spare money and time to spend on politics.
parts.text: Who holds wealth and market power, and how scarce essentials are.

parts.story: Officials hear from people all the time, and some voices arrive louder than others. Campaign money and paid lobbying reach them directly. In many places the local reporters who once covered city hall are gone, which leaves fewer people watching. Turnout matters as well. When some groups vote far less often, officials learn whose views carry weight on election day.
parts.text: Money, organized interests, local news and public attitudes that reach officials.

parts.story: Accountability depends on a real chance of losing. In most districts the general election is easy to predict, so the contest that decides the seat is a low-turnout primary. Incumbents also help write the rules for their own races, from district maps to voting procedures. When few officials face a competitive race, the pressure to serve the whole electorate fades.
parts.text: Whether officials can lose their seats, and who controls the rules of elections.

parts.story: Once in office, officials work inside a set of checks. Congress writes the laws and is supposed to oversee the executive branch. Courts settle fights over the rules, while inspectors general and agencies enforce them. When Congress lacks staff and expertise, more decisions shift to a president acting alone, and weakened watchdogs make the next shortcut easier. Most people meet all of this through public services, such as a benefit claim or a long wait on the phone.
parts.text: Congress, the presidency, courts, watchdogs and the public services they run.

parts.plain_question: Whose side are the rules on?
parts.story: Here the two questions meet. Policy can spread its benefits widely or send most of them to wealthy people and organized groups, and several studies find that the preferences of wealthier Americans get a stronger response. Trust follows what people see, and it grows when services work for them. From here the story loops back: tax breaks and rules that favor those at the top add to the wealth where it began.
parts.text: Whose interests policy favors, and whether public trust follows performance.

parts.formal_title: How the economy reaches a household
parts.story: This layer is the kitchen-table economy: pay, prices, benefits and debts, and what is left at the end of the month. It sits under the five areas because this is where policy lands. A tax change or a new wage rule shows up here first. Strain here also flows back up, since households stretched thin have less time and money for taking part.
parts.text: How does production become pay, household resources and essential costs?

parts.story: Software now sits between people and many of the things they need. The ranking of a social feed shapes what news people see, and pricing software helps set some rents and prices. AI is changing how work gets done and who keeps the gains. Government decides the rules these systems run under, which is why several lines here are lines of authority.

domains.title: News, records and public information
domains.everyday_question: How can I find out what my local officials are doing, and whether what I read about them is true?
domains.overview: Voters depend on information they cannot gather themselves: what the council decided, whether a claim about an election holds up, what the unemployment rate was last month. This domain follows how that information is paid for, how it reaches people and who can distort it. Local newsrooms lost most of the advertising that once paid reporters, and a few large platforms now rank much of what people see. Congress, the Federal Trade Commission, the Federal Communications Commission, courts and state legislatures set the rules. Newsrooms, platforms, records offices and statistical agencies make daily choices within them. When reporting thins out, challengers enter fewer races and officials face less scrutiny, which weakens the electoral pressure traced under Elections and representation. Missing records and weaker watchdogs also make favoritism harder to detect, a link followed under Money, lobbying and influence.

domains.title: Elections and representation
domains.everyday_question: Does my vote change who represents me and what they do in office?
domains.overview: Elections are the main way residents reward or replace the people who govern them. This domain follows each step: registering, casting a ballot, drawing districts, choosing nominees, counting votes and certifying results. States write most of these rules, and the legislators who write them often have a stake in the outcome. Congress sets some floors for federal elections, and courts decide which rules stand. In most House districts one party is sure to win, so a low-turnout primary picks the officeholder and the November election carries little threat. Incumbents who face little risk of losing feel less pressure to perform, a path that leads to the quality of public services. Who votes also shapes whose interests policy serves, which connects elections to political money and to household finances.

domains.title: Money, lobbying and influence
domains.everyday_question: Who gets a meeting with my representative, and what does it cost them?
domains.overview: Between elections, officials hear most from the people and groups who can pay for campaigns, lobbyists and expert advice. This domain traces those channels: campaign contributions and outside spending, disclosure of who pays, lobbying and the move between public office and industry jobs, officials' personal financial stakes, public contracting, and the tax and regulatory favors that can follow. Congress, state legislatures and the Federal Election Commission write and enforce the rules, and Supreme Court rulings under the First Amendment set their outer limits. Evidence that donors get more access is strong. Evidence on how far that access changes policy is weaker and contested. The money comes disproportionately from the households with the most wealth, and the advantages it secures can protect that wealth. Weak enforcement by agencies and watchdogs lets the cycle run with fewer checks.

domains.title: Congress, agencies and public services
domains.everyday_question: Why does it take so long to get a benefit, a permit or a new law?
domains.overview: A law helps people only when Congress can write it well and an agency can carry it out. This domain covers both halves. On the legislative side it looks at Congress's own staff and research agencies, the floor rules that decide what gets a vote, budget deadlines that can shut the government down, and the power to demand information from the executive branch. On the delivery side it looks at hiring, civil-service protection, aging software, contracting, paperwork that keeps eligible people from benefits, and permitting. Congress funds and structures agencies, the President and agency heads run them, and courts police the limits. When Congress lacks its own experts it leans on industry for drafting. Service failures feed a proposed loop in which trust and funding fall together, which ties this domain to elections and to presidential power.

domains.title: Checks on power and equal justice
domains.everyday_question: What stops a president, a court or the police from overstepping, and can I get a fair hearing if they do?
domains.overview: Every office in this Atlas works within legal limits set by the Constitution, by statutes and by court rulings. This domain asks whether those limits hold. It covers emergency powers, executive orders, withheld funds, war powers, pardons and the removal of watchdogs and regulators. It looks at how judges are appointed, assigned and held to ethics rules. It also asks whether the law treats people equally when they deal with police, prosecutors, surveillance or discrimination. Congress can write limits and refuse funds, courts decide disputes, and inspectors general and independent commissions investigate. Since 2024 several Supreme Court rulings have widened presidential control over agencies, while rulings on tariffs and the National Guard have bounded it. When Congress cannot legislate, more policy moves into executive action. Court rulings on maps and political money feed back into elections and influence.

domains.title: Competition and market power
domains.everyday_question: Why do I have so few choices, and such high prices, for things like prescriptions, hospital care or concert tickets?
domains.overview: Competition is supposed to keep prices in check: if one seller charges too much, another can win the customer. This domain looks at what weakens that check. Mergers, including strings of small acquisitions, can leave a market with few sellers. A firm that controls a gateway, such as a search engine, a pharmacy benefit network or a regional hospital system, can favor itself or raise rivals' costs. Hidden fees, forced arbitration, patent tactics and licensing rules add other barriers. The Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general and the courts enforce antitrust law, and Congress sets their budgets and powers. Concentration among employers can also hold down wages, and platforms' share of advertising has drained money from local news. The 2025 and 2026 court record shows liability findings against some firms and losses for enforcers in other cases.

domains.title: Work, pay and bargaining power
domains.everyday_question: Why is it so hard to get a raise, a predictable schedule or a fair hearing at work?
domains.overview: Most households live on what they earn, so the rules that shape pay and working conditions reach almost everyone. This domain looks at workers' bargaining power: whether they can organize and win a contract, switch to a better job, recover unpaid wages, get predictable hours and paid leave, work safely and have a say when employers bring in new technology. Congress writes the core labor laws. The National Labor Relations Board and the Labor Department enforce them, and states and cities set many floors of their own. Union membership fell from 20.1% of wage and salary workers in 1983 to 10.0% in 2025. Where workers bargain from weakness, a smaller share of each dollar of output goes to wages, which feeds wealth concentration and, through political spending, influence over policy. Employer concentration ties this domain to competition policy.

domains.title: Taxes, wealth and economic security
domains.everyday_question: Why can some families build wealth while others cannot cover a $400 emergency?
domains.overview: Income is what a household receives over a year. Wealth is what it owns after debts. This domain follows the rules that decide how both are taxed, protected and passed on: tax rates on wages compared with investment gains, inheritance, audits, profits shifted abroad, tax breaks, cash support for families, Social Security, household debt, financial crises, recession support and the federal budget. Congress writes the tax code and benefit laws, and the IRS, the Treasury, the Federal Reserve and financial regulators carry them out. In 2025, 37% of adults could not cover a $400 expense with cash. Wealth at the top is held mostly in stocks, while middle-class wealth is mostly home equity, which ties this domain to housing. Concentrated wealth funds political spending, and rules shaped by that spending can protect it, the cycle shown as loop R1: Wealth and political influence reinforce each other.

domains.title: Housing, health care and getting ahead
domains.everyday_question: Why do rent, child care and medical bills take so much of my paycheck, and does where I grew up decide where I end up?
domains.overview: Households spend most of their income on housing, health care, child care, food, transportation and energy. This domain asks why those costs run high and why the chance of doing better than one's parents depends so much on place and family. Local zoning boards and state legislatures decide how many homes can be built. Congress, the states and insurers shape health coverage and prices. States and school districts fund schools. When homes are scarce, existing owners gain equity and often oppose new building, which keeps rents high (loop R8: Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building). High costs for essentials leave less for savings and add to household insecurity, and financial strain makes it harder to take part in public decisions. Absolute mobility, the chance of out-earning one's parents, fell from about 90% for children born in 1940 to about 50% for those born in the 1980s.

domains.title: Taking part, trust and shared norms
domains.everyday_question: Why does showing up feel pointless, and why do people across the party divide distrust each other so much?
domains.overview: Democracy depends on more than election rules. People need time, skills and a reason to believe that taking part matters, and enough shared ground to accept results they dislike. This domain looks at who takes part between elections, how civic organizations and everyday contact across groups have thinned, how hostility toward the other party has grown, and how threats, false fraud claims and party tolerance for misconduct strain democratic norms. Cities, schools, libraries, civic groups and parties shape these conditions more than Congress does. Hostility toward the other party gives voters a reason to excuse misconduct by their own side, which weakens the threat of losing office. Financial strain and weaker worker organizations reduce participation, so policy answers less to the households under the most pressure. A belief that nothing can change keeps people home and leaves decisions to the organized few.

hubs.title: Cost of living
hubs.question: Why does it cost so much to live here?
hubs.intro: Housing, groceries, electricity and insurance take the largest share of most household budgets. A landlord, a grocer, a utility or an insurer sets each of those prices, and public rules shape the market where they set it. Zoning decides how many homes can exist near jobs. A state utility commission rules on what a power company may charge, and in many states the insurance department reviews home insurance rates before they take effect. Interest rates, droughts, animal disease and storms push prices from outside any single office. Each pathway below follows one bill to the people who set it and to the offices that can change the rules behind it. It also reports what the evidence says about proposed responses.

hubs.title: Health and care
hubs.question: Why is care so hard to get and to pay for?
hubs.intro: Getting care depends on whether a plan or program will pay and whether a clinician, a child care center or a home care aide is available to provide it. Employers, insurers, state Medicaid agencies and Congress settle most of the payment question. Licensing rules, training slots and wages settle much of the availability question, and state legislatures, state boards and the federal programs that pay for care set those. Prices add another layer: hospitals and insurers negotiate them privately, and pharmacy benefit managers stand between drug makers and pharmacies. The pathways here start with an appointment, a bill, a child care slot or care for an aging parent, and trace each one to the office that controls the decision.

hubs.title: Work and financial security
hubs.question: Why doesn't my paycheck go further?
hubs.intro: What a household keeps depends on what it earns and on what taxes and benefits add or subtract. Employers set pay inside a labor market shaped by how many employers compete for workers, by minimum wage laws and by the rules that govern unions. Congress and state legislatures then decide how much of that pay goes to taxes and which households qualify for credits, food assistance or health coverage. Social Security replaces part of a worker's earnings in retirement or after a disability, under a formula Congress wrote and can change. These pathways show where each decision is made and how proposed changes would reach different households over different periods.

hubs.title: Public services where you live
hubs.question: Who keeps the water, roads and schools working?
hubs.intro: Drinking water, streets, buses and public schools are run close to home, usually by a city, a county, a special district or an elected school board. Much of the money and many of the rules come from farther away. Federal law sets drinking water standards and states enforce them. Federal formulas and state budgets pay for a large part of road and transit work, and state aid formulas decide much of what each school district can spend. When a pipe fails or a repair stalls, the office that answers the phone may not be the one that controls the budget. Each pathway names both and shows how a resident can bring a problem to the body able to fix it.

hubs.title: Voice, power and information
hubs.question: How do my vote and my voice reach the people who decide?
hubs.intro: Every pathway in this Atlas ends at an office: a council, a commission, a legislature or an agency. This topic asks how residents reach those offices and how much that contact matters. In many districts a primary with low turnout settles who holds the seat, so the general election decides little. Who draws district lines and when local elections are held both change whose views officials need to weigh, and so does the way campaigns are paid for. Technology raises a newer question, since software now sets some prices, screens job applicants, ranks the news people see and decides eligibility for some public benefits. The two pathways here explain those mechanisms and connect them to the model of accountability at the center of the Atlas.

pathways.title: Housing costs
pathways.question: Why did my rent go up?
pathways.short_answer: Rent rises when more households compete for a limited number of homes where they need to live. City and town councils adopt zoning rules that set how many homes each lot may hold, and planning boards apply them project by project; in many high-demand regions those rules keep building below demand. Asking rents for professionally managed apartments were 29% higher in early 2026 than in 2020. For buyers, the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose from $1,240 at the end of 2020 to $2,420 in late 2025 as prices and mortgage rates climbed, and rates passed 7% in October 2026.

pathways.title: Grocery prices
pathways.question: Why is my grocery bill higher?
pathways.short_answer: Grocery prices are still rising slowly: the Consumer Price Index for food at home, the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure of grocery prices, rose 1.8% in the year to September 2026. Farms receive about 12 cents of each food dollar, so wages, fuel, transport and store costs set most of the price. Particular foods jump when supply shrinks, as eggs did during bird flu outbreaks and beef has as cattle numbers fell. Tariffs add a cost that U.S. importers mostly pay first. Whether large meatpackers and grocers use market power to widen margins is disputed; the Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforce the competition laws.

pathways.title: Electric and utility bills
pathways.question: Why is my electric bill going up?
pathways.short_answer: Your rate is approved by a regulator or a board. For an investor-owned utility, the state public utility commission sets rates in a rate case; for public power and cooperatives, a city council, utility board or co-op board does. Rates recover the cost of power plants, fuel, transmission lines and local wires, and investor-owned utilities also earn a regulated return on what they invest. Recent increases trace mainly to grid spending, natural gas prices and disaster recovery. In the 13-state PJM grid region, a capacity auction overseen by federal regulators has added costs, and its market monitor attributes $23.1 billion over three auctions to data center demand.

pathways.title: Home and auto insurance
pathways.question: Why did my home insurance premium go up?
pathways.short_answer: Home insurance costs more because each claim costs more to pay and more homes stand where storms and wildfires strike. Reinsurance, the coverage insurers buy for themselves, also became more expensive. Average monthly premiums rose 72% from 2019 to 2025, to $201. Insurers propose rates, and each state's insurance commissioner or department reviews them under rules the state legislature writes, including which costs may count. Where approved rates fall below expected losses, some insurers stop renewing policies and households turn to state-created insurers of last resort. Flood damage needs a separate policy, mostly from a federal program that Congress has extended through December 11, 2026.

pathways.title: Health coverage and access
pathways.question: Why is it hard to find an appointment?
pathways.short_answer: An appointment depends on coverage and on whether a clinician near you has time. Whether you have coverage turns on your employer's plan, on marketplace subsidies that Congress sets, and on your state Medicaid agency, which checks eligibility at each renewal. Insurers then choose which clinicians join a plan's network. The number of clinicians nearby depends on Medicare funding for residency training, state licensing laws and what each payer pays. As of December 2025, 92.3 million people lived in federal primary care shortage areas. A 2025 survey of offices in 15 large metro areas, run by a staffing company, found an average wait of 31 days for a new patient.

pathways.title: Medical bills and drug prices
pathways.question: Why can the same care produce different bills?
pathways.short_answer: Most of a medical bill's price comes from a private contract. Each insurer or employer plan negotiates its own rates with each hospital and clinician, so a scan can cost widely different amounts within one city. Hospitals with few nearby rivals win higher rates, and Medicare pays more for some services in hospital outpatient departments than in doctors' offices. RAND, a nonprofit research organization, found private plans paid hospitals 254% of Medicare rates in 2022. For medicines, the manufacturer sets a list price protected by patents, and pharmacy benefit managers negotiate rebates off that price, so a patient's coinsurance can still be based on the full list price.

pathways.title: Childcare and family care
pathways.question: Why does childcare cost so much, and why can't I find an opening?
pathways.short_answer: Childcare costs a lot because young children need many adults per child, and staff pay makes up most of a program's budget. State licensing agencies set those staff-to-child ratios. Pay stays low anyway: childcare workers earned a median $16.82 an hour in May 2025, and programs struggle to hire and keep staff. Parents cover most of the bill, an average of $13,184 a year in 2025 by the count of Child Care Aware of America, an advocacy group. Subsidies reached 16 percent of children eligible under federal rules in 2022, and each state legislature decides how much more to add.

pathways.title: Long-term care and disability
pathways.question: Why is it so hard to get help at home as I age or live with a disability?
pathways.short_answer: Most paid long-term care runs through Medicaid, which paid 61 percent of the $415 billion spent in 2022 on long-term services, meaning help with daily tasks such as bathing and dressing. Federal Medicaid law requires states to cover nursing home care but leaves most home and community services optional, so states cap enrollment: more than 710,000 people were on waiting or interest lists in 2024. Medicare does not cover ongoing personal care. Home care depends on aides paid a median $17.21 an hour in May 2025, and family members fill the gaps. Each state's Medicaid agency decides who gets services and what providers are paid.

pathways.title: Pay and working conditions
pathways.question: Why isn't my pay keeping up with what my work produces?
pathways.short_answer: Pay rises when workers produce more, though by less than the full gain, and bargaining power decides the split. In the U.S. nonfarm business sector, output per hour has grown about 2.1% a year since 1947. Workers' share of business income fell to 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest on record. Your bargaining power depends on how easily you can leave for a better offer, how many employers compete to hire you, whether you can bargain as a group, and the legal wage floor. Congress, the National Labor Relations Board, state legislatures and state labor departments set or enforce most of those rules.

pathways.title: Taxes, benefits and financial security
pathways.question: How do taxes and benefit rules change what my household keeps?
pathways.short_answer: What a household keeps depends on rules Congress writes and agencies carry out. Workers pay 7.65% of wages in payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare from the first dollar. Federal income tax applies above the standard deduction, and refundable credits, which pay out even when no tax is owed, add money back for low earners with children. Benefits such as SNAP food aid and Medicaid shrink or end as earnings rise, so a raise can leave a family little better off. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the 2025 federal law, Public Law 119-21, lowers resources for the lowest-income tenth of households and raises them for the top tenth.

pathways.title: Social Security and retirement
pathways.question: What will I get from Social Security, and could the rules change before I retire?
pathways.short_answer: Your benefit depends on your earnings record, the formula in the Social Security Act and the age you claim. The formula averages your highest 35 years of wage-indexed earnings and replaces a larger share of lower earnings. Benefits rise each year with inflation; the increase for 2027 is 3.6 percent. The 2026 Trustees Report projects that the retirement trust fund's reserves run out in late 2032, after which incoming taxes would cover 78 percent of scheduled benefits. Congress decides how to close that gap, and each option falls on different earners and birth years.

pathways.title: Clean drinking water
pathways.question: Who makes sure my tap water is safe?
pathways.short_answer: Your water utility tests and treats the water. It follows national limits set by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and in most states a state drinking water program enforces them. The utility can be a city department, a regional authority or a private company. Customers' bills pay for most pipes and treatment: in 2017, state and local sources covered 96% of public spending on water utilities. A city council or utility board sets rates for most publicly owned systems, and a state utility commission regulates many private ones. For a problem, start with the utility. If it is not resolved, contact the state drinking water program.

pathways.title: Roads, bridges and transit
pathways.question: Why is the repair on my street taking so long?
pathways.short_answer: It depends first on who owns the road. Counties, cities and towns own about three-quarters of public road miles, and state transportation departments own most of the rest. A pothole waits for the local public works budget and crew schedule. Larger work that uses federal aid must be listed in a multi-year program adopted by the regional planning organization and approved by the governor, so it waits for money and its place in line. Federal money is under strain: CBO projects the highway account of the Highway Trust Fund will run out in 2028, and the 2021 infrastructure law covered fiscal years through 2026.

pathways.title: Public schools
pathways.question: Why does my child's school have less than schools in other districts?
pathways.short_answer: Most school money comes from local property taxes and state aid. In 2020-21, local sources supplied 44% of public school revenue and states 46%, and 83% of the local share came from property taxes. A district with more taxable property can raise more per student at the same tax rate. The state aid formula, written by the legislature, decides how much of that gap is closed, and state courts have ordered changes when formulas fall short of state constitutions. Studies comparing students before and after state finance reforms estimate that sustained increases raised schooling and adult earnings, most for children from low-income families.

pathways.title: Voting and public influence
pathways.question: Which election decides who represents me, and how can I influence the people who decide?
pathways.short_answer: The election that decides an office is the one whose outcome is still in doubt. In a district one party wins reliably, that is the party primary, a nominating election often held months before November with far fewer voters. Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe for 2026. Unite America, an advocacy group, counts 383 as effectively decided in primaries, by 9.4% of eligible voters. State legislatures, or commissions in some states, draw the districts that make seats safe. Between elections, randomized experiments in two state legislatures found that constituent calls and emails about a specific bill changed legislators' votes.

pathways.title: Algorithms in daily life
pathways.question: How do algorithms affect the prices I pay, my job, what I see online and the services I get?
pathways.short_answer: Companies and public agencies use software to set prices, screen job applicants, rank what you see online and decide benefit renewals, and the effects depend on the data fed in and the rules around it. Rent-pricing software that pooled competitors' private data led to a Justice Department case against RealPage. Large experiments found that changing a feed shifts what people see, with small measured effects on how they feel about the other party. Evidence on AI and jobs is early: one payroll study finds fewer jobs for workers aged 22 to 25 in exposed occupations, while others find no broad effect. Federal agencies, state legislatures and courts set the limits.

A1.title: Concentration of household wealth
A1.label: Wealth at the top
A1.description: How much of all household wealth belongs to the households at the top. Wealth here means assets minus debts, built up over time.
A1.increase_means: A higher value means the wealthiest households hold a larger share of all household wealth.
A1.why: When wealth piles up at the top, so does the money available to shape elections and laws.
A1.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
A1.indicator: Top 1% share of household net worth (Fed DFA): 32.5% in 2026 Q2, the highest since the series began in 1989 (W003); top 0.1% 15.0% (W005)

A2.title: Workers' bargaining power
A2.label: Workers' bargaining power
A2.description: Workers' ability to negotiate pay and conditions, alone or together. Union membership and the share of business income paid to workers help track it.
A2.increase_means: A higher value means workers have more say over their pay and working conditions.
A2.why: It decides whether you can ask for a raise or a better schedule and expect a real answer.
A2.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
A2.indicator: Union density (BLS, 10.0% 2025); nonfarm business labor share (BLS, 52.8% in 2026 Q2, lowest since 1947; W008)

A3.title: Market concentration
A3.label: Market concentration
A3.description: How much of a market a few firms control. Concentration can weaken competition, with effects that depend on the market and on how hard it is for new firms to enter.
A3.increase_means: A higher value means fewer firms hold more of the market.
A3.why: With fewer sellers, prices can stay high and choices narrow, from prescriptions to concert tickets.
A3.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
A3.indicator: Average markups (De Loecker, Eeckhout, Unger); sector HHI (Census)

A4.title: Households' financial security
A4.label: Households' financial security
A4.description: A household's ability to meet basic needs and absorb an unexpected expense. Poverty rates and emergency savings show how much room families have.
A4.increase_means: A higher value means more households can cover their needs and a surprise bill.
A4.why: A family with little cushion has less time and money to show up in politics, and one surprise bill can set it back for months.
A4.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
A4.indicator: SPM poverty (Census P60); share able to cover a $400 expense (Fed SHED)

A5.title: Housing scarcity
A5.label: Housing scarcity
A5.description: A shortage of homes where people need or want to live. Homes per household and rent relative to income show the pressure.
A5.increase_means: A higher value means homes are harder to find or afford in the places people want to live.
A5.why: Too few homes near good jobs pushes rents up and keeps people from moving to better work.
A5.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
A5.indicator: Housing units per household; rent-to-income for renters (JCHS)

B1.title: Money spent to influence politics
B1.label: Money spent on influence
B1.description: Campaign contributions, spending by outside groups and paid lobbying used to influence public decisions. Each channel has its own rules and reporting periods, and disclosure rules decide how clearly the original funders can be identified.
B1.increase_means: A higher value means more money flowing into campaigns, outside groups and lobbying.
B1.why: Money buys access: meetings, ads and lobbyists who know which line in a bill to change.
B1.indicator: Dollars per cycle; outside-spending share; undisclosed share (FEC, OpenSecrets)

B2.title: Availability of local reporting
B2.label: Local reporting
B2.description: The reporters and news organizations that cover local decisions. Measures include places with no local news source and reporters per resident.
B2.increase_means: A higher value means more reporting on local government and local elections.
B2.why: Reporters at council meetings are often the only outsiders watching how local money gets spent.
B2.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
B2.indicator: Counties with no local news source (Medill: 213 in 2025; N31); journalists per 100k

B3.title: Civic ties across social and political groups
B3.label: Ties across groups
B3.description: Relationships formed through organizations and shared work that connect people across party or income lines. These ties help people cooperate and learn about opportunities.
B3.increase_means: A higher value means more people have regular ties to people of another party or income group.
B3.why: Unions, congregations and clubs put people from different backgrounds in the same room, which makes cooperation easier.
B3.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
B3.indicator: Economic connectedness (Chetty et al. 2022); cross-partisan membership (GSS)

B4.title: Hostility toward the other political party
B4.label: Hostility to the other party
B4.description: How strongly people dislike or distrust supporters of the other party. It measures feelings toward people, which can change separately from disagreement over policy.
B4.increase_means: A higher value means people feel colder and more hostile toward the other party's supporters.
B4.why: When people fear the other side more than they judge their own, officials pay less for breaking norms.
B4.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
B4.indicator: ANES in-party minus out-party feeling thermometer gap

B5.title: Equality of voter turnout
B5.label: Equal turnout
B5.description: How evenly people vote across income groups. A smaller gap between turnout at high and low incomes means participation is more equal.
B5.increase_means: A higher value means turnout is more similar across income groups.
B5.why: Officials pay closest attention to the people who vote, so gaps in turnout become gaps in influence.
B5.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time). Turnout is observed once per election, so the reading behaves like a condition measured each cycle; the habits and organizations behind it build up over time.
B5.indicator: Turnout gap between top and bottom income quintiles (CPS)

B6.title: Exposure to hostile political content
B6.label: Hostile content
B6.description: How often people see political material that attacks the other party or its supporters. It measures what reaches people, and connection L47 covers how that material changes attitudes.
B6.increase_means: A higher value means a larger share of the political content people see attacks the other side.
B6.why: Posts that attack the other side travel fast and keep the temperature high between elections.
B6.indicator: Share of political posts seen that attack the out-party (platform research APIs)

C1.title: Seats with little electoral competition
C1.label: Safe seats
C1.description: Districts where one party wins by a wide margin, so its candidates face little risk in the general election. The model counts seats won by more than 10 percentage points.
C1.increase_means: A higher value means more seats are safe for one party.
C1.why: In a safe seat the November winner is close to certain, so the race that matters happens earlier.
C1.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
C1.indicator: Share of House and state legislative seats won by over 10 points

C2.title: How often the primary decides the winner
C2.label: Seats settled in the primary
C2.description: The share of seats where the general election is so predictable that the primary settles who takes office. Turnout in that deciding contest can be far lower than in November.
C2.increase_means: A higher value means more seats are settled in the primary.
C2.why: A small, low-turnout primary electorate ends up choosing the representative for everyone.
C2.indicator: Share of House seats effectively decided in the primary (Unite America, from Cook ratings: 88% in 2026, decided by 9.4% of eligible voters; 87% in 2024 on a voting-age denominator; W017)

C3.title: Risk of losing office
C3.label: Risk of losing office
C3.description: The credible threat that an incumbent will lose the next election. Where seats are competitive, the threat pushes officials to respond to voters before anyone is removed.
C3.increase_means: A higher value means incumbents face a more credible chance of defeat.
C3.why: The chance of losing is what makes officials listen. Without it, voters lose their strongest tool.
C3.indicator: Electoral pressure: the credible chance an incumbent loses (share of competitive seats). Defined as pressure; the sanction applied is node C5.

C4.title: Officeholders' control over election rules
C4.label: Incumbents control election rules
C4.description: The power of people already in office to set district maps, voting-access rules and local election choices. This is rule-setting authority, and each rule's effect needs its own evidence.
C4.increase_means: A higher value means incumbents have more say over the rules of their own elections.
C4.why: The people who benefit from today’s maps and voting rules are often the ones who write them.
C4.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
C4.indicator: Share of congressional and legislative maps drawn by the party they favor; count of access restrictions enacted by trifectas; count of state preemptions of local electoral choice

D1.title: Congress's ability to write and check policy
D1.label: Congress's capacity
D1.description: The staff and independent expertise Congress needs to investigate problems, draft laws and oversee how agencies carry them out. Committee staffing and the budgets of its support agencies help track that ability.
D1.increase_means: A higher value means Congress has more staff and expertise to draft laws and oversee agencies.
D1.why: Without enough staff and experts, Congress leans on lobbyists and the executive branch for answers.
D1.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D1.indicator: Committee staff FTE; CRS, GAO, CBO budgets; substantive bills enacted per Congress

D2.title: Presidential action without new legislation
D2.label: Presidential action alone
D2.description: How far the executive sets policy through orders, emergency powers or other action without a new law. Different actions carry different legal limits.
D2.increase_means: A higher value means more policy is set by presidential order or emergency power without a new law.
D2.why: Orders and emergency powers let a president act fast, and they can also skip the debate a law requires.
D2.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D2.indicator: National emergencies in force; executive orders per year; impoundments; removals of protected officials

D3.title: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition
D3.label: Rulings favoring appointers
D3.description: Rulings on political money, election rules and executive power that benefit the coalition that appointed the judges. It is a proposed pattern read across decisions, with exceptions recorded in the evidence.
D3.increase_means: A higher value means more of the body of rulings favors the coalition responsible for the appointments.
D3.why: Courts decide many fights over money and election rules. This tracks whether those rulings tend to help the side that appointed the judges.
D3.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D3.indicator: Index of rulings on money, maps, access and removal (Buckley to Callais)

D4.title: Ability to investigate and enforce the rules
D4.label: Watchdogs and enforcement
D4.description: Whether watchdogs can obtain records, investigate wrongdoing and secure a response. Vacancies, quorums and enforcement of subpoenas decide whether that authority works in practice.
D4.increase_means: A higher value means watchdogs can get records, investigate and make findings stick.
D4.why: Inspectors general, auditors and regulators are how wrongdoing gets found and fixed.
D4.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D4.indicator: IG vacancies; FEC and NLRB quorum status; GAO recommendations implemented; subpoena enforcement outcomes

D5.title: Quality of public services
D5.label: Quality of public services
D5.description: How reliably government delivers the services people use. Waiting times, error rates and the time needed to finish a task make performance visible.
D5.increase_means: A higher value means services are delivered faster and with fewer errors.
D5.why: Wait times, errors and paperwork are where most people meet their government.
D5.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D5.indicator: IRS answer rate; SSA wait times; permitting durations; federal civilian workforce down about 256,000 (over 11%) at CFO Act agencies, Dec 2024 to Jan 2026, after about 378,000 separations in 2025 (GAO-26-108583, W010)

D6.title: State and local testing of reforms
D6.label: State and local reform tests
D6.description: The ability of states and local governments to try a policy and learn from its results. Adoption, spread to other places and state limits on local choice help track it.
D6.increase_means: A higher value means states and localities try more new policies and pass on what they learn.
D6.why: States and cities can try a fix first, and others can copy it if it works.
D6.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time). The listed indicators count adoptions per year, which is a flow; the stock would be the number of reforms in force or the legal room states and localities have to act.
D6.indicator: Reforms adopted per year by initiative or statute; diffusion count; preemption count

E1.title: Policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests
E1.label: Policy tilt to insiders
E1.description: How far rules favor wealthy people or well-organized groups over less organized residents. Tax benefits and research on whose preferences receive a response give partial measures.
E1.increase_means: A higher value means rules deliver more of their benefits to wealthy people and organized groups.
E1.why: This is the heart of both questions: whose interests the rules end up serving.
E1.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
E1.indicator: Share of tax expenditures to top decile (CBO); responsiveness gap (Gilens data, with caveats)

E2.title: Trust earned through performance
E2.label: Earned trust
E2.description: Confidence in institutions that rests on evidence of how competently and honestly they act. Survey trust is an imperfect measure because performance is one of several influences on what people believe.
E2.increase_means: A higher value means more of the public's confidence rests on evidence that institutions perform.
E2.why: Trust that rests on results lets government ask more of people when it matters.
E2.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
E2.indicator: Pew trust in federal government (17%, Sept 2025, the latest Pew reading); Gallup confidence in Congress (9%, June 2026; W020); Gallup trust in mass media (33%, Sept 2026; W018); Gallup trust in the judicial branch (46%, Sept 2026; W019)

X1.title: What new technology can do
X1.label: New technology
X1.description: Technical advances that change which tasks can be automated and how much workers can produce. Their effects on pay and jobs depend on how employers use them.
X1.increase_means: A higher value means machines and software can do more tasks.
X1.why: Automation changes which jobs exist and who keeps the gains from higher output.
X1.indicator: Labor share; automation exposure; productivity growth

X2.title: Population patterns and residential sorting
X2.label: Residential sorting
X2.description: Where people live and how communities differ by age, education or party. These patterns can make districts politically lopsided before any map is drawn.
X2.increase_means: A higher value means communities are more sorted by party, age or education.
X2.why: When neighbors increasingly share a party, districts tilt before anyone draws a map.
X2.indicator: Urban-rural partisan gap; age structure; education realignment

X3.title: Trade and the movement of capital
X3.label: Trade and capital
X3.description: The movement of goods, investment and wealth across borders. Import competition and offshore assets connect this wider setting to local jobs and bargaining power.
X3.increase_means: A higher value means more import competition and more capital moving across borders.
X3.why: Global trade and mobile capital change local jobs and how much bargaining room workers have.
X3.indicator: Import penetration by commuting zone; offshore wealth share. Chinese import competition explains about a quarter of the 1990-2007 manufacturing job decline (W067), with effects persisting through 2019 (W068)

X4.title: Foreign interference
X4.label: Foreign interference
X4.description: Documented efforts by foreign actors to influence U.S. political information or processes. Showing that an operation happened takes different evidence from showing that it changed votes.
X4.increase_means: A higher value means more foreign efforts to influence U.S. political information or processes.
X4.why: Foreign efforts to sway U.S. politics add noise to what voters see and hear.
X4.indicator: Documented operations (ODNI); measured exposure (Eady et al. 2023)

X5.title: Major external shocks
X5.label: Major shocks
X5.description: Events such as wars, pandemics and climate disasters that strain households and public institutions. The model treats them as outside pressures and does not explain how each begins.
X5.increase_means: A higher value means more frequent or more severe wars, pandemics and disasters.
X5.why: Wars, pandemics and disasters test whether institutions can protect households under strain.
X5.indicator: Disaster losses; insurance availability; emergency declarations

A6.title: Homeowners' equity
A6.label: Homeowners' equity
A6.description: The value owners hold in their homes after mortgage debt. The housing loop follows this stake and the wealth gap between owners and renters, which is a separate measure from the top 1% share of wealth.
A6.increase_means: A higher value means owners hold more value in their homes, relative to their mortgages and to renters' wealth.
A6.why: Rising home values build owners’ wealth, which gives many owners a stake in keeping new building out.
A6.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
A6.indicator: Owner-renter net worth gap (Fed SCF, 1989 to 2022); owner home equity share of household net worth

C5.title: Incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement
C5.label: Incumbents defeated
C5.description: Officeholders who lose an election or retire under threat of defeat. This consequence is measured separately from the pressure they face while still in office.
C5.increase_means: A higher value means more incumbents lose or retire under threat of defeat in an election cycle.
C5.why: Defeats are how the system corrects itself. They show that poor performance has a cost.
C5.indicator: Incumbents defeated or retiring under threat, by cycle (House and Senate); state legislative incumbent defeats

D7.title: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions
D7.label: Entrenched majority control
D7.description: Lasting control of a legislature or another body that sets election rules or confirms judges. The model tracks how safe seats help a majority keep this control and use it again.
D7.increase_means: A higher value means the same majority holds rule-setting bodies longer and is harder to unseat.
D7.why: A majority that cannot lose can keep redrawing the rules in its own favor.
D7.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D7.indicator: Years the same party has held a state legislature or trifecta; seat share needed to flip a chamber versus vote share needed (seats-votes curve); share of rule-setting bodies (legislatures that draw maps, the Senate that confirms judges) held by a majority insulated by safe seats

EC1.title: Output produced per hour of work
EC1.label: Productivity
EC1.description: How much workers produce in an hour. Higher productivity can support higher living standards, and the rules governing pay decide who receives the gains.
EC1.increase_means: A higher value means workers produce more per hour.
EC1.why: Workers produce far more per hour than a generation ago. How that gain is shared is set by rules people make.
EC1.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time). Output per hour is a ratio of two flows; the model treats its level as the result of accumulated capital, skills and know-how.
EC1.indicator: Nonfarm business output per hour (BLS): +2.1% a year 2019 Q4 to 2026 Q2 (W007)

EC2.title: Public investment in research and infrastructure
EC2.label: Public investment
EC2.description: Government funding for research and for the systems that support economic activity. Money committed to a project and money spent on it can differ for years.
EC2.increase_means: A higher value means more public money going to research and infrastructure each year.
EC2.why: Roads, research and broadband paid for today shape the jobs available tomorrow.
EC2.indicator: Federally funded R&D share of GDP: 1.86% (1964) to 0.63% (2022) (W053); IIJA DOT funds 75.7% obligated, 46.6% spent by July 2026 (W054)

EC3.title: Workers' share of income
EC3.label: Workers' share of income
EC3.description: The portion of business income paid to workers as compensation. It describes how income is divided as it is earned, which is separate from how accumulated wealth is distributed.
EC3.increase_means: A higher value means workers receive a larger share of the income businesses produce.
EC3.why: This is how much of what businesses earn goes to the people doing the work.
EC3.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time). The share is a ratio of income flows in each period, so it behaves like a condition (auxiliary); the model treats it as a stock because it changes slowly.
EC3.indicator: Nonfarm business labor share 52.8% (2026 Q2), lowest since 1947 (W008); corporate profits 13.0% of gross domestic income in 2025 (W016, W052)

EC4.title: Concentration of stock ownership
EC4.label: Stock ownership concentration
EC4.description: How much of households' corporate stock and mutual fund holdings belongs to the wealthiest groups. This decides who receives much of the gain when those assets rise in value.
EC4.increase_means: A higher value means the wealthiest households hold a larger share of household stocks and mutual funds.
EC4.why: When stocks rise, most of the gain goes to the households that already own the most.
EC4.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
EC4.indicator: Top 1% hold 50.9% and the next 9% hold 37.2% of household corporate equities and mutual fund shares (2026 Q2, W112)

EC5.title: Where newly created credit goes
EC5.label: Where credit goes
EC5.description: Banks create deposits when they lend, so lending directs new purchasing power toward homes, businesses and other uses. The model tracks where credit goes and the risks that grow with it.
EC5.increase_means: A higher value means more new credit flowing to the use being discussed, such as mortgages or loans to nonbank lenders.
EC5.why: Lending decides whether new money flows into homes and businesses or into bidding up assets people already own.
EC5.indicator: Bank loans $14.09T: real estate 41.4%, business 21.0%, consumer 13.7%, loans to nonbank lenders 14.6% (H.8, Oct 2026, W060); private credit about $1.4T (W062); banks create deposits when they lend, and reserve requirements have been zero since March 2020 (W058, W059)

EC6.title: Net support from taxes and public benefits
EC6.label: Net support from taxes and benefits
EC6.description: Taxes collect resources and public benefits return income or services to households. In this model a higher value means more net support or redistribution toward the households being discussed, and who pays and who receives decide the effect.
EC6.increase_means: A higher value means taxes and benefits leave the households being discussed with more net support.
EC6.why: Taxes and benefits decide how much of a paycheck a family keeps and what help arrives when times are hard.
EC6.indicator: Top 1% income share 18% before and 14% after taxes and transfers (CBO, 2022, W063); Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of SPM poverty in 2025 (W001)

EC7.title: Household income
EC7.label: Household income
EC7.description: Money a household receives over a period, including earnings and other income. It pays current expenses and can add to savings; wealth records what the household has kept after debts.
EC7.increase_means: A higher value means households receive more money over the year.
EC7.why: What comes in each month sets what a family can spend, save and plan for.
EC7.indicator: Real median household income $87,460 (2025), +2.6% (W002); consumer spending was 67.6% of GDP in 2025 (W016)

EC8.title: Household assets and debts
EC8.label: Household assets and debts
EC8.description: What households own and what they owe. Savings, home equity and debt shape their ability to withstand a lost paycheck or an unexpected bill.
EC8.increase_means: A higher value means households hold more assets relative to their debts.
EC8.why: Savings and debts decide how long a household can last after a lost paycheck.
EC8.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
EC8.indicator: Median net worth: homeowners $396,200, renters $10,400 (SCF 2022, W072); household debt $18.77T (Q2 2026, W012); 63% could cover a $400 expense with cash (W074)

EC9.title: Cost of essentials
EC9.label: Cost of essentials
EC9.description: What households pay for necessities such as housing, care and insurance. Costs measured against income show pressure that national growth figures can miss.
EC9.increase_means: A higher value means necessities take more of a household's income.
EC9.why: Rent, care and insurance take a growing share of many paychecks.
EC9.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time). Costs are paid each period, so the measures behave like flows or conditions; the model treats the level of prices as persistent.
EC9.indicator: 49% of renter households cost-burdened (W013); child care $13,184 a year (W015); family health premium $26,993 (W014); home insurance premiums +72% 2019-2025 (W013)

EC10.title: Costs of tariffs and trade rules
EC10.label: Tariff costs
EC10.description: Import taxes and related trade rules can raise costs for U.S. buyers. The burden depends on prices, purchasing choices and which households or businesses use the affected goods.
EC10.increase_means: A higher value means tariffs add more to what U.S. buyers pay.
EC10.why: Import taxes are paid at the border and often passed on in store prices.
EC10.indicator: Average statutory tariff rate about 11.0% (Aug 2026); about $1,100 per household a year (W069); 86-94% of the cost borne by U.S. buyers (W070)

EC11.title: Climate hazards and insurance costs
EC11.label: Climate and insurance costs
EC11.description: The financial risk from climate-related damage and the cost or availability of insurance against it. Exposure varies by location and by a household's ability to adapt or move.
EC11.increase_means: A higher value means greater risk of climate damage and higher costs to insure against it.
EC11.why: In disaster-prone places, insurance is getting harder to buy and costlier to keep.
EC11.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
EC11.indicator: Highest-risk fifth of ZIP codes paid 82% more for home insurance (W076); 23 billion-dollar disasters in 2025 (W080)

EC12.title: Energy demand and emissions
EC12.label: Energy demand
EC12.description: The energy the economy uses and the greenhouse gases released in producing and using it. These are separate quantities: electricity demand affects the grid, and its emissions depend on the sources that supply it.
EC12.increase_means: A higher value means more energy use or more emissions; the two can move apart when cleaner sources meet new demand.
EC12.why: How much power the economy uses shapes electric bills and the pace of climate change.
EC12.indicator: Electricity use forecast +1% (2026) and +3% (2027) (W079); emissions +2.4% in 2025, preliminary (W078)

TC1.title: How platforms rank feeds and seek attention
TC1.label: Feed ranking
TC1.description: The choices platforms make about which posts and recommendations people see. Ranking can change exposure a great deal even when measured changes in political attitudes are small or absent.
TC1.increase_means: A higher value means more of what people see is chosen by ranking built to hold attention, compared with a time-ordered feed.
TC1.why: A few ranking choices decide which posts millions of people see each day.
TC1.indicator: Share of time in algorithmically ranked feeds; ranking objectives disclosed by platforms

TC2.title: Concentration of platforms and digital advertising
TC2.label: Platform concentration
TC2.description: The share of digital advertising and distribution held by a few platforms. It affects publishers' revenue and the choices open to advertisers and users.
TC2.increase_means: A higher value means a few platforms take a larger share of digital advertising and distribution.
TC2.why: A few platforms take most digital advertising, which squeezes the publishers who pay reporters.
TC2.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
TC2.indicator: Worldwide digital ad share 2026: Meta 26.8%, Google 26.4%, Amazon 9.0% (eMarketer forecast, W099)

TC3.title: Use of AI at work
TC3.label: AI at work
TC3.description: How workers and employers adopt generative AI for their tasks. Measured time savings in particular settings leave the wider effects on jobs and pay to be assessed separately.
TC3.increase_means: A higher value means more workers and employers use generative AI in their tasks.
TC3.why: AI tools are changing tasks at work, and the rules decide whether workers share the gains.
TC3.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
TC3.indicator: Share of workers and firms using generative AI at work; task-time savings (W105, W107)

TC4.title: Concentration of AI funding and computing power
TC4.label: AI capital concentration
TC4.description: How much of the capital and computing infrastructure used to build advanced AI sits with a few firms. The amount built is a separate variable, TC8: Computing capacity built for AI.
TC4.increase_means: A higher value means a few firms hold more of the capital and computing power used for advanced AI.
TC4.why: Building advanced AI takes enormous capital, so a handful of firms hold most of it.
TC4.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
TC4.indicator: Nearly 90% of notable 2024 models from industry (W113)

TC5.title: Government's ability to build and run digital services
TC5.label: Government digital teams
TC5.description: The public teams and skills needed to deliver services through reliable software. Aging systems and dependence on outside contractors affect how quickly agencies can improve a service.
TC5.increase_means: A higher value means agencies can build, run and fix their own digital services.
TC5.why: Strong software teams are why some agencies can process a benefit in days.
TC5.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
TC5.indicator: Eleven most critical legacy systems 23-60 years old; about 80% of IT spending on operations (W116); 18F closed March 2025 (W119); Direct File not offered for 2026 (W120)

TC6.title: Data centers' demand on the electricity grid
TC6.label: Data-center load
TC6.description: The power and grid capacity data centers need. Large new loads can raise system costs, and the effect on households depends on how regulators assign those costs.
TC6.increase_means: A higher value means data centers draw more power and need more grid capacity.
TC6.why: New data centers need huge amounts of power, and regulators decide who pays for the grid upgrades.
TC6.indicator: Data centers 4.4% of U.S. electricity (2023), 6.7-12% projected by 2028 (W081); PJM monitor: $23.1B added by data-center load across three auctions (W126)

TC7.title: Use of pricing algorithms
TC7.label: Pricing algorithms
TC7.description: Software that sellers or landlords use to set prices. Software fed with competitors' private information raises different competition questions from software that uses public data or a firm's own data.
TC7.increase_means: A higher value means more sellers and landlords set prices with software, especially software fed with competitors' nonpublic data.
TC7.why: Software that sets rents and prices can push them up when competitors feed it the same private data.
TC7.indicator: Landlords and sellers using shared nonpublic data in pricing software; state and local bans (W127, W128, W129)

TC8.title: Computing capacity built for AI
TC8.label: AI computing build-out
TC8.description: How much computing infrastructure, mostly data centers filled with specialized chips, has been built to train and run AI systems. TC4 measures how few firms hold that capacity, a separate quantity.
TC8.increase_means: A higher value means more computing capacity has been built for AI.
TC8.why: The race to build data centers is drawing hundreds of billions of dollars in private investment.
TC8.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
TC8.indicator: 2025 capex Amazon $134.7B, Microsoft $118B, Alphabet $91.5B, Meta $72.2B (secondary compilation, W111)

L01.name: Concentrated wealth funds more political spending
L01.plain: People with more wealth can give more to campaigns, outside groups and lobbyists, so wealth concentrated at the top raises the money spent to influence politics.
L01.sign_meaning: When wealth becomes more concentrated at the top, spending to influence politics tends to rise.
L01.mechanism: Contributions and lobbying scale with wealth; top 0.01% of donors give about 40% of itemized money

L02.name: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors
L02.plain: Donors gain meetings with officeholders and a say in which issues reach the agenda and how bills are drafted, which can shift rules toward their interests.
L02.sign_meaning: When more money is spent to influence politics, policy tends to favor wealthy and organized interests more.
L02.qualification: A 2016 field experiment (Kalla and Broockman) found congressional offices granted meetings more often to people identified as donors; affluent and middle-income Americans want the same policy about 90% of the time, so any tilt shows on the issues where they differ.
L02.mechanism: Access, agenda and drafting; donors get meetings; affluent and median preferences agree about 90% of the time so the tilt shows at the margin

L03.name: Policy advantages add to wealth at the top
L03.plain: Tax breaks for investment income and rules that protect existing profits deliver most of their value to the top tenth of households, which adds to their wealth.
L03.sign_meaning: When policy favors wealthy and organized interests more, wealth tends to become more concentrated at the top.
L03.qualification: CBO estimated that about 75% of the benefit of lower tax rates on capital gains and dividends went to the top 1% of households in 2019; asset prices also move the top share, so policy is one cause among several.
L03.mechanism: Tax expenditures, capital-income preferences and rent-protecting rules accrue to the top decile

L04.name: Political money helps shape judicial confirmations
L04.plain: Outside groups pay for campaigns for and against judicial nominees and bring test cases, which can affect who reaches the bench and which questions courts decide.
L04.sign_meaning: When more money is spent on politics, court rulings favoring the appointing coalition tend to increase.
L04.qualification: The evidence is a history of organized legal movements (Teles 2008); it does not show that any donation caused a particular confirmation or ruling.
L04.mechanism: Funding of confirmation campaigns and litigation; influence on Senate outcomes

L05.name: Court rulings widen permitted political spending
L05.plain: Supreme Court decisions from Buckley v. Valeo (1976) through NRSC v. FEC (2026) struck limits on political spending and opened new channels for money.
L05.sign_meaning: As rulings of this kind accumulate, more money tends to flow into politics.
L05.qualification: The rulings are on the record, but the variable they come from has no published scoring rule, so read it through the named decisions: Buckley (1976), Citizens United (2010), McCutcheon (2014) and NRSC v. FEC (2026).

L06.name: Court rulings expand incumbents' control of election rules
L06.plain: Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) closed federal courts to partisan-map claims, and Shelby County (2013) and Louisiana v. Callais (2026) removed federal checks on changes to voting rules.
L06.sign_meaning: When rulings of this kind accumulate, officeholders tend to gain more control over maps and voting rules.
L06.qualification: Each ruling removed one federal check; state courts and state constitutions still limit maps in some states, so the effect differs from state to state.
L06.mechanism: Rucho removes federal review of partisan maps; Shelby and Callais remove preclearance and most Section 2 constraints on access rules

L08.name: Safe seats make the primary decisive
L08.plain: When one party is sure to win the general election, the real choice happens in that party's primary.
L08.sign_meaning: More safe seats go with more seats effectively decided in the primary.
L08.qualification: Unite America, a reform advocacy group, counted 88% of House seats (383 of 435) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries using Cook Political Report ratings; the count depends on the group's own definition of a decided seat.
L08.mechanism: When the general election is settled, the primary decides

L09.name: Decisive primaries may deepen partisan hostility
L09.plain: Nominees chosen by a party's most engaged voters may campaign to the base and send hostile signals about the other party to their supporters.
L09.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: when more seats are decided in primaries, hostility toward the other party tends to rise.
L09.qualification: Contested. The strongest tests (McGhee and coauthors 2014) found that opening primaries did not measurably change legislators' voting records, and they measured legislators; this link concerns voters' feelings toward the other party. A study of one Alaska election cycle found some moderation (Reilly, Wright and Lublin 2025).
L09.mechanism: Base-oriented nominees and party leaders' cues; the best tests of primary openness on legislator extremism are null

L10.name: Partisan hostility weakens Congress's capacity
L10.plain: Polarized chambers pass fewer major laws and move decisions to party leaders, which leaves committees and their staff with less work and less say.
L10.sign_meaning: When hostility toward the other party rises, Congress's ability to write and check policy tends to fall.
L10.qualification: The studies (Binder 2003; Lee 2016) measure polarization among members of Congress and the number of laws passed; they did not measure public hostility or committee staff capacity directly.
L10.mechanism: Polarized chambers legislate less and centralize in leadership

L11.name: A weaker Congress invites presidential action
L11.plain: When Congress does not legislate, presidents fill the gap with executive orders, emergency declarations, tariffs and spending freezes.
L11.sign_meaning: When Congress's capacity falls, presidential action without new legislation tends to rise.
L11.mechanism: Legislative abdication is filled by orders, emergencies, tariffs and impoundment

L12.name: Presidential action erodes Congress's will to legislate
L12.plain: When the executive settles questions alone, members of Congress have less reason to build the staff and skills needed to write laws.
L12.sign_meaning: When presidents act more without new laws, Congress's capacity tends to fall further.
L12.qualification: This return effect rests on legal and historical analysis (Chafetz 2017) and has no quantitative test.
L12.mechanism: Atrophy of the incentive and capacity to legislate

L13.name: Recent rulings, on balance, expand presidential power
L13.plain: Rulings on presidential immunity and the removal of officials widened what a president can do alone, while rulings on tariffs, the National Guard and the Federal Reserve set limits.
L13.sign_meaning: On the 2024 to 2026 record, more rulings of this kind go with more presidential action without new legislation.
L13.qualification: The positive sign is a net reading of 2024 to 2026 decisions: Trump v. United States and Trump v. Slaughter widened presidential power, and Learning Resources, Trump v. Illinois and Trump v. Cook limited it. A different set of rulings could reverse the sign.
L13.mechanism: Immunity and removal rulings expand unilateral power; tariff, Guard and Fed rulings bound it. Net positive 2024 to 2026

L14.name: Presidential removals weaken watchdog agencies
L14.plain: Firing inspectors general and commissioners, leaving boards without a quorum and cutting staff all reduce what watchdogs can investigate and enforce.
L14.sign_meaning: When presidential action without new legislation rises, the ability to investigate and enforce the rules tends to fall.
L14.mechanism: Removal of inspectors general and commissioners; quorum losses; reductions in force

L15.name: Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action
L15.plain: Audits, lawsuits and enforcement raise the cost of acting without a law, provided the enforcer does not answer to the official being checked.
L15.sign_meaning: When oversight grows stronger, presidential action without new legislation tends to fall.
L15.qualification: GAO found several 2025 impoundments unlawful, and its findings carry no penalty of their own; the restraint depends on courts and Congress acting on them.
L15.mechanism: Audits, litigation and enforcement restrain unilateral action when the enforcer is independent

L16.name: Watchdogs reduce favoritism and waste in policy
L16.plain: Investigators who find an agency captured by the industry it regulates, or money wasted, can force corrections that remove some advantages built into rules and contracts.
L16.sign_meaning: When oversight grows stronger, policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests tend to shrink.
L16.qualification: GAO credits its High Risk List work with about $84 billion in financial benefits since 2023 by its own accounting; most of that is waste and payment errors, a broader category than favoritism toward organized interests.
L16.mechanism: Detection and remedy of capture and waste

L17.name: Visible favoritism can prompt investigations
L17.plain: When a scandal or obvious harm comes to light, prosecutors, auditors and legislators open inquiries into it.
L17.sign_meaning: When policy favoritism grows and becomes visible, investigation and enforcement tend to increase in response.
L17.qualification: Investigations follow only some scandals, such as the federal case over Ohio House Bill 6 that ended in convictions in 2023; a response needs a watchdog with the staff and legal power to act.
L17.mechanism: Visible harm and scandal trigger scrutiny and investigations

L18.name: Congressional expertise may reduce insider influence
L18.plain: Committees with their own experts rely less on bill text and analysis supplied by interested groups.
L18.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: more congressional capacity goes with fewer policy advantages for insiders.
L18.qualification: Hypothesis. The cited research shows reliance on lobbyists' expertise (Drutman 2015) and on model bills in state legislatures (Hertel-Fernandez 2019); no study tests what added congressional staff would change.
L18.mechanism: Own expertise reduces dependence on interested drafting

L19.name: Insider-tilted policy may weaken congressional expertise
L19.plain: Rules shaped by outside interests can reduce the demand for independent analysis inside Congress, which makes staff cuts easier to pass.
L19.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: more policy advantages for insiders go with less congressional capacity.
L19.qualification: Hypothesis. The cited evidence is one event, the 1995 House staff cuts and the closing of the Office of Technology Assessment, and it does not show that insider influence caused them.
L19.mechanism: Insider-tilted policy weakens support for public expertise

L20.name: Better public services build earned trust
L20.plain: People who receive a service that works on time have a reason to trust the agency that delivered it.
L20.sign_meaning: When public services improve, trust based on performance tends to rise.
L20.qualification: Survey trust also moves with which party holds office (Hetherington 2005), so the share of trust that comes from performance is uncertain.
L20.mechanism: Experienced competence; trust also tracks partisanship of the incumbent, so the causal share is uncertain

L21.name: Earned trust supports compliance and service funding
L21.plain: People who trust an agency are more likely to pay taxes and follow its rules, which gives it the revenue and cooperation to keep services working.
L21.sign_meaning: When earned trust rises, the quality of public services tends to rise.
L21.qualification: Studies of tax morale (Luttmer and Singhal 2014) and COVID-19 rules (Bargain and Aminjonov 2020) support the compliance channel; the claim that trust raises political support for funding is a hypothesis.
L21.mechanism: Compliance and revenue channel (well-supported); support-for-funding channel (hypothesis)

L22.name: Insider-tilted policy cuts public service capacity
L22.plain: Tax cuts and budget austerity often fall on the staff who run programs, so agencies answer fewer calls and process claims more slowly.
L22.sign_meaning: When policy favors insiders more, the quality of public services tends to fall.
L22.qualification: Staff losses are documented in agency data, including TIGTA and OPM figures for the IRS in 2025; the step from favoritism in tax law to a specific agency's cuts passes through budget decisions with several causes.
L22.mechanism: Austerity and tax cuts fall on administrative capacity; IRS lost about a quarter of staff in 2025

L23.name: Poor service raises incumbents' risk of losing
L23.plain: Voters judge officeholders on results, so visible failures make a challenger more credible and an incumbent easier to replace.
L23.sign_meaning: When public services get worse, the risk of losing office tends to rise; better service lowers it.
L23.qualification: Retrospective voting is well documented (Healy and Malhotra 2013), and voters also punish officials for events outside their control, such as natural disasters, so the pressure does not track performance alone.
L23.mechanism: Poor performance raises pressure to replace officials (retrospective voting)

L24.name: Electoral pressure leads to actual defeats
L24.plain: Where seats are competitive, a credible threat turns into an incumbent's defeat or a retirement taken to avoid one.
L24.sign_meaning: When the risk of losing office rises, more incumbents tend to be defeated or pushed to retire.
L24.qualification: Pressure can change an official's behavior before any defeat occurs, so testing the whole chain needs evidence on both the threat and the defeats over several election cycles.
L24.mechanism: Credible pressure becomes an actual removal or a forced retirement where seats are competitive

L25.name: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure
