R-40.summary: Employers would have to tell workers when AI is used to hire, schedule or evaluate them, explain decisions and offer human review, and negotiate how tools are used where workers have a union. Workers in jobs exposed to AI would gain once the rules are enforced. Employers would bear compliance costs.
R-40.what_it_changes: AI adoption may weaken the position of entry-level workers in exposed jobs (LT05: AI adoption may weaken entry-level workers' position, rated contested). Notice, a way to contest decisions and a say through bargaining aim to protect A2: Workers' bargaining power. The reform operates on loop R6 (Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other).
R-40.who_decides: Unions and employers can bargain over AI, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; the Writers Guild's 2023 contract is an example. States can pass notice and review laws (medium), and Colorado's SB 26-189 takes effect January 1, 2027. City audit laws are rated low, since enforcement of New York City's Local Law 144 has been weak.
R-40.legal_authority: Authority to require notice is clear. Bargaining over how tools are deployed requires a union.
R-40.implementation: Notice comes first. Explanations of decisions and human review follow. Audits come next, and complaints are tracked. Enforcement capacity is a prerequisite.
R-40.costs: The public cost is small. Employers bear compliance costs once enforcement begins.
R-40.failure_risks: Employers and AI vendors are expected to resist, mainly by writing narrow definitions of covered tools. The biggest risk is no enforcement. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Whether AI is hurting entry-level workers is disputed. Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen (2025) found a 13% relative employment decline for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations, a pattern consistent with an AI effect that does not prove one. A study of Denmark ruled out earnings effects above 1% to 2%, and the Yale Budget Lab found no clear unemployment trend by exposure. Research by Anthropic, a company that makes AI tools, found job-finding for 22- to 25-year-olds entering exposed occupations about 14% lower than in 2022, a barely significant result.

remedy_evidence.text: The remedy is a hypothesis. Main limitation: enforcement has been weak where these rules have been tried, as in New York City, so there is little evidence on what working rules would achieve.

R-40.tradeoffs: Compliance costs rise, and the rules may slow useful adoption of AI.
success_measures: Complaints filed and resolved
Union contracts with clauses on AI
R-40.alternatives: Funding for worker retraining is the main alternative. Rejected option: bans on AI use.

status.text: Colorado SB 26-189, signed May 14, 2026 according to a law-firm summary, takes effect January 1, 2027. When automated decision tools are used in consequential decisions, including employment decisions, it requires notice, a plain-language explanation within 30 days of an adverse outcome, and rights to correct data, request human review and appeal. It replaces Colorado's 2024 AI Act, which never took effect.

routes.note: Writers Guild 2023 contract.
Colorado SB 26-189 from Jan 1, 2027.

New York City Local Law 144 requires employers that use automated hiring tools to commission and post bias audits. A December 2025 audit by the New York State Comptroller found that the city's consumer protection agency received two complaints from July 2023 to June 2025 and found one violation among 32 companies it reviewed, while the auditors found at least 17 potential violations at the same companies.

R-41.title: Large power users pay their grid costs
R-41.summary: Large new electricity users, such as data centers, would pay for the grid capacity and upgrades their demand requires, through rates set by state utility commissions. Households in fast-growing grids would gain at the next rate case, the proceeding in which regulators set a utility's prices. Data-center operators would pay more.
R-41.what_it_changes: Data-center load raises electricity demand and, through capacity prices, household bills (LT11: Data-center load raises household electricity bills, rated plausible). Charging large loads for the costs they cause aims to keep those costs out of EC9: Cost of essentials, and it acts on TC6: Data centers' demand on the electricity grid. The reform sits on no feedback loop.
R-41.who_decides: For an investor-owned utility, the state public utility commission sets retail rates; tariffs set by commissions under state law are rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. For public power or a cooperative, a city council or co-op board decides. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which oversees wholesale markets, can change market rules (low), and in the PJM region the grid operator's capacity auction also feeds into bills.
R-41.legal_authority: State commissions set retail electricity rates, and FERC oversees wholesale markets.
R-41.implementation: Regulators first design the tariff. Large loads then take on minimum demand charges or long-term contracts, which keep them paying for capacity even if their usage drops. Bill impacts are measured afterward.
R-41.costs: No public cost is identified. Data-center operators pay more starting with the next rate case.
R-41.failure_risks: Data-center developers are likely to oppose it, and they can adapt by locating in states with more permissive terms. Loads moving to states that spread these costs across all customers is the chief risk. Reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: In the PJM region, the independent market monitor attributes about $23.1 billion in capacity costs across three auctions to data-center load (January 2026 analysis). PJM estimated bill increases of 1.5% to 5% for some customers after its 2026/2027 auction. The pass-through to household bills is documented for PJM; other grids differ.

remedy_evidence.text: The case rests on design logic. Main limitation: no evaluation of these tariffs has been found, and loads may move to places offering different terms.

success_measures: Change in residential bills attributable to large new loads
Capacity prices in grid auctions
R-41.alternatives: Rules requiring large users to bring their own generating capacity are the main alternative. Rejected option: spreading these costs across all customers.

status.text: States set retail electricity rates, so tariffs that make data centers and other customers with the largest power demands pay for the grid costs they cause come from state utility commissions, and a growing number of utilities have adopted data-center-specific terms (Congressional Research Service, May 2026). Transmission rules are federal: on June 18, 2026 the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission ordered all six regional grid operators it oversees to file, within 60 days, rules on how large loads connect to the grid, including measures against shifting transmission costs onto other customers, or to show that their current rules are adequate.

routes.note: Large-load tariffs are proposed or pending before several state commissions.

R-42.title: Congress votes on lasting tariffs
R-42.summary: Tariffs, which are taxes on imports, could stay in place beyond a short period only if Congress voted to approve them. Households and importers would gain when existing tariffs come up for review. Producers protected by tariffs would lose that protection unless Congress chose to keep it.
R-42.what_it_changes: Presidents now set tariff rates under statutes that delegate the power (LE19: The executive sets tariff rates), and U.S. buyers pay most of the cost (LE18: Tariffs raise prices U.S. buyers pay). Requiring a vote returns a tax power to Congress, the branch the Constitution assigns it to. The reform touches loop R13 (Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action).
R-42.who_decides: Congress decides by statute, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; bills have been introduced in earlier sessions. Courts police individual statutes through suits over statutory authority (medium), as in Learning Resources v. Trump (February 20, 2026), where the Supreme Court held that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs.
R-42.legal_authority: Article I of the Constitution gives Congress the power to impose tariffs. A statute requiring approval would need a President willing to sign it or a majority large enough to override a veto.
R-42.implementation: Congress passes the statute. Existing tariffs are then reviewed and put to a vote.
R-42.costs: Federal revenue changes as tariffs end or continue. Producers that benefit from protection lose it when tariffs lapse without a vote.
R-42.failure_risks: Any administration is expected to resist, along with protected industries. The main adaptation is shifting to other statutes: after the 2026 ruling, most tariffs imposed under the emergency-powers law were replaced under Sections 122, 232 and 301. A veto poses the biggest risk. Once enacted, a statute would be durable.

problem_evidence.text: Tariffs cost about $1,100 per household per year as of August 2026, according to the Yale Budget Lab. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that U.S. importers bore 94% of tariff costs from January to August 2025 and 86% by November.

remedy_evidence.text: The approach is plausible. Learning Resources shows that courts police one statute at a time. Main limitation: no U.S. experience shows how a general vote requirement would work in practice.

R-42.tradeoffs: Responses in trade disputes would be slower.
success_measures: Tariffs in force without a vote of Congress
Tariff cost per household
R-42.alternatives: Narrowing each statute that delegates tariff power is the main alternative. Rejected option: relying on courts alone, because the executive can shift to other statutes.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, no law requiring congressional approval of tariffs has been enacted. On February 20, 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in Learning Resources v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs. The administration then imposed a 10% global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, effective February 24, 2026; that section limits such tariffs to 150 days unless Congress extends them. On May 7, 2026 the Court of International Trade ruled 2 to 1, for the plaintiffs in one case, that those tariffs were not justified under Section 122, and the Federal Circuit put that ruling on hold in June 2026.

routes.note: Bills have been introduced in earlier sessions of Congress.
Learning Resources.

R-43.title: Building codes and mitigation against disaster losses
R-43.summary: States and cities would adopt and enforce stronger building codes and fund retrofits that reduce damage when storms and other hazards strike. Owners and renters in hazard areas would gain at the next disaster, and insurance would stay more available. Builders would face higher construction costs now.
R-43.what_it_changes: Higher hazard raises insurance premiums and nonrenewals (LE20: Climate hazard raises insurance costs), and in high-hazard places insurance costs weigh on home values (LE23: Climate risk weighs on home equity). Stronger codes and mitigation cut losses when hazards hit, which aims to lower EC11: Climate hazards and insurance costs. The reform sits on no feedback loop.
R-43.who_decides: States can adopt statewide codes, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Local governments adopt and enforce codes (medium). Congress funds mitigation grants (low), and FEMA administers federal mitigation money.
R-43.legal_authority: States and local governments have the authority to adopt building codes.
R-43.implementation: Governments adopt modern codes first. Enforcement follows, then funding for retrofits of existing buildings, then measurement of insurance claims after events. Inspection capacity is a prerequisite.
R-43.costs: Construction costs rise for builders, and the price of new homes goes up. Mitigation grants come from public budgets.
R-43.failure_risks: Some builders tend to oppose it, and local opt-outs are the likely adaptation. Codes that are adopted but not enforced are the main failure risk. Codes are durable, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: The Treasury Department's Federal Insurance Office found that from 2018 to 2022, homeowners in the riskiest fifth of ZIP codes paid 82% more for insurance ($2,321 on average) than those in the least risky fifth, and saw about 80% more nonrenewals. Insurance industry groups disputed the figures.

remedy_evidence.text: The Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety, a research group supported by property insurers, studied closed claims from Hurricane Charley (2004) in Charlotte County, Florida. Homes built after stricter codes took effect there in 1996 had 40% lower damage frequency and 60% lower damage severity. Main limitation: that study covers one storm in one county, and higher upfront costs and weak enforcement can limit the benefit.

R-43.tradeoffs: Codes raise the cost of new homes, which works against adding housing supply (R-30) at the margin.
success_measures: Insurance claims after hazard events
Insurance premiums in high-risk ZIP codes
R-43.alternatives: Relying on insurance pricing alone to signal risk is the main alternative. Rejected option: rebuilding to old codes after disasters.

status.text: Building codes are adopted state by state, and in many states each city or county decides which code to adopt and enforce.

routes.note: Federal mitigation grants depend on annual appropriations.

R-44.title: Competition remedies for search and ad markets
R-44.summary: Courts and agencies would impose remedies that open search and online advertising markets to rivals, such as bans on exclusive deals and requirements to share data. Publishers and advertisers would gain over years if the share of ad money captured by a few platforms falls. The dominant platforms would lose some control over these markets.
R-44.what_it_changes: Platforms took the advertising that paid for local reporting (LT03: Platforms drew ad revenue from local news), and concentrated ownership may entrench the goals that govern feeds (LT02: Platform concentration may entrench engagement ranking, a hypothesis). Remedies that open these markets aim to lower TC2: Concentration of platforms and digital advertising. The reform acts on loop R16 (Local news loss and weak electoral pressure may reinforce each other).
R-44.who_decides: The Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission and states enforce through litigation, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; the Google search and ad-tech remedies are the main cases. Congress could legislate (low).
R-44.legal_authority: The Sherman Act, the main federal antitrust law, supplies the authority.
R-44.implementation: A court orders a remedy first. A monitor then oversees compliance. Ad market shares and the share of ad revenue reaching publishers are measured afterward.
R-44.costs: The public cost is small. Dominant platforms lose some revenue and control.
R-44.failure_risks: Platforms would likely push back through appeals and by launching new products outside a decree's reach. Remedies too weak to change market shares are the main failure risk. Decrees last only for their terms, and appeals can overturn them.

problem_evidence.text: Newspaper advertising revenue fell from about $49.4 billion in 2005 to about $9.8 billion in 2022, according to Pew Research Center. Where Craigslist arrived, newsroom staff fell 6% and coverage of local House members dropped about 30% (Djourelova, Durante and Martin, 2021). That study covers classified ads; for search and social advertising the link is plausible.

remedy_evidence.text: Conduct remedies, which regulate a company's behavior without breaking it up, are untested at this scale. Courts found Google liable in search (August 2024) and ad tech (April 2025) and ordered conduct remedies without divestiture, and the FTC lost its case against Meta in November 2025. Main limitation: the market effect depends on the remedy, and some cases remain unresolved.

R-44.tradeoffs: Benefits from integrated services may be lost.
success_measures: Shares of the digital advertising market
Share of advertising revenue that reaches publishers
R-44.alternatives: Interoperability mandates, which require platforms to work with rivals' products, are the main alternative.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, both federal antitrust cases against Google are past the liability stage. In the search case, Judge Amit Mehta's remedies of September 2, 2025 barred exclusive default-search contracts and required Google to share some search-index and user-interaction data with qualified competitors, and they did not require a sale of Chrome or Android; Google and the Justice Department each appealed parts of the judgment in early 2026, according to news reports. In the ad-tech case, Judge Leonie Brinkema issued remedies in early September 2026: a six-year order with interoperability and nondiscrimination requirements and a court-appointed monitor, without a forced sale of Google's ad exchange.

routes.note: Search case: remedies ordered September 2, 2025, with appeals filed by Google and the Justice Department in early 2026. Ad-tech case: a six-year behavioral order with a court-appointed monitor, issued in early September 2026.

R-45.title: Verifiable elections with paper records and audits
R-45.summary: Every vote would leave a paper record, results would be audited, officials would face firm deadlines to certify, and election workers would be protected from threats. Every voter would gain at every election, because results could be checked and accepted. Officials who refuse to certify lawful results would face court orders.
R-45.what_it_changes: Paper records, audits and certification on a schedule make results provable, so that C5: Incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement can happen and be accepted. Every reform that works through elections rests on this floor. The reform is linked to B5: Equality of voter turnout and to E2: Trust earned through performance, and to loop R4b (Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable) and loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance).
R-45.who_decides: States can pass certification and audit statutes, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; 39 states and the District of Columbia have laws protecting election officials. Counties run elections and can strengthen administration directly (high). Congress can fund recurring grants (low).
R-45.legal_authority: States run elections. The Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022 governs the federal count of presidential electoral votes; it clarified certification duties and raised the threshold for objections in Congress.
R-45.implementation: Paper records and audits come first. Certification duties with deadlines follow. A system for responding to threats against officials comes next.
R-45.costs: The cost is small, paid mainly by state and county election offices.
R-45.failure_risks: Officials who refuse to certify are expected to resist, mainly through litigation. Underfunded staff and refusals to certify are the main failure risks. Durability is high, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: An AP-NORC and USAFacts survey published in September 2026 found that 34% of U.S. adults trust the certification of the 2026 midterm results a great deal or quite a bit. In a 2025 Brennan Center survey of 858 local election officials, 38% reported threats, harassment or abuse.

remedy_evidence.text: Evidence is strong that paper records and audits catch errors. A risk-limiting audit, one common design, checks a statistical sample of paper ballots against the reported outcome. Main limitation: audits help only when trained staff run them and officials complete certification lawfully.

R-45.tradeoffs: Audits take time, which can delay final results.
success_measures: Risk-limiting audits completed
Certifications completed on time
Threats against election officials investigated and resolved
R-45.alternatives: No alternative to this floor is listed. It rejects replacing voting machines with hand counts, which raise error rates.

status.text: Nearly all U.S. voters now cast ballots on paper or on machines that produce a paper record that can be audited.

routes.note: Since 2020 many states have passed laws protecting election officials from threats, harassment or publication of their home addresses.

R-46.title: Expand the House of Representatives
R-46.summary: Congress would add seats to the House, so each member would represent fewer people, with a plan for apportionment and staffing. Residents of large states would gain at the next apportionment after the change. A larger chamber could also give party leaders more control.
R-46.what_it_changes: More seats mean smaller districts and more representatives per person, and pairing expansion with multi-member districts (R-03) multiplies the effect. The reform is linked to C1: Seats with little electoral competition and B5: Equality of voter turnout, and to loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates).
R-46.who_decides: Congress decides by statute, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030.
R-46.legal_authority: Congress fixed the House at 435 seats by statute in 1929, so it can change the number by statute. A bill would need 60 Senate votes or filibuster reform (R-12).
R-46.implementation: Congress passes a statute. The new size applies at the next apportionment, when House seats are divided among the states after the census.
R-46.costs: The cost is small: offices, staff and space for the added members.
R-46.failure_risks: Incumbents are likely to oppose it. The main failure risk is that a larger chamber concentrates power in party leadership. Once enacted, the change is durable, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: After the 2020 census, the average House district had 761,169 residents, according to the Census Bureau.

remedy_evidence.text: Frederick (2010), in observational research, found that larger districts reduce members' contact with constituents and constituents' approval of the member, with modest effects. Main limitation: the effect of expansion on electoral competition is untested.

R-46.tradeoffs: A larger chamber can concentrate power in its leadership.
success_measures: Residents per House member
R-46.alternatives: Proportional multi-seat districts (R-03) are the main alternative.

status.text: The number of House seats has been fixed at 435 by federal law since the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929. Enlarging the House would take a new federal statute, and none has been enacted.

R-47.title: Fusion voting and public funding for parties
R-47.summary: More than one party could nominate the same candidate, so a voter could back a candidate on a smaller party's ballot line without splitting the vote. Public funding could also go to parties as well as candidates. Minor parties and their voters would gain in the first election cycle, and major parties would have reason to absorb the smaller lines.
R-47.what_it_changes: Fusion voting lets two parties nominate the same candidate, and party-centered funding helps organized coalitions form without spoiling races. The reform is linked to C2: How often the primary decides the winner and C3: Risk of losing office, and to loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates).
R-47.who_decides: States can legalize fusion by statute, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; it is legal in New York and Connecticut. Party-centered public funding at the federal level is rated low.
R-47.legal_authority: In Timmons (1997), the Supreme Court held that states may ban fusion, so each state decides whether to allow it.
R-47.implementation: A statute comes first. It runs for two election cycles, and then it is evaluated.
R-47.failure_risks: Major parties tend to oppose it, mainly through ballot-access rules that make it harder for small parties to qualify. The chief risk is major parties absorbing the smaller lines. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Party organizations are weak, and getting on the ballot is harder for minor parties than for major ones, as state-by-state signature and fee requirements compiled by Ballotpedia show.

remedy_evidence.text: Experience in New York, where fusion is legal, informs the proposal. Main limitation: evidence comes from few states, and stronger party leaders and absorption of smaller lines are known risks.

success_measures: Votes cast on minor-party ballot lines
How long coalitions between parties last
R-47.alternatives: All-party primaries (R-01) are the main alternative.

status.text: Fusion voting lets one candidate appear on the ballot lines of more than one party. It is legal and in regular use in New York and Connecticut. Minor parties in Kansas and New Jersey have gone to court to overturn their states' bans. Massachusetts Question 3, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would let a party endorse a candidate in a single all-candidate primary and show that endorsement on the ballot. Party-centered public funding remains a proposal.

routes.note: Legal in New York and Connecticut.

R-48.title: Agency independence after the Slaughter ruling
R-48.summary: After the Supreme Court's June 2026 decision in Trump v. Slaughter, Congress would protect independent agencies through other tools: public reasons and records for removals, protected budgets, agency structures the ruling leaves intact, and a written exception for the Federal Reserve. People affected by federal regulation would gain over years if those designs hold. The designs are untested, and their durability depends on how courts apply the decision.
R-48.what_it_changes: When officials can be removed at will, watchdogs and regulators weaken (L14: Presidential removals weaken watchdog agencies), and fewer independent enforcers are left to restrain unilateral action (L15: Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action). After Slaughter, independence has to come from structure, such as records, stated reasons for removal, budget protection and the design of lower-level offices, because tenure protection no longer works for many officials. The reform works through loop R18 (Weakening watchdogs lowers the cost of further unilateral action).
R-48.who_decides: Congress can legislate, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Litigation can test the designs (low); in Trump v. Cook, the Supreme Court denied a stay, and the case continues on the merits.
R-48.legal_authority: In Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026), the Supreme Court held 6 to 3 that the Federal Trade Commission's protection against removal without cause violates the separation of powers, and it overruled what remained of Humphrey's Executor, the earlier precedent that had allowed such protection. The Court reserved the question of the Federal Reserve.
R-48.implementation: Congress first maps which agencies the ruling exposes. It then passes a statute with new protections, which are tested in litigation.
R-48.costs: There is no fiscal cost. Presidents would face more process before removing officials.
R-48.failure_risks: Administrations would likely push back, mainly by removing officials anyway. The likeliest way it falls short is that the Court extends Slaughter to these designs. Durability depends on court doctrine.

problem_evidence.text: The Supreme Court decided Trump v. Slaughter 6 to 3 on June 29, 2026, striking down the FTC's protection against removal without cause.

remedy_evidence.text: The proposed designs are untested. Main limitation: their durability depends on how courts apply Slaughter, and no court has yet ruled on designs like these.

R-48.tradeoffs: Agencies would have less insulation from presidential control than they had before the ruling.
success_measures: Removals of agency officials accompanied by stated reasons
Days each year that multi-member agencies have a quorum
R-48.alternatives: Congressional oversight is the main alternative. Rejected option: re-enacting the tenure protections that Slaughter struck down.

status.text: On June 29, 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in Trump v. Slaughter that the President may remove Federal Trade Commission members at will, and it overruled Humphrey's Executor (1935). The same day, in Trump v. Cook, the Court voted 5 to 4 to deny the government's request to let the President remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook while her case continues. Cook is an interim order: she stays in office for now, and the Court has not decided whether the Fed's for-cause protection is valid.

routes.note: Cook stay denied; merits continue.

R-49.title: Civic work that crosses party lines
R-49.summary: Membership groups and service programs would bring people of different parties together for shared work, such as serving as poll workers, again and again over time. Members and their communities would gain on an ongoing basis. Measured drops in hostility tend to fade quickly, so lasting effects across the population are uncertain.
R-49.what_it_changes: Ties formed through shared work across party lines can reduce hostility (L33: Cross-group ties reduce partisan hostility, rated plausible) and make turnout more equal (L34: Civic ties make turnout more equal, rated well-supported). The reform builds variable B3: Civic ties across social and political groups and operates on loop R15 (Unions, civic ties and equal turnout reinforce each other).
R-49.who_decides: Membership organizations can act now, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. States and election offices can run poll-worker programs (high); more than 163,000 veterans and military family members served as poll workers from 2022 to 2024.
R-49.legal_authority: Civil-society programs need no government authority.
R-49.implementation: Organizations recruit members across party lines. Members work together on shared projects, and effects are measured over time.
R-49.failure_risks: Few groups resist. The biggest risk is that effects fade. Durability depends on keeping members engaged, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: Hostility toward the other party is high.

remedy_evidence.text: A 2024 megastudy of 32,059 participants tested 25 interventions: 23 reduced partisan animosity, and the effects faded within about two weeks. A randomized evaluation of Braver Angels workshops at four universities found reduced polarization, with implicit and behavioral effects still present at the study's end (Baron and colleagues, 2025). Main limitation: most effects decay, and lasting change across the population is unmeasured.

success_measures: Membership drawn from more than one party
Animosity toward the other party among members
R-49.alternatives: Dialogue programs are the main alternative. Rejected option: one-off dialogue events.

status.text: Cross-partisan membership groups and national-service programs continue to operate; this reform has no single bill or rule whose status can be tracked.

routes.note: Over 163,000 veterans and military family members served as poll workers 2022-24.

R-50.title: Popular-vote compact and constitutional amendment options
R-50.summary: R-50 covers long-term options for how senators and presidents are chosen: constitutional amendments on Senate apportionment and the Electoral College, and the National Popular Vote compact, which needs no amendment. Under the compact, member states would award their electoral votes to the national popular-vote winner once states holding 270 electoral votes have joined. Voters in states that are not competitive in presidential races would gain if it takes effect.
R-50.what_it_changes: A durable Senate majority shapes the courts over decades, and Senate malapportionment, the unequal populations of states that each have two senators, is a fixed feature of that link (L57: Durable Senate majorities shape court appointments). These options act on D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions and D3: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition, and on loop R12 (Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules).
R-50.who_decides: A constitutional amendment requires two-thirds of each house of Congress and three-quarters of the states, or a convention; it gets the lowest feasibility rating for 2026 to 2030. The National Popular Vote compact is an interstate compact, a set of matching state laws that take effect at a threshold, rated low; it needs states with 270 electoral votes and has 222.
R-50.legal_authority: Article V of the Constitution sets the amendment process. Whether the compact needs congressional consent under the Constitution's Compact Clause is an open question that courts would decide.
R-50.implementation: The compact takes effect once member states reach 270 electoral votes. Litigation is expected to follow.
R-50.failure_risks: Small states and the parties advantaged under current rules are expected to resist. Litigation and states withdrawing from the compact are the main risks. An amendment, once ratified, would be durable.

problem_evidence.text: Senate malapportionment is documented: every state has two senators regardless of population, so senators from small states represent far fewer people.

remedy_evidence.text: The compact is untested, and no court has ruled on it. Main limitation: it has not taken effect, so neither its legal standing nor its effects on campaigns are known.

R-50.tradeoffs: Member states could withdraw from the compact.
success_measures: Electoral votes held by states in the compact
R-50.alternatives: No alternative is listed and no option is rejected here.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, 18 states and the District of Columbia, holding 222 electoral votes, have enacted the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. It takes effect only when its members hold at least 270 electoral votes, so it is 48 short. Virginia joined in April 2026.

routes.note: 18 states plus DC, 222 electoral votes of 270 needed.

I001.title: Local newsrooms close and fewer reporters watch local government
I001.summary: When a local paper or station closes, fewer reporters attend council meetings, read budgets or question officials. Residents lose a shared source of facts about local decisions, and local officials face less public scrutiny.
I001.mechanism: When local news outlets close, fewer reporters examine local government, and residents share less common knowledge about the decisions made in their name.
I001.evidence_note: Well supported. The 2025 State of Local News census counted 212 U.S. counties with no local news source (the report's landing page gives 213). A 2020 study by Gao, Lee and Murphy linked newspaper closures to higher borrowing costs for local governments. Hayes and Lawless (2021) found that shrinking local coverage goes with lower political engagement and knowledge; their panel and content data support associations, and the authors limit their causal claims.
I001.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Public funds for local news already operate, including New Jersey's Civic Information Consortium and Canada's Local Journalism Initiative. No published study has measured whether these funds improve accountability, such as closer scrutiny of officials.
I001.response: State legislatures and local philanthropies would create an independently governed local-news fund. It would pay formula grants, keep funders away from editorial decisions and publish data on every award.
I001.tradeoff: Public money can invite political control of coverage. The design keeps the people who appoint the fund's board separate from the people who make editorial decisions.
I001.success_measure: Counties with a local news source, reporters per resident, and the corrections that funded outlets publish.

aimed_reforms.why: Pays reporters to cover local government with an editorial firewall, which is the fund this record proposes.

problem_example.headline: Gallup, New Mexico, loses its paper after 62 years
problem_example.text: In January 2026, the Gallup Independent in Gallup, New Mexico, printed its last issue after 62 years. Its circulation had fallen from 18,000 in 2006 to under 5,000. Bob Zollinger, whose family ran the paper, worries the city council and county commission will now meet with no reporter present.

source.title: NM news desert grows with closure of longtime Gallup newspaper

fix_example.headline: New Jersey funds local news through a state-created consortium
fix_example.text: New Jersey's 2018 law created the Civic Information Consortium, a nonprofit that funds local journalism with donations and state money. It has issued more than $12 million in grants. State support fell from $4 million in fiscal 2024 to $2.5 million in fiscal 2026, and Gov. Mikie Sherrill's first budget proposal would zero it out.
fix_example.result: Sen. Andrew Zwicker's bill would direct at least $5 million a year to the consortium but had not reached a committee vote, and the article cites no study of whether the grants brought closer scrutiny of officials.

source.title: Lawmakers eye funding stream for NJ PBS, local news

I002.title: Chain owners cut local reporting
I002.summary: When one company buys many local papers or stations, it often cuts local staff and shares content across its outlets. The strongest study, of one TV station owner, found coverage moved toward national politics and viewers left.
I002.mechanism: Chains that buy local outlets often cut local reporting staff. One strong study found that one owner, Sinclair Broadcast Group, shifted its acquired stations toward national political coverage; whether common owners in general centralize the news agenda is untested.
I002.evidence_note: Plausible. Martin and McCrain (2019, American Political Science Review) found that local TV stations bought by Sinclair shifted toward national and right-leaning political coverage and lost viewers. The study covers one ownership group. Staff cuts at chain-owned outlets appear in industry counts such as the 2025 State of Local News report.
I002.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Merger review that weighs the number of independent news voices has not been tested for U.S. media. The Federal Communications Commission has loosened its ownership rules, and no evaluation has measured what those changes did to coverage.
I002.response: Congress, the Federal Communications Commission and the federal antitrust agencies would review local news mergers for their effect on competition and on the number of independent outlets. Owners would disclose who ultimately owns each outlet and how many newsroom staff it employs.
I002.tradeoff: Owning many outlets proves neither biased coverage nor illegal market power, so each deal needs its own evidence.
I002.success_measure: More distinct owners in each local market and more original local reporting.

aimed_reforms.why: Funds independent local reporters, which offsets the staff cuts that follow acquisitions; ownership itself stays unchanged.

problem_example.headline: Stations bought by Sinclair shift toward national politics
problem_example.text: In September 2017, Sinclair Broadcast Group finished buying 14 local TV stations from Bonten Media Group. A study in the American Political Science Review found the stations' coverage of national politics rose about 25% while local politics coverage fell. Their coverage also moved to the right, and a small drop in viewership was not statistically significant.
problem_example.where: Seven U.S. TV markets served by former Bonten stations

source.title: Local News and National Politics
source.publisher: American Political Science Review (Martin and McCrain)

fix_example.headline: Regulators' review stops Sinclair's bid for Tribune Media
fix_example.text: In July 2018, the Federal Communications Commission sent Sinclair's $3.9 billion bid for Tribune Media to a hearing before a judge. Commissioners questioned whether planned sales of stations to buyers close to Sinclair were a sham that would let Sinclair keep running them. Tribune walked away from the deal in August.
fix_example.result: The merger collapsed, Sinclair said it had not misled the commission, and no study has measured what the outcome meant for local coverage.

source.title: CNN Money report on Tribune ending the Sinclair merger (lede: 'The Sinclair Broadcast Group acquisition of Tribune Media is dead.')

I003.title: Platforms take the advertising that once paid for reporting
I003.summary: Most of the advertising money that used to support newspapers now goes to large online platforms. News organizations still pay the cost of reporting, so they cover fewer public decisions.
I003.mechanism: Large online platforms now collect most of the advertising money that once paid for news, while publishers still carry the cost of reporting.
I003.evidence_note: Well supported. Industry estimates compiled by the Pew Research Center show U.S. newspaper advertising revenue falling from about $49 billion in 2005 to under $10 billion in 2022. The 2025 State of Local News census counted 212 counties with no local news source.
I003.remedy_note: Hypothesis. No U.S. evaluation of reader vouchers or refundable subscription credits exists. Canada's digital news subscription tax credit has data on how many people claim it and no measure of its effect on reporting.
I003.response: A state legislature would pilot reader vouchers and refundable tax credits for local news subscriptions. Nonprofit and small independent outlets would qualify alongside established publishers.
I003.tradeoff: Subsidies can flow mostly to large, established publishers. Eligibility rules need to be neutral about viewpoint and simple enough for small outlets to use.
I003.success_measure: New subscribers, readers reached in places with little coverage, and public cost per reader.

aimed_reforms.why: Replaces part of the lost advertising money with public and philanthropic funding behind an editorial firewall.
Opens search and ad-tech markets so a smaller share of advertising money is captured by a few platforms.

problem_example.headline: Judge finds Google illegally dominated online ad tools
problem_example.text: In April 2025, a federal judge in Virginia ruled that Google held an illegal monopoly over some of the technology websites use to sell ads. Publishers pay a 20% fee on Google's ad exchange. In September 2026 the judge ordered six years of rule changes and declined to force a sale, and Google said it would appeal.
problem_example.where: United States (federal court in Alexandria, Virginia)

source.title: Google should relax ad tech rules, appoint antitrust monitor, US judge finds

fix_example.headline: Canada tried a tax credit for news subscriptions
fix_example.text: Canada let taxpayers claim a credit worth 15% of up to $500 spent on qualifying digital news subscriptions. About 302,000 people filed for it in 2020, roughly 1% of the country's more than 27 million tax filers, and the average credit was $36.
fix_example.result: Uptake was about 1% in the first year, and the article reports no measured effect on subscriptions; one publisher called the result negligible.

source.title: Canada offered a tax credit to encourage digital news subscriptions. Here's how it's going

I004.title: False claims outlast their corrections
I004.summary: People who hear a false claim several times tend to keep believing part of it after it is corrected. Researchers infer that this makes it harder for voters to judge officials, though that step has not been measured.
I004.mechanism: Repeating a false claim raises belief in it, and corrections reduce that belief only partly and fade over time. The further step, that this weakens voters' ability to hold officials to account, is inferred; no study listed for this record measures it.
I004.evidence_note: Well supported for the psychology of belief. A 2022 review in Nature Reviews Psychology (Ecker and colleagues) found that repetition raises belief and that corrections work partly and fade. A 2020 meta-analysis by Walter and Tukachinsky found that corrections reduce reliance on misinformation without removing it. These lab and field studies measure belief; none measures election outcomes. In US Dominion v. Fox (March 2023), a Delaware court ruled at summary judgment that specific broadcast claims about Dominion were false; the ruling covers those claims only.
I004.remedy_note: Well supported. A meta-analysis found that corrections and prominent retractions reduce belief in a false claim without erasing it. Defamation judgments punish a publisher, and audiences who already absorbed the claim keep part of their belief.
I004.response: Newsrooms, courts and funders would each act. Funders would pay for public-interest reporting that shows its sources. Courts would apply existing defamation law with due process, and newsrooms would run corrections as prominently as the original error.
I004.tradeoff: Opinion and honest mistakes need protection, and no government body should license what counts as true.
I004.success_measure: How many people see a correction compared with the original claim, and whether they later recall the accurate facts.

aimed_reforms.why: Funds source-transparent public-interest reporting, the funding half of this record's response.

problem_example.headline: A retracted vaccine claim still finds believers
problem_example.text: A 1998 Lancet paper by Andrew Wakefield claimed a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, and the journal later retracted it. In an April 2024 Annenberg Public Policy Center survey of 1,522 U.S. adults, 24% called the statement that no evidence links the measles vaccine to autism inaccurate.

source.title: False belief in MMR vaccine-autism link endures as measles threat persists
source.publisher: Annenberg Public Policy Center, University of Pennsylvania

fix_example.headline: Fox agrees to pay Dominion $787.5 million over false claims
fix_example.text: Dominion Voting Systems sued Fox News for defamation over falsehoods the network broadcast after the 2020 presidential election. In April 2023, with the case underway in Wilmington, Delaware, Fox agreed to pay $787.5 million and acknowledged the court's rulings finding certain claims about Dominion false. NPR's David Folkenflik reported that no on-air apology had been disclosed.
fix_example.result: Dominion will get about half the $1.6 billion it sought, and no on-air apology was disclosed as part of the deal.

source.title: Fox News averts major defamation trial by settling with Dominion Voting Systems

I005.title: Readers cannot tell reporting from opinion or paid content
I005.summary: Many readers cannot tell whether a piece reports verified facts, gives an opinion or promotes a sponsor. Clear labels help a little, and their effect depends on how they are written and placed.
I005.mechanism: Many readers cannot reliably tell reported fact from opinion, or news from sponsored content.
I005.evidence_note: Well supported. In a 2018 Pew Research Center survey of 5,035 U.S. adults, 26% correctly classified all five factual statements and 35% all five opinion statements. Amazeen and Wojdynski (2020) found that fewer than one in ten readers recognized native ads, paid articles styled to look like news, as advertising.
I005.remedy_note: Plausible. Disclosure labels raise recognition of sponsored content modestly, and the gain depends on wording and placement. No study shows that labels change trust or the beliefs that bear on voting.
I005.response: The Federal Trade Commission, within its existing authority, and publishers would act. Paid content would carry clear labels, and publishers would post standards that separate reported facts from opinion.
I005.tradeoff: Labels have small effects on their own, and readers can skip them.
I005.success_measure: The share of people in user tests who correctly identify who sponsored a piece.

problem_example.headline: Many adults mix up news facts and opinions
problem_example.text: In a 2018 Pew Research Center survey, 5,035 U.S. adults sorted 12 news statements as factual or opinion, including five of each type. For each set of five, roughly a quarter got most or all wrong. Even among the most politically aware, only 36% correctly identified all five factual statements.

source.title: Distinguishing Between Factual and Opinion Statements in the News

fix_example.headline: FTC acts against Lord & Taylor's paid posts
fix_example.text: In March 2016, the Federal Trade Commission charged that retailer Lord & Taylor deceived consumers through a paid article in an online fashion magazine and paid Instagram posts by 50 fashion influencers. The company settled, and a final order in May 2016 prohibits those deceptive advertising techniques.
fix_example.result: The order binds the company, but no study measured whether readers became better at spotting paid content afterward.

source.title: In the Matter of Lord & Taylor, LLC (FTC File No. 152 3181)

I006.title: Feeds built for attention reward attacks on the other side
I006.summary: Platforms rank posts to keep people scrolling, and posts attacking an opposing group draw more shares. Studies show ranking changes what people see far more clearly than it changes how they feel about the other party.
I006.mechanism: Feeds ranked to hold attention give more reach to posts that attack an out-group (people seen as the opposing side) and to misleading claims.
I006.evidence_note: Well supported for engagement and exposure. Rathje, Van Bavel and van der Linden (2021) examined 2.7 million posts and found an association: each word about the opposing political group went with about 67% more shares. On X in 2023, a seven-week randomized experiment with 4,965 U.S. users showed the ranked feed changed what people saw, though one platform, period and sample limit how far that generalizes. When researchers reranked hostile partisan posts for 1,256 users over ten days of the 2024 campaign, feelings toward the other party shifted.
I006.remedy_note: Plausible. In one experiment, reranking feeds to show fewer hostile partisan posts lowered hostility toward the other party over ten days. In a larger randomized experiment during the 2020 election, moving Facebook and Instagram users to a chronological feed for three months changed what they saw and how long they stayed, and researchers found no significant change in polarization or political knowledge. Rules giving users a choice of feed have mixed evidence, and Moody v. NetChoice (2024) limits how far government can direct a platform's editorial choices.
I006.response: Congress and the platforms would act. Users would choose how their feed is ranked, independent researchers would get platform data under privacy safeguards, and independent risk audits would be tied to remedies when they find problems.
I006.tradeoff: Effects differ from platform to platform, and auditor access can expose users' private information. Obligations have to fit the limits on regulating editorial discretion and compelled disclosure set out in Moody v. NetChoice.
I006.success_measure: Quality of the content users are shown, measured hostility toward the other party, and privacy incidents.

aimed_reforms.why: Gives users a choice of ranking and gives researchers data to measure what attention-based ranking does.

problem_example.headline: More hostile posts in X feeds deepen partisan dislike
problem_example.text: During the 2024 presidential campaign, researchers reranked the X feeds of 1,256 volunteers for ten days. Feeds showing more posts with partisan animosity and antidemocratic attitudes made feelings toward the other party about two points colder on a 100-point scale. Showing fewer such posts warmed them by a similar amount.

source.title: Social media algorithms and affective polarization, Piccardi et al.

fix_example.headline: Europe makes big platforms offer unpersonalized feeds
fix_example.text: Under the European Union's Digital Services Act, people using platforms with more than 45 million monthly EU users can now opt for feeds that are not personalized. These largest platforms must also identify and analyze widespread risks and take measures to reduce them, with the European Commission primarily responsible for enforcing these extra duties.
fix_example.result: The European Commission reports no figures on how many users switched feeds or on any change in hostility between groups.

source.title: The Digital Services Act

I007.title: People cannot see or challenge platform decisions
I007.summary: Platforms decide which posts people see and which they remove, often with little explanation or route to appeal. No one has measured how often those decisions are wrong, so the size of the problem remains a hypothesis.
I007.mechanism: Users of large platforms cannot see how content reaches them or contest moderation errors. The scale is unmeasured: no source counts moderation errors or appeal outcomes.
I007.evidence_note: Hypothesis. The only U.S. evidence concerns perception. In a 2020 Pew Research Center survey, 73% of U.S. adults said social media sites censor political viewpoints. That figure measures belief; it does not show how often platforms make mistakes.
I007.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The European Union's Digital Services Act requires explanations and appeal routes, and no evaluation of its effects has been found. Similar U.S. mandates face First Amendment limits.
I007.response: Congress would require large platforms to explain moderation decisions in terms a user can act on, offer appeal routes and publish aggregate enforcement data. The platforms would carry out these duties.
I007.tradeoff: Trade secrets limit full disclosure, and detailed rules can teach abusers how to evade enforcement. Obligations must fit the limits on regulating editorial discretion set out in Moody v. NetChoice.
I007.success_measure: How quickly appeals are resolved, how many errors are reversed, and whether platforms pass compliance audits.

aimed_reforms.why: Researcher access to platform data would let independent teams measure how content reaches users, the unmeasured part of this record.

problem_example.headline: Twitter blocks news links without saying why
problem_example.text: In October 2020, Twitter blocked users from sharing links to two New York Post stories about Joe Biden and at first declined to explain why. Users saw only a notice calling the link potentially harmful. Chief executive Jack Dorsey later called blocking links with zero context unacceptable.

source.title: Facebook and Twitter limit sharing 'New York Post' story about Joe Biden

fix_example.headline: EU requires platforms to explain removals and allow appeals
fix_example.text: Under the European Union's Digital Services Act, platforms that remove or suspend a user's content must explain why. Users who disagree can appeal through the platform itself or through an out-of-court dispute settlement body, which the European Commission says is faster and cheaper than going to court.
fix_example.result: The Commission's page sets out these rights but reports no figures on how many removals are explained, appealed or overturned.

source.title: The Digital Services Act

I008.title: A few platforms control how news reaches people
I008.summary: About half of U.S. adults get news from social media at least sometimes, so a handful of companies decide how much of it they see. When one of them changes its rules, news outlets can lose much of their audience overnight.
I008.mechanism: News organizations lose reach when a few platforms change who gets access or how content is discovered.
I008.evidence_note: Plausible. In 2024 about half of U.S. adults got news from social media at least sometimes, according to the Pew Research Center, which shows how much distribution runs through a few platforms. When Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada in 2023, Canadian outlets lost reach.
I008.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Portable subscriptions and interoperability remedies (rules that let users and content move between services) have not been tested for news. Canada's 2023 news block showed outlets losing reach; it produced no evidence about which remedy would help.
I008.response: Congress and competition regulators would support subscriptions readers can carry between services, tools for publishers to reach readers directly, and public-interest ways to find news. Market-wide interoperability remedies would follow the response in I087: Exclusive data makes dominant platforms hard to challenge.
I008.tradeoff: Interoperability can let spam travel more easily between services and can weaken privacy.
I008.success_measure: The cost of switching services for readers and publishers, and the number of competing services in active use.

problem_example.headline: Meta pulls news from Facebook in Canada
problem_example.text: After Canada's Online News Act required tech companies to pay news organizations for their content, Meta blocked news media posts and links from its top networks. Almost a year later, the Reuters Institute reported in 2024 that small local and regional outlets that relied heavily on Facebook traffic said they were suffering.

source.title: Digital News Report 2024: Canada
source.publisher: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, University of Oxford

I009.title: Foreign sponsors disguise political messages as domestic speech
I009.summary: Foreign governments have run covert campaigns that hide who is paying, so their political messages look like ordinary American speech. The operations are documented; the strongest study of one campaign found no measurable change in attitudes or votes.
I009.mechanism: Foreign governments run covert operations that hide their sponsorship so strategic political messages look like ordinary U.S. speech. The operations are documented. Their effect on votes is unestablished, and the one strong study found no measurable effect.
I009.evidence_note: Documented. A declassified 2021 assessment by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence found that Russia and Iran ran covert influence operations during the 2020 federal elections and found no evidence that votes were altered. In September 2024 the Justice Department indicted two RT employees; the indictment states allegations of covert financing and direction. A 2023 study of the Russian Internet Research Agency's 2016 Twitter campaign (Eady and colleagues, Nature Communications) found exposure concentrated among a small group of strongly Republican users and no measurable relationship with attitudes or votes.
I009.remedy_note: Plausible. Enforcement of the Foreign Agents Registration Act and of campaign-finance law are established tools. Their effect on audiences is unproven, and the best study of 2016 Russian activity found no measurable attitude change.
I009.response: The Justice Department, the Federal Election Commission and election agencies would enforce foreign-agent and campaign-finance law, require disclosure of who pays for political messages and publish threat notices grounded in evidence.
I009.tradeoff: An indictment is an allegation. Enforcement must protect domestic dissent and legitimate foreign journalism.
I009.success_measure: Undisclosed networks disrupted, and how accurately operations are traced to their sponsors.

aimed_reforms.why: Disclosure of the original funders of political spending targets the hidden sponsorship at the center of this record.

problem_example.headline: Russia's troll farm targeted Americans on Twitter in 2016
problem_example.text: During the 2016 U.S. election, Russia's Internet Research Agency ran a foreign influence campaign on Twitter. A 2023 study in Nature Communications, using a survey of 1,496 Americans, found 1% of users accounted for 70% of exposures, mostly people who strongly identified as Republicans. It found no meaningful link to changes in attitudes or votes.

source.title: Exposure to the Russian Internet Research Agency foreign influence campaign on Twitter in the 2016 US election and its relationship to attitudes and voting behavior

fix_example.headline: Prosecutors charge RT staff over hidden video funding
fix_example.text: In September 2024, the Justice Department charged two employees of Russia's state-controlled RT with conspiring to violate the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Prosecutors allege RT spent about $10 million on a Tennessee company whose nearly 2,000 videos never told viewers RT was paying. Both Russian defendants were at large when charged.
fix_example.result: The indictment put the alleged funding on the public record; its effect on viewers has not been measured.
fix_example.where: United States (Southern District of New York; Tennessee company)

source.title: DOJ indictment of two RT employees (press release)

I010.title: Fake audio and video can impersonate candidates
I010.summary: Cheap software can fake a candidate's voice or face and reach voters just before they decide. The harm depends on timing, reach and whether a verified correction reaches the same people.
I010.mechanism: Cheap fabricated audio and video can mislead voters at decisive moments, such as the days before an election.
I010.evidence_note: Plausible. In January 2024 an AI-generated robocall imitating President Biden's voice reached New Hampshire voters before the primary. The Federal Communications Commission imposed a $6 million forfeiture on the consultant behind it and reached a $1 million settlement with the carrier. The case shows the method in use; no study listed for this record measures its effect on votes.
I010.remedy_note: Hypothesis. More than 25 states have enacted election deepfake laws, according to a tracker kept by the advocacy group Public Citizen. The laws are new, a federal court blocked California's law on First Amendment grounds in X Corp. v. Bonta, and no study has measured whether any of them deter fakes.
I010.response: Congress and the states would ban fraudulent election impersonation under narrow definitions. Platforms would add provenance records showing where a file came from, and channels for fast, authenticated corrections.
I010.tradeoff: Satire, journalism and lawful anonymous speech need protection.
I010.success_measure: How fast fakes are verified and corrected, and how many lawful posts are removed by mistake.

problem_example.headline: Cloned Biden voice tells New Hampshire voters to stay home
problem_example.text: In January 2024, potential primary voters in New Hampshire got robocalls in a voice that sounded like President Biden. The voice told them to stay home and "save your vote" by skipping the state's primary. Federal Communications Commissioner Geoffrey Starks later called them voice cloning calls.

source.title: Implications of Artificial Intelligence Technologies on Protecting Consumers from Unwanted Robocalls and Robotexts, Declaratory Ruling (FCC 24-17), Statement of Commissioner Starks

fix_example.headline: FCC rules AI-cloned voices fall under robocall law
fix_example.text: In February 2024, weeks after the New Hampshire calls, the Federal Communications Commission ruled that AI-generated voices count as "artificial" voices under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. Callers now need a person's prior consent before using one, with limited exceptions. State attorneys general can pursue the people behind such calls and seek damages.
fix_example.result: The ruling gave regulators and states a clear legal basis to pursue AI voice robocalls; no study has measured whether it deters them.

source.title: Implications of Artificial Intelligence Technologies on Protecting Consumers from Unwanted Robocalls and Robotexts, Declaratory Ruling (FCC 24-17)

I011.title: Targeted political ads escape public scrutiny
I011.summary: Campaigns and groups can send different political claims to different audiences, out of view of everyone else. A searchable record of every ad, its funder and its targeting would let the public examine them.
I011.mechanism: Microtargeted political ads let sponsors send different claims to different groups without the wider public seeing them.
I011.evidence_note: Plausible. Kim and colleagues (2018) collected 2016 Facebook ads from a volunteer panel and found that most divisive issue ads came from groups that could not be identified or looked suspicious. The study covers one election cycle and one volunteer panel. Meta's Ad Library shows spending ranges and audiences, though only for one company and only for ads that advertisers declare as political.
I011.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Ad archives exist voluntarily at Meta and Google and by law in the European Union. No study shows that an archive changes advertiser behavior or what voters know.
I011.response: Congress would require, and platforms would maintain, searchable archives of political ads, including issue ads. Each entry would show the sponsor, the spending, the targeting criteria and the ad itself.
I011.tradeoff: Archives must protect the privacy of the people targeted, and the law has to define an issue ad carefully.
I011.success_measure: How complete the archive is, and whether each ad can be traced to its sponsor.

problem_example.headline: Russian group's Facebook ads reached 11.4 million Americans
problem_example.text: From 2015 to 2017, Russia's Internet Research Agency bought 3,393 Facebook ads, and more than 11.4 million American users saw them. The ads became public when House Intelligence Committee Democrats released them, along with others Facebook later found, for a total of 3,519.

source.title: Social Media Advertisements
source.publisher: U.S. House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, Democratic staff

fix_example.headline: Meta ends EU political ads under new transparency law
fix_example.text: Meta has kept political ads in a public Ad Library showing each ad's spending and targeting, with a "paid for by" label. When the European Union's new political ad law added extensive limits on ad targeting, Meta stopped delivering political and social issue ads in the EU on October 6, 2025, citing legal uncertainty.
fix_example.result: Meta stopped selling political ads in the EU instead of running them under the new rules, and politicians there can still post without paying to promote it.

source.title: Ending political, electoral and social issue advertising in the EU

I012.title: Threats drive reporters and researchers out of public debate
I012.summary: Threats and harassment lead some journalists, researchers and election officials to stop speaking or leave their work. Residents then have fewer people able to investigate and explain public problems.
I012.mechanism: Threats push journalists and researchers out of public debate, leaving fewer people to investigate and explain public problems.
I012.evidence_note: Well supported. In a 2021 global survey by the International Center for Journalists and UNESCO, 73% of 901 women journalists reported online violence and 30% said they censored themselves; respondents chose to take part. In the Brennan Center's survey of 858 U.S. local election officials (April to May 2025), 38% reported threats, harassment or abuse and 52% worried about their staff's safety.
I012.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Press-freedom groups recommend threat investigation and legal-defense support as standard practice. No study has measured whether that support keeps reporters in their jobs.
I012.response: The Justice Department, the states and news organizations would investigate threats, fund legal defense and help people whose home details are published to target them (doxxing), under narrowly drawn laws.
I012.tradeoff: The law has to separate threats from harsh criticism that is lawful.
I012.success_measure: Threat cases resolved, and reporters who stay in their jobs.

problem_example.headline: Online abuse pushes women journalists to self-censor
problem_example.text: In a 2020 global survey by the International Center for Journalists and UNESCO, 73% of 714 women journalists said they had faced online violence. The most common response, given by 30%, was censoring themselves on social media, and 4% said they quit their jobs. Respondents chose to take part.
problem_example.where: Global (respondents in many countries, including the United States)

source.title: The Chilling: Global study of online violence against women journalists
source.publisher: International Center for Journalists (ICFJ) and UNESCO

I013.title: Public records arrive too late to be useful
I013.summary: Federal agencies take weeks or months to answer requests for public records, and backlogs keep growing. Slow answers stall investigations by reporters and residents.
I013.mechanism: Slow responses to public-records requests obstruct investigations. The claim that delay favors people with inside access is an inference the sources do not test.
I013.evidence_note: Documented. The Justice Department reported 1.50 million federal Freedom of Information Act requests in fiscal year 2024, up 25%, with simple requests taking 44 days on average, the longest since 2011. A tabulation of FOIA.gov data by the Brechner Center counted a year-end backlog of 267,056 requests, up 33%, and a record-low 12% of requests granted in full.
I013.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Response deadlines already exist in law, and agencies miss them. More funding and rules requiring agencies to publish records before anyone asks are plausible fixes; neither has been evaluated for its effect on backlogs.
I013.response: Congress, federal agencies and the states would fund records officers, publish records openly in machine-readable form and enforce response deadlines with an appeal that works.
I013.tradeoff: Redactions still have to protect privacy and legitimate security interests.
I013.success_measure: Age of the request backlog, and how complete agencies' proactive publication is.

problem_example.headline: Federal records backlog jumps by a third in 2024
problem_example.text: In fiscal 2024, the backlog of overdue federal Freedom of Information Act requests grew 33%, to 267,056, by the Brechner Center's count of federal data. Simple requests took 44 days on average, up from 39 the year before. Agencies spent an estimated $723 million processing requests.

source.title: FOIA requests, denials, backlogs, delays, costs surge in FY 2024
source.publisher: Brechner Center for Freedom of Information, University of Florida

I014.title: Removals and cuts put public statistics at risk
I014.summary: Jobs, price and population figures depend on statistical agencies that work free of political pressure. The 2025 removal of the labor statistics chief and budget cuts raised that risk, though no measurement yet shows the numbers have worsened.
I014.mechanism: Removal of agency heads, budget cuts and interference can weaken the official statistics people rely on. The August 2025 removal at the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the cuts are documented; no measurement yet shows that data quality has declined.
I014.evidence_note: Plausible. On August 1, 2025, the President removed the commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics after a jobs report, the first such removal, as documented in Urban Institute commentary. The American Statistical Association's 2024 and 2025 reviews documented budget, staffing and independence pressures across federal statistical agencies. Effects on data quality have not been measured.
I014.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Laws protecting release schedules and methods have been proposed. The view that independent statistical agencies sustain trust in data rests on expert consensus and has not been measured.
I014.response: Congress would protect statistical agencies' methods, release schedules and career experts by law. The agencies would publish revision logs and submit to independent audits.
I014.tradeoff: Independent agencies still have to answer for their methods.
I014.success_measure: Releases published on schedule, and how openly revisions are explained.

aimed_reforms.why: Builds agency independence from public reasons for removal, protected records and budget protection, which would cover statistical agency heads.

problem_example.headline: President fires labor statistics chief after jobs report
problem_example.text: On August 1, 2025, the day the July jobs report showed a slowing labor market, President Trump fired Bureau of Labor Statistics Commissioner Erika McEntarfer. The administration cited large revisions to earlier job numbers. She is the only commissioner ever fired, according to the Urban Institute.

source.title: Why the Firing of the BLS Commissioner Should Concern Every Data User

fix_example.headline: Canada shields its chief statistician by law
fix_example.text: In December 2017, Canada amended its Statistics Act so the chief statistician serves a term of up to five years and can be removed only for cause. Decisions on methods must rest strictly on professional statistical standards, and any government order on them must be tabled in Parliament within 15 days.
fix_example.result: The protections are now in statute; no study has measured their effect on public trust in Canada's statistics.

source.title: Bill C-36, An Act to amend the Statistics Act (royal assent)

I015.title: Public information is out of reach for some residents
I015.summary: Slow or missing internet service and websites that do not work with screen readers can keep people from public services and civic information. Residents need formats that fit their devices, languages and assistive tools.
I015.mechanism: Gaps in internet access and in accessible design keep some residents from public services and reliable civic information.
I015.evidence_note: Plausible. The Pew Research Center's 2024 survey put home broadband adoption at about 80% of U.S. adults, with gaps by income, age and rural residence. The survey measures access; it does not measure how many people fail to complete a public service.
I015.remedy_note: Plausible. A 2024 Justice Department rule under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act requires state and local government websites and apps to meet a set accessibility standard (WCAG 2.1 AA). Deadlines fall in 2026 and 2027, so compliance and outcome data do not exist yet.
I015.response: Federal and state agencies and libraries would make public records and civic information work with assistive technology, slow connections, plain language and several languages. Broadband construction belongs with the infrastructure response in I142: Poor transport and utility connections raise the cost of living.
I015.tradeoff: Construction grants for broadband need conditions on affordability and maintenance.
I015.success_measure: Affordable broadband coverage, and the share of people who complete a public service using accessible tools.

problem_example.headline: More than one in five adults lack home broadband
problem_example.text: In a 2025 Pew Research Center survey, 78% of U.S. adults said they subscribe to broadband internet at home, leaving more than one in five without home broadband. Adults with lower incomes and less formal education were less likely to have it.

source.title: Internet, Broadband Fact Sheet

fix_example.headline: Justice Department sets web accessibility rule for local governments
fix_example.text: In April 2024, the Justice Department required state and local government websites and apps to meet a set accessibility standard, WCAG 2.1 Level AA, under the Americans with Disabilities Act. In April 2026 it extended the deadlines to April 2027 for governments serving 50,000 or more people and April 2028 for smaller ones.
fix_example.result: No deadline has arrived yet, so there is no data on whether residents can now reach public services more easily.

source.title: Fact sheet: ADA Title II web and mobile accessibility rule

I016.title: People share claims before checking them
I016.summary: Material often spreads before anyone looks at where it came from or what supports it. Checking what other sources say about an unfamiliar claim is a skill that can be taught.
I016.mechanism: Many people share material without checking its origin or the evidence behind it.
I016.evidence_note: Well supported. A national study of 3,446 U.S. students (Breakstone and colleagues, 2021) found that large majorities failed basic checks of where online material came from.
I016.remedy_note: Well supported. A randomized study across one school district found that teaching lateral reading (checking what other sources say about a source) improved students' evaluation of online material. Prompts asking people to consider accuracy modestly improved the quality of what they shared in lab tests and a field experiment on Twitter (Pennycook and colleagues, 2021).
I016.response: Schools, libraries and civic groups would teach lateral reading with real comparisons between sources, and test whether the skill holds up on unfamiliar examples.
I016.tradeoff: Training individuals cannot change every incentive in the media market.
I016.success_measure: Whether verification skills carry over to new material, and the accuracy of what people share.

problem_example.headline: Students take a Russian video as U.S. fraud evidence
problem_example.text: In a national study published in 2021, 3,446 U.S. high school students evaluated online material on the live internet. More than half believed an anonymously posted Facebook video was strong evidence of U.S. voter fraud, though it was filmed in Russia. Two-thirds could not tell news stories from ads on a popular website's home page.

source.title: Students' Civic Online Reasoning: A National Portrait

fix_example.headline: A nudge to check accuracy improves what people share
fix_example.text: In a field experiment published in 2021, researchers sent 5,379 Twitter users a private message asking them to rate the accuracy of one nonpolitical headline. Afterward, the quality of news sites they shared rose about 2% across all days and about 5% on days they tweeted.
fix_example.result: A one-question prompt raised the quality of shared news by a small amount; the study did not test lateral reading lessons.

source.title: Shifting attention to accuracy can reduce misinformation online

I017.title: Registration hurdles and roll errors keep eligible people from voting
I017.summary: Eligible people can miss an election because registering is hard or because their record was wrongly removed from the rolls. The burden falls hardest on people who move often.
I017.mechanism: Registration hurdles and flawed maintenance of voter rolls keep some eligible people from voting, and the burden falls unevenly.
I017.evidence_note: Well supported. The Brennan Center for Justice, a voting-rights research and advocacy organization, counted about 16 million voters removed from rolls nationwide between 2014 and 2016, with removal rates rising in places formerly covered by federal preclearance after Shelby County v. Holder (2013). These are removal rates. The count does not show how many removals were mistakes.
I017.remedy_note: Well supported for registration. Across seven early-adopting states, automatic voter registration raised registration by 9% to 94% after adjusting for trends, according to a Brennan Center analysis; effects on turnout are smaller and debated. As of November 2025, 24 states plus DC had automatic registration.
