I046.mechanism: Narrow exceptions in tax law and regulation give concentrated gains to a few and spread the costs thinly across many.
I046.evidence_note: Well supported. The Joint Committee on Taxation estimates federal tax expenditures, the revenue lost to special deductions, exclusions and credits, at about $2.3 trillion in fiscal year 2026. The largest items are the exclusions for retirement saving and employer health coverage and the lower rates on capital gains; the total covers broad provisions and narrow ones alike. The Government Accountability Office reported in 2012 that most tax expenditures are never evaluated.
I046.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The Government Accountability Office has published a framework for evaluating tax expenditures. Systematic review with expiry dates has never been enacted, so there is no evidence on its effect.
I046.response: Congress and agencies would publish estimates of who benefits from major tax expenditures and regulatory exemptions, and schedule unjustified preferences for review and expiry.
I046.tradeoff: Some targeted provisions correct real failures in a market.
I046.success_measure: Cost of preferences, and the share of renewals that follow an evaluation.

aimed_reforms.why: Narrows two large preferences, untaxed gains at death and lower rates on capital income.

problem_example.headline: 2004 tax holiday mostly helped a few large firms
problem_example.text: The 2004 tax law let U.S. companies bring home foreign profits at a tax rate equal to 5.25%. Only 843 of about 9,700 eligible corporations used it, and 15 firms accounted for 52% of the $312 billion returned. Studies cited by the Congressional Research Service found a rise in stock buybacks and little effect on domestic investment or jobs.

source.title: Tax Cuts on Repatriation Earnings as Economic Stimulus: An Economic Analysis (R40178)

fix_example.headline: States began requiring reviews of their tax breaks
fix_example.text: In 2015 and 2016, 13 states passed laws requiring regular evaluations of their economic development tax incentives, which together cost states billions of dollars a year. A 2017 Pew review found that lawmakers in states including Indiana and Washington changed incentives in line with what the evaluations found.
fix_example.result: Several states changed incentives after reviews, though Pew did not report how much money the changes saved.

source.title: How States Are Improving Tax Incentives for Jobs and Growth

I047.title: Residents with less time and money have less say between elections
I047.summary: People with more time, money and organizational backing take part far more often in hearings, public comments and meetings. Officials making detailed decisions hear mostly from them.
I047.mechanism: Advantages in time and money skew who takes part in public decisions between elections.
I047.evidence_note: Well supported. Schlozman, Verba and Brady (2012), drawing on surveys and a census of organizations, found that participation and organized interests tilt heavily toward affluent people and business. In Massachusetts planning and zoning meeting minutes, Einstein, Glick and Palmer (2019) found that participants were older, whiter and more likely to own homes than other residents, and mostly opposed new housing.
I047.remedy_note: Plausible. Citizen panels chosen by lottery produce more representative participants by design, according to an OECD review. Evidence that their proposals change policy comes from individual cases.
I047.response: Legislatures and foundations would fund accessible public hearings, paid citizen panels and legal help for underrepresented groups.
I047.tradeoff: Whoever selects panel members and sets the agenda can tilt the results toward the sponsor.
I047.success_measure: How representative participants are, and how many of their proposals receive an official answer.

problem_example.headline: Housing hearings drew older homeowners who opposed building
problem_example.text: Researchers coded thousands of comments residents made at local planning and zoning board meetings about housing development and matched the speakers to a voter file. Speakers were disproportionately older, male, longtime residents and homeowners, and they opposed new housing far more strongly than the general public did.

source.title: Who Participates in Local Government? Evidence from Meeting Minutes
source.publisher: Einstein, Glick and Palmer, Perspectives on Politics

fix_example.headline: Massachusetts panel of chosen voters reviewed a ballot question
fix_example.text: In 2018, a Massachusetts pilot drew 20 voters from a pool of 15,000 to mirror the state's population and review a ballot question on nurse staffing in hospitals. The panel wrote a statement for voters. It was the state's second such review, after one on marijuana in 2016.
fix_example.result: Penn State professor John Gastil's team found such statements easier to understand than summaries by election officials, and lawmakers were considering making the review an official part of state elections.

source.title: Lawmakers Consider Including 'Citizens' Statements' In The State's Voter Guide

I048.title: Court rulings limit what campaign-finance laws can do
I048.summary: Supreme Court rulings under the First Amendment have struck down many limits on political spending and contributions. Disclosure and public financing remain legal options, while broader limits would need a constitutional amendment.
I048.mechanism: Current First Amendment doctrine blocks many proposed limits on political money.
I048.evidence_note: Documented. Citizens United v. FEC (2010) allowed unlimited independent spending by corporations and unions and upheld disclosure. McCutcheon v. FEC (2014) struck down aggregate contribution limits and held that only quid pro quo corruption or its appearance justifies limits. NRSC v. FEC (June 30, 2026) struck down limits on party spending coordinated with candidates.
I048.remedy_note: Hypothesis. A constitutional amendment would be legally sufficient and has no realistic path to ratification. Disclosure and public financing remain the feasible tools.
I048.response: Congress and the states would pursue disclosure and public financing now, and separately draft a constitutional amendment authorizing reasonable limits on political money with safeguards for speech.
I048.tradeoff: Amendments are hard to pass, and vague language could give officials power to censor.
I048.success_measure: A route to enactment, review for effects on rights, and durable compliance.

aimed_reforms.why: Public financing is one of the tools current doctrine allows.
Disclosure survived Citizens United and is the other tool current doctrine allows.

problem_example.headline: Supreme Court struck down overall caps on giving
problem_example.text: In 2014, the Supreme Court struck down federal caps on the total one person could give to candidates and political committees combined in a two-year cycle. Alabama resident Shaun McCutcheon and the Republican National Committee had challenged the 2012 cap of $117,000. The 5 to 4 ruling found the caps did not serve the only government interest the Court had accepted.

source.title: McCutcheon, et al. v. FEC

fix_example.headline: New York State's match raised the share from small donors
fix_example.text: New York State began matching small donations to legislative candidates in 2024, matching the first $50 of a constituent's gift 12 to 1. In the first cycle, 328 candidates took part. A Brennan Center study found that small gifts plus matching funds made up 45% of campaign money, up from 5% in earlier cycles.
fix_example.result: In-district small donors doubled to about 50,800, and the share of money from large donors and organizations fell from 72% in 2022 to 38% in 2024.

source.title: New York Used a New Public Campaign Financing Program in 2024. How Did It Work?

I049.title: Low pay and turnover drain Congress's staff expertise
I049.summary: Committee staff have fallen by roughly a third since the 1980s, and low pay drives experienced aides out. With less knowledge in house, Congress has a harder time judging competing claims on its own.
I049.mechanism: Low pay and turnover reduce Congress's institutional knowledge and its independence when weighing claims from outside interests.
I049.evidence_note: Well supported. The Brookings Institution's Vital Statistics on Congress, compiled from official counts, shows committee staff down roughly a third since the 1980s. Hertel-Fernandez, Mildenberger and Stokes (2019) surveyed senior staff and found that they misjudge constituent opinion and rely on contacts from interest groups.
I049.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The House raised staff pay floors and caps in 2022, and no study of the effect on retention has been published.
I049.response: Congress, through its appropriations and the administration of each chamber, would raise pay and build career paths for specialist staff, expand committee capacity and publish data on retention and workload.
I049.tradeoff: More staff alone does not raise quality, so professional standards have to stay in place.
I049.success_measure: Staff tenure, and the share of legislation that receives technical review.

aimed_reforms.why: Funds congressional staff and support agencies directly, which is this record's response.

problem_example.headline: House committee staff fell by a third in a year
problem_example.text: In 1995, the House had 1,258 committee staff, down from 1,947 the year before. A Congressional Research Service count found 1,170 in 2023, a decline of 38% since 1977 and the steepest drop of any House staff category.

source.title: House of Representatives Staff Levels, 1977-2023 (R43947)

fix_example.headline: House sets its first pay floor for staff
fix_example.text: In May 2022, Speaker Nancy Pelosi set a $45,000 minimum salary for House staff, effective that September, and raised the top pay limit to $203,700. LegiStorm, a firm that tracks congressional staff, found turnover eased in 2022 and 2023, though the 2023 rate was still tied for the third-worst since at least 2001.
fix_example.result: No study has isolated the pay floor's effect, and LegiStorm's counts show turnover improving after 2022 while staying near its highest levels in two decades.

source.title: House tees up vote on union protections for staffers

I050.title: Congress's research agencies cannot keep up with technical questions
I050.summary: Questions about new technology and the federal budget can outrun the capacity of Congress's nonpartisan research agencies. Members then decide with less neutral analysis in hand.
I050.mechanism: Technology and budget questions outrun the neutral expertise available to Congress.
I050.evidence_note: Well supported. Brookings' series on congressional support-agency staffing documents the long decline in Congress's in-house capacity. The Government Accountability Office created a technology assessment team in 2019, a partial answer to the gap left when Congress closed its Office of Technology Assessment in 1995.
I050.remedy_note: Hypothesis. GAO's technology assessment team rebuilt part of the lost capacity, and its output has been measured only by counts of requests.
I050.response: Congress would expand the Congressional Research Service, the Congressional Budget Office and the Government Accountability Office, and establish a modern technology-assessment function with public methods.
I050.tradeoff: The agencies have to stay nonpartisan, and new units should avoid duplicating existing offices.
I050.success_measure: Requests completed, turnaround time, and external peer review of the work.

aimed_reforms.why: Expands support-agency capacity, including technical analysis.

problem_example.headline: Congress closes its technology research office
problem_example.text: In 1995, Congress stopped funding its Office of Technology Assessment, which had produced about 750 full studies since 1972. Lawmakers gave it $3.6 million for fiscal 1996 to close down. From 2002 to April 2020, the Government Accountability Office published 16 technology assessments.

source.title: The Office of Technology Assessment: History, Authorities, Issues, and Options (R46327)

fix_example.headline: GAO builds a larger science and technology team
fix_example.text: The Government Accountability Office's science and technology team, created in 2019, almost tripled its staff to 149 by March 2023. In that span it issued 17 in-depth technology assessments and 38 two-page Science and Tech Spotlights for Congress.
fix_example.result: The team's output is measured in counts of reports and staff, and no study has judged whether its work changes congressional decisions.

source.title: Testimony of Comptroller General Gene L. Dodaro before the House Appropriations Subcommittee on the Legislative Branch

I051.title: A few leaders decide which bills get debated
I051.summary: House and Senate leaders control floor time and which amendments get a vote, which limits committee work and open debate. Most enacted laws still pass with support from both parties.
I051.mechanism: A few leaders control access to the floor and to amendments.
I051.evidence_note: Well supported. The Bipartisan Policy Center's Healthy Congress Index tracks open and closed rules, committee activity and days in session, and finds that closed rules, which bar or limit floor amendments, dominate recent Congresses. Curry and Lee (2020) found that most enacted laws remain bipartisan, so leadership control has not produced purely partisan output.
I051.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Restoring open rules and committee markups is a choice each chamber can make. Evidence that it improves outcomes is contested, since bipartisan lawmaking persists under current practice.
I051.response: The House and Senate would change their rules to restore regular committee consideration, reasonable access to amendments and published exceptions for real emergencies.
I051.tradeoff: Unlimited amendments can become obstruction, and time limits have to be applied fairly.
I051.success_measure: Committee markups held, amendment access, and time to read bills before votes.

problem_example.headline: House leaders shut down floor amendments
problem_example.text: The House last used a fully open rule, which lets any member offer amendments on the floor, in 2014 under Speaker John Boehner. Under Speaker Nancy Pelosi from 2019 to 2023, the Rules Committee approved no open rules. In 2025 it issued 95 closed rules that barred floor amendments.

source.title: Influence Shrinks as House Limits Members' Power to Change Bills

fix_example.headline: Senate passes spending bills on time in 2018
fix_example.text: In 2018, Senate appropriators moved spending bills in what Chairman Richard Shelby called an open, bipartisan process, and the Defense and Labor-Health-Education package passed the Senate 93 to 7. Five spending bills became law that September, the most enacted on time since fiscal 1997, according to the committee.
fix_example.result: The on-time bills covered more than half of discretionary spending, and the remaining bills lapsed that December into a 35-day partial shutdown.

source.title: President Signs Defense Package into Law, Enacts Most On-Time Spending Bills in Two Decades

I052.title: The Senate filibuster lets a minority block ordinary bills
I052.summary: Most Senate bills need 60 votes to end debate, so a minority can stop measures a majority supports. Voters then have a harder time telling who could have acted and who blocked action.
I052.mechanism: Minority vetoes through the Senate's cloture rule block ordinary legislation and blur who is responsible for the result.
I052.evidence_note: Well supported. Senate records show cloture motions, votes to end debate that usually need 60 senators, rising from single digits per Congress before 1970 to 200 to 300 in recent Congresses.
I052.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The Senate changed its rules for nominations by simple majority in 2013 and 2017, which shows that rule change is feasible. The effects of a talking filibuster or a declining vote threshold are untested.
I052.response: The Senate would reform cloture with a threshold that declines over time or a majority vote on final passage, keeping protected debate and amendments for the minority.
I052.tradeoff: Protection of rights should not depend entirely on temporary majorities.
I052.success_measure: Debates completed, votes held on substance, and outcomes for rights.

aimed_reforms.why: Lets a Senate majority reach a final vote on ordinary legislation.

problem_example.headline: Background check plan wins 54 votes and fails
problem_example.text: In April 2013, a Senate amendment by Joe Manchin of West Virginia to expand gun background checks won 54 votes to 46. It failed because the Senate required three-fifths of its members, or 60 votes, to adopt it.

source.title: Roll Call Vote 113th Congress, 1st Session, Vote Number 97 (Manchin Amdt. No. 715 to S. 649)

fix_example.headline: Senate drops the 60-vote rule for nominations
fix_example.text: In November 2013, the Senate voted to let a simple majority end debate on all nominations except Supreme Court picks. In April 2017 it extended that change to the Supreme Court, and the next day it confirmed Neil Gorsuch 54 to 45.
fix_example.result: Nominations now move by simple majority, while most legislation still needs 60 votes to end debate.

source.title: Senate Proceedings Establishing Majority Cloture for Supreme Court Nominations: In Brief (R44819)

I053.title: Deadline bills bundle unrelated choices with little scrutiny
I053.summary: Congress often passes sprawling spending bills right before a deadline, combining unrelated policies in one vote. Members and the public get little time to read individual provisions.
I053.mechanism: Bills passed at crisis deadlines bundle unrelated provisions and limit scrutiny.
I053.evidence_note: Plausible. The Congressional Research Service documents the frequency and size of omnibus and consolidated appropriations acts since the 1980s. It records the practice; no source listed for this record measures how many provisions escape review.
I053.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The House has a rule requiring bill text 72 hours before a vote and often waives it. Change logs and separate votes on unrelated provisions have not been evaluated.
I053.response: Congress would set earlier committee calendars, publish readable bill texts and change logs, and hold separate recorded votes on major unrelated provisions.
I053.tradeoff: Some packages are needed to reach a bargain, so rules should avoid forcing every provision into its own bill.
I053.success_measure: Time bill text is public before votes, and riders passed without review.

aimed_reforms.why: Automatic continuing funding removes the shutdown deadline that drives last-minute bundling.

problem_example.headline: Congress passes a 5,593-page bill within hours
problem_example.text: On December 21, 2020, congressional leaders released a 5,593-page bill at 2 p.m., and both chambers passed it that night. The Associated Press reported that it joined $900 billion in pandemic relief with $1.4 trillion in yearly spending and folded in unrelated items such as new copyright rules and two Smithsonian museums.

source.title: Too big to read: Giant bill a leap of faith for Congress

fix_example.headline: Oklahoma splits a bundled law into 23 bills
fix_example.text: In June 2013, the Oklahoma Supreme Court struck down a sweeping 2009 lawsuit overhaul because it packed multiple subjects into one bill, which the state constitution forbids. Governor Mary Fallin called a five-day special session, and in September she signed 23 separate bills that rewrote the state's civil lawsuit rules.
fix_example.result: Lawmakers voted on each piece of the overhaul separately, and all 23 bills became law within three months of the ruling.

source.title: Governor Signs Special Session Bills

I054.title: Shutdown threats interrupt government services
I054.summary: When Congress misses a funding deadline, agencies close or slow down, federal workers go without pay and planning stalls. The threat of a shutdown also becomes a bargaining tool.
I054.mechanism: Lapses in appropriations damage planning, services and workers, and the threat of a lapse becomes a tool in budget negotiations.
I054.evidence_note: Documented. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the 43-day lapse in 2025, the longest on record, cut fourth-quarter growth by 1.0 to 2.0 percentage points and permanently lost $7 billion to $14 billion of output; the estimate is a scenario. The Congressional Research Service summarized the lapse's effects on services. CBO estimated that the 35-day shutdown ending in January 2019 permanently cost $3 billion of GDP.
I054.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Automatic continuing resolutions have been proposed repeatedly and never enacted. The concern that they weaken the incentive to pass budgets is theoretical.
I054.response: Congress would adopt automatic temporary funding, with rules that keep old priorities from being frozen in place, and require timely votes on budgets.
I054.tradeoff: Automatic funding can reduce the pressure to finish full-year appropriations.
I054.success_measure: Shutdown days, and full-year appropriations passed on time.

aimed_reforms.why: Continues funding at the prior level if appropriations lapse, so services do not stop.

problem_example.headline: The 2025 shutdown erases billions in output
problem_example.text: Federal funding lapsed on October 1, 2025, starting a government shutdown. On October 29, the Congressional Budget Office estimated, in scenarios lasting four to eight weeks, that the shutdown would cut fourth-quarter growth by 1.0 to 2.0 percentage points and permanently erase $7 billion to $14 billion of output.

source.title: A Quantitative Analysis of the Effects of the Government Shutdown on the Economy (as of Oct 29, 2025)

fix_example.headline: North Carolina keeps funding flowing without a budget
fix_example.text: After a long budget fight in 2015, North Carolina passed a law the following year that keeps state money flowing when lawmakers miss the budget deadline. It first kicked in on July 1, 2019, letting the state budget director fund operations at no more than the prior year's spending, with state and public school employee salaries frozen.
fix_example.result: State operations continued under the automatic funding, and by November 2019 lawmakers still had not enacted a complete budget to replace it, leaving spending and pay at old levels.

source.title: Automatic Continuing Appropriations and Government Shutdowns

I055.title: Debt-limit standoffs create a risk of default
I055.summary: Congress passes spending and tax laws, then votes separately on whether the Treasury may borrow to pay for them. Standoffs over that second vote raise borrowing costs and the risk of missed payments.
I055.mechanism: Separating borrowing authority from fiscal decisions Congress has already enacted creates default risk and extra cost.
I055.evidence_note: Documented. The Government Accountability Office estimated that the 2011 debt-limit delay raised Treasury borrowing costs by about $1.3 billion in fiscal year 2011. Fitch Ratings cited repeated debt-limit standoffs as a governance factor when it downgraded the United States to AA+ in 2023.
I055.remedy_note: Plausible. From 1979 to 1995 a House rule, known as the Gephardt rule, automatically linked borrowing authority to the budget Congress adopted. No formal evaluation of it exists.
I055.response: Congress would tie borrowing authority automatically to the spending and tax laws it enacts, and publish debt projections.
I055.tradeoff: The change leaves the underlying gap between spending and revenue untouched.
I055.success_measure: Events that raise the risk of default, and disruptions to Treasury financing.

problem_example.headline: Debt limit delay adds $1.3 billion in costs
problem_example.text: In 2011, Congress did not raise the federal debt limit until August 2, when it passed the Budget Control Act. Before then, the Treasury stayed under the limit by suspending investments of federal retirement funds. The Government Accountability Office estimated the delay raised borrowing costs by about $1.3 billion in fiscal 2011.

source.title: Debt Limit: Analysis of 2011-2012 Actions Taken and Effect of Delayed Increase on Borrowing Costs (GAO-12-701)

fix_example.headline: The House ties borrowing to its budget vote
fix_example.text: In 1979, the House adopted the Gephardt rule, which automatically produced a debt-limit bill when it passed a budget plan. Fifteen of the 20 resolutions created this way became law. The Congressional Research Service found that over 80% of the 57 debt-limit measures enacted from 1980 to 2022 still needed a separate House vote.
fix_example.result: The Congressional Research Service described the rule's role in debt-limit lawmaking as limited, and the House repealed it in 2023.

source.title: Debt Limit Legislation: The House "Gephardt Rule" (RL31913)

I056.title: Congress's demands for information can expire unanswered
I056.summary: When the executive branch resists a congressional subpoena, the court case can outlast the two-year Congress that issued it. Delay weakens oversight even when Congress has a valid claim to the information.
I056.mechanism: Slow litigation over subpoenas weakens congressional checks within a two-year Congress.
I056.evidence_note: Documented. The Congressional Research Service explains why civil enforcement of subpoenas against the executive branch routinely outlasts a Congress. In Trump v. Mazars USA (2020), the Supreme Court set a new balancing test for subpoenas of a President's records, and the records reached Congress years after the request.
I056.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Expedited civil enforcement has been proposed. Constitutional limits on standing and executive privilege remain unresolved.
I056.response: Congress, with the courts, would create expedited civil enforcement and clear standing where the Constitution allows, with procedures for privilege claims and sanctions after review.
I056.tradeoff: Disputes over executive privilege require fair adjudication.
I056.success_measure: Time to final compliance, and requests resolved.

aimed_reforms.why: Provides timely subpoena enforcement and records access when oversight is obstructed.

problem_example.headline: Fast and Furious subpoena fight outlasts several Congresses
problem_example.text: In 2012, Attorney General Eric Holder did not comply with a House Oversight Committee subpoena for documents on the Fast and Furious gun-trafficking operation, and the committee sued. A federal court ordered compliance in 2016, and in 2019 the case was still on appeal after spanning several Congresses and two presidents.
problem_example.where: Washington, D.C. (U.S. House and Justice Department)

source.title: Congressional Subpoenas: Enforcing Executive Branch Compliance (R45653)

I057.title: Programs continue without evidence of results
I057.summary: Many federal programs and tax breaks run for years without a credible check on whether they work. A 2018 law created evaluation officers, and agencies still rarely use findings when deciding renewals.
I057.mechanism: Spending and rulemaking continue without anyone learning what works.
I057.evidence_note: Documented. The Government Accountability Office reported in 2012 that most tax expenditures are never evaluated. Its 2025 High Risk List names 38 areas where government effectiveness depends on leadership, capacity, monitoring and demonstrated progress. The Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018 requires evaluation officers and learning agendas, and GAO finds implementation uneven.
I057.remedy_note: Plausible. The 2018 Evidence Act created evaluation officers and learning agendas. GAO finds uneven implementation and little use of evaluations when programs come up for renewal.
I057.response: Congress and agencies would require evaluation plans in proportion to a program's size, open administrative data to evaluators and base renewal decisions on published findings.
I057.tradeoff: Poor metrics can push aside long-term public value that is hard to measure.
I057.success_measure: Share of spending evaluated, and program changes that follow findings.

problem_example.headline: A trillion dollars in tax breaks goes unevaluated
problem_example.text: In fiscal 2011, the federal government gave up an estimated $1 trillion in revenue through 173 tax breaks. In a 2012 review, the Government Accountability Office found the executive branch had made little progress in building a way to judge whether these breaks work.

source.title: Tax Expenditures: Background and Evaluation Criteria and Questions (GAO-13-167SP)

fix_example.headline: Evidence Act sets a framework for testing programs
fix_example.text: The Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018 created a framework to strengthen the federal government's capacity to build and use evidence about whether programs work. In a 2020 survey, the Government Accountability Office found that an estimated 95% of federal managers had at least one type of evidence on their programs, and about half to two-thirds of those used it in decisions such as allocating resources.
fix_example.result: Use of evidence remains partial, and only about a third to half of managers said parts of their evidence-building capacity were present to a great or very great extent, according to GAO.

source.title: Evidence-Based Policymaking: Survey Data Identify Opportunities to Strengthen Capacity across Federal Agencies (GAO-21-536)

I058.title: Slow hiring and lost staff leave public jobs vacant
I058.summary: Federal agencies took about 101 days on average to hire someone in 2023, and in 2025 they lost more than 11% of their workforce. Vacancies hold up benefits and permits and weaken enforcement.
I058.mechanism: Vacancies in public agencies hold up permits, benefits and enforcement.
I058.evidence_note: Documented. Office of Personnel Management dashboard figures, reported by FEDmanager, put the average time to hire at 101.2 days in fiscal year 2023, up from 97.2 in 2021. Across 22 major agencies, the Government Accountability Office found that about 378,000 employees left in 2025 and headcount fell by about 256,000, more than 11%, between December 2024 and January 2026. GAO's 2025 High Risk List ties government effectiveness to agency capacity.
I058.remedy_note: Plausible. Skills-based hiring and the Chance to Compete Act are law. The loss of more than 11% of the workforce in 2025 outweighs any effect the hiring reforms could have shown.
I058.response: Congress, the Office of Personnel Management and agencies would use skills-based hiring, competitive pay for technical roles and simpler recruitment, within a protected career service that manages performance.
I058.tradeoff: Faster hiring must keep merit selection and equal opportunity.
I058.success_measure: Time to hire, service backlogs, and staff retention.

aimed_reforms.why: Protects merit hiring and career staff, which keeps expertise in agencies.

problem_example.headline: Federal agencies lose more than a tenth of staff
problem_example.text: In 2025, 22 major federal agencies lost nearly 378,000 employees and hired about 127,000, the Government Accountability Office found. Their combined workforce fell by almost 256,000, more than 11%, between December 2024 and January 2026. The Department of Education shrank by more than 45%.

source.title: Federal Agency Workforce Changes: Update for July 2025 to January 2026 (GAO-26-108583)

I059.title: Leadership turnover interrupts long-term delivery
I059.summary: Frequent changes of political leadership scatter knowledge and stop projects before they show results. Programs run by career managers have scored better on management ratings than programs run by political appointees.
I059.mechanism: Frequent leadership changes interrupt the long-term work of delivering programs.
I059.evidence_note: Well supported. Lewis (2008) found that programs run by political appointees scored lower on federal management ratings than programs run by career managers; the evidence is observational and drawn from the government's own program assessments. The Partnership for Public Service, using Office of Personnel Management data, reports the federal workforce down 12% from September 2024 to January 2026, including 136,822 deferred resignations.
I059.remedy_note: Plausible. Evidence on appointee performance supports protecting career expertise. Transition plans and limits on acting officials' terms have not been evaluated.
I059.response: Congress and agencies would protect career expertise, document decisions, and create transition plans and limits on how long acting officials can serve.
I059.tradeoff: Elected leaders keep their lawful authority to set policy direction.
I059.success_measure: Knowledge passed on at transitions, and days that leadership posts sit vacant.

aimed_reforms.why: Keeps career expertise in place through changes of political leadership.

problem_example.headline: Homeland Security cycles through acting leaders
problem_example.text: Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen resigned on April 10, 2019, a year after the deputy secretary post went vacant, and the department's management chief resigned the same day. Two acting secretaries followed within seven months. In August 2020, the Government Accountability Office found that acting secretary Chad Wolf and Ken Cuccinelli, the official performing the deputy's duties, were named under an invalid order of succession.

source.title: Department of Homeland Security: Legality of Service of Acting Secretary of Homeland Security (B-331650)

I060.title: Aging government software fails the people using it
I060.summary: Some critical federal systems are 23 to 60 years old, and about 80% of federal technology spending goes to keeping existing systems running. Old, fragmented software raises errors and paperwork and makes fraud harder to catch.
I060.mechanism: Aging, fragmented software systems raise errors, fraud and paperwork.
I060.evidence_note: Documented. A 2025 Government Accountability Office report identified 11 critical federal systems aged 23 to 60 years, seven with known security weaknesses, and found that about 80% of more than $100 billion in annual IT spending goes to operating and maintaining existing systems.
I060.remedy_note: Plausible. Modular modernization and digital service teams are practices GAO endorses. Agencies' completion rates are mixed, and no evaluation has been done at scale.
I060.response: Congress, agencies and states would fund modernization in modular stages, public-interest digital teams, open standards and independent security testing.
I060.tradeoff: Large contracts can lock in failure, so delivery should come in stages.
I060.success_measure: Share of transactions completed, system downtime, and cost per transaction.

aimed_reforms.why: Builds public teams that can replace and run agency software.

problem_example.headline: Federal agencies run critical systems up to 60 years old
problem_example.text: In July 2025, the Government Accountability Office reviewed 11 of the most critical federal legacy systems and found them 23 to 60 years old. Seven were running with known cybersecurity weaknesses, and both Treasury systems in the review ran on COBOL, a decades-old programming language. Agencies typically spend about 80% of their technology money on operating and maintaining existing systems.

source.title: Information Technology: Agencies Need to Plan for Modernizing Critical Decades-Old Legacy Systems (GAO-25-107795)

fix_example.headline: Agencies finish three of ten flagged system upgrades
fix_example.text: In June 2019, the Government Accountability Office named 10 critical federal computer systems most in need of modernization. By February 2025, agencies had completed three of those upgrades. Four more were due within a few years, and one had no completion date.
fix_example.result: Progress has been slow, with three of the 10 modernizations finished nearly six years after GAO's list.

source.title: Information Technology: Agencies Need to Plan for Modernizing Critical Decades-Old Legacy Systems (GAO-25-107795)

I061.title: Contracting rules can reward paperwork over results
I061.summary: Rigid procurement rules and weak management of contracts can drive capable suppliers away and let vendors miss useful goals. The scale of the problem has not been measured.
I061.mechanism: Rigid procurement and weak contract management deter capable suppliers and leave vendors unaccountable for results.
I061.evidence_note: Plausible. The Government Accountability Office's 2025 High Risk List covers 38 areas where effectiveness depends on leadership, capacity and monitoring, and GAO's 2025 review of legacy systems shows most technology money going to maintain old systems. Neither measures how often procurement rules cause a failure.
I061.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Outcome-based pilots are recommended practice, and no controlled evaluation has been found.
I061.response: Congress and procurement agencies would use small competitive pilots, milestones tied to outcomes, open procurement data and trained contracting officers.
I061.tradeoff: Flexibility has to keep the controls that guard against favoritism and fraud.
I061.success_measure: Range of vendors, milestones delivered, and cost overruns.

problem_example.headline: HealthCare.gov contract costs climb as site stumbles
problem_example.text: The Government Accountability Office found in 2014 that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services built HealthCare.gov without a required acquisition strategy and issued work orders before key requirements were known. Money committed to the main marketplace contract rose from $56 million in September 2011 to more than $209 million by February 2014. The site launched in October 2013 without proof that it met performance requirements.

source.title: Healthcare.gov: Ineffective Planning and Oversight Practices Underscore the Need for Improved Contract Management (GAO-14-694)

fix_example.headline: Rikers program tests paying only for results
fix_example.text: Rikers Island in New York City was home to the nation's first social impact bond, a pay-for-success deal that funded a program for jailed young people called the Adolescent Behavioral Learning Experience. In July 2015, the Vera Institute of Justice, the independent evaluator, found that the program did not reduce reoffending among participants.
fix_example.result: The independent evaluation found no drop in reoffending, the outcome the pay-for-success deal was set up to reward.

source.title: Impact Evaluation of the Adolescent Behavioral Learning Experience (ABLE) Program at Rikers Island

I062.title: Paperwork pushes eligible people off benefits
I062.summary: Repeated forms and renewal steps cause people who still qualify to lose benefits. When pandemic-era Medicaid coverage rules ended, more than 25 million people were disenrolled, 69% of them for procedural reasons.
I062.mechanism: Repeated documentation and renewal requirements cause eligible people to lose support.
I062.evidence_note: Well supported. KFF's analysis of state-reported data found that more than 25 million people were disenrolled from Medicaid when pandemic-era continuous coverage ended, 69% for procedural reasons such as missing paperwork. Herd and Moynihan's Administrative Burden (2018) synthesizes program evidence that the costs of learning about, applying for and staying in a program reduce take-up.
I062.remedy_note: Well supported. During the same Medicaid renewals, the share completed automatically from data the state already held ranged from 11% to over 90% by state, and states with high rates had fewer procedural losses. The evidence is descriptive.
I062.response: Federal and state agencies would share data with consent, renew eligibility automatically, use common applications and keep human channels for appeals.
I062.tradeoff: Automation can multiply errors, so correction routes and privacy safeguards have to stay in place.
I062.success_measure: Take-up among eligible people, wrongful denials, and time people spend on paperwork.

aimed_reforms.why: Agencies that build and run their own systems can renew eligibility from data they already hold.

problem_example.headline: Medicaid renewals cut millions over paperwork
problem_example.text: In April 2023, states resumed regular Medicaid eligibility checks as a pandemic-era rule that kept people continuously enrolled came to an end. By September 2024, more than 25 million people had been disenrolled, and KFF found 69% of them were cut for paperwork or procedural reasons.

source.title: An Examination of Medicaid Renewal Outcomes and Enrollment Changes at the End of the Unwinding

fix_example.headline: Some states renew Medicaid coverage automatically
fix_example.text: Arizona and Rhode Island completed 90% or more of their Medicaid renewals automatically during 2023 and 2024, using data the state already had, while Pennsylvania and Texas did so for 11% or less. KFF concluded that raising these automatic renewal rates can help people keep coverage.
fix_example.result: KFF ties higher automatic renewal rates to better coverage retention, though its evidence is descriptive and does not measure the effect state by state.

source.title: An Examination of Medicaid Renewal Outcomes and Enrollment Changes at the End of the Unwinding

I063.title: Overlapping federal, state and local roles leave gaps
I063.summary: When several governments share a task, they can impose conflicting rules or leave parts of it with no owner. Residents then cannot tell which office is responsible for fixing a failure.
I063.mechanism: Duplicated authority across levels of government creates gaps, conflicting requirements and shifting of blame.
I063.evidence_note: Documented. The Government Accountability Office's 2026 report on duplication, overlap and fragmentation identified 97 new actions and counted $774 billion in savings realized since 2011, with 77% of its earlier recommendations addressed.
I063.remedy_note: Plausible. GAO's consolidation actions, with $774 billion realized since 2011, show that assigning an accountable lead works in specific cases.
I063.response: Congress, governors and agencies would assign an accountable lead for each shared service, set common data standards and fund agreements between levels of government.
I063.tradeoff: National consistency has to leave room for useful local adaptation.
I063.success_measure: Delays at handoffs between agencies, and obligations left unmet.

problem_example.headline: Flint's water crisis falls between state and federal regulators
problem_example.text: In April 2014, Flint, Michigan, switched water sources for a system serving nearly 100,000 residents. Michigan's environmental agency, which supervised the system, took no formal enforcement action until August 2015. The EPA's inspector general found that management weaknesses at the federal agency, which kept oversight power, delayed its response until an emergency order in January 2016.

source.title: Management Weaknesses Delayed Response to Flint Water Crisis (Report 18-P-0221)
source.publisher: U.S. EPA Office of Inspector General

I064.title: Permitting reviews lack a predictable path to a decision
I064.summary: Federal environmental impact statements took a median of 3.5 years from 2010 to 2018, and reviews often run one after another. Coordinated schedules can speed decisions while keeping protections for communities and the environment.
I064.mechanism: Sequential reviews and thin staffing delay public investment.
I064.evidence_note: Documented. The Council on Environmental Quality found that environmental impact statements completed from 2010 to 2018 took a median of 3.5 years and a mean of 4.5 years; the data measure time and leave outcome quality unjudged. In Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County (May 29, 2025), the Supreme Court narrowed the scope of review under the National Environmental Policy Act and directed courts to defer to agencies.
I064.remedy_note: Plausible. Coordinated schedules under FAST-41 and the 2023 amendments to the National Environmental Policy Act shorten some reviews, and the Seven County ruling narrowed court review. Effects on the quality of outcomes are unmeasured.
I064.response: Congress, the states and agencies would set coordinated review schedules, staff permitting offices adequately and publish reasons for decisions, while keeping substantive environmental and community protections.
I064.tradeoff: A fast decision can still be wrong, so speed is only one measure of success.
I064.success_measure: Time to decision, litigation, and environmental outcomes.

aimed_reforms.why: Treats getting appropriated investment to actual work as part of the reform, and permitting delay is one place it stalls.

problem_example.headline: Utah rail line approval swings through the courts
problem_example.text: In December 2021, the Surface Transportation Board approved an 88-mile railroad line in northeastern Utah after an environmental impact statement of more than 3,600 pages. A federal appeals court vacated the approval in 2023, finding numerous flaws in that review. In May 2025, the Supreme Court reversed and told courts to give agencies substantial deference.

source.title: Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, No. 23-975 (opinion text)
source.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)

I065.title: Emergency powers outlast the emergency
I065.summary: Federal law gives the President about 150 special powers once a national emergency is declared, and some declared emergencies have lasted for decades. Requiring Congress to renew them would make officials justify keeping exceptional powers in force.
I065.mechanism: Broad emergency delegations let a temporary crisis justify durable policy.
I065.evidence_note: Documented. The Brennan Center's 2025 guide catalogs about 150 statutory powers that become available when a national emergency is declared, with dozens of emergencies in effect, some for decades. In Learning Resources v. Trump (February 20, 2026), the Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs; other tariff authorities need separate analysis.
I065.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Requiring an affirmative vote of Congress to renew an emergency, the model in the ARTICLE ONE Act, is untested at the federal level. The Learning Resources ruling shows that courts can police one emergency statute.
I065.response: Congress would require its own affirmative vote to renew major emergencies, along with public findings of fact and judicial review.
I065.tradeoff: Congress has to be able to act quickly in a real emergency.
I065.success_measure: Emergencies allowed to lapse without renewal, and review dates met.

aimed_reforms.why: Makes emergencies lapse unless Congress renews them.

problem_example.headline: A 1979 Iran emergency is still in force
problem_example.text: In November 1979, President Jimmy Carter declared a national emergency over Iran by executive order. Presidents of both parties have renewed it every year since, and in November 2025 it was continued again, 46 years later. Each renewal is a notice signed by the President alone.

source.title: Notice on the Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to Iran (DCPD-202501097)
source.publisher: Daily Compilation of Presidential Documents, GovInfo (U.S. Government Publishing Office)

fix_example.headline: Pennsylvania voters made the legislature renew emergencies
fix_example.text: In May 2021, Pennsylvania voters approved amendments that end a governor's emergency declaration after 21 days unless lawmakers vote to extend it. The legislature can also end one by simple majority without the governor's signature. In June 2021, lawmakers used that power to end the COVID-19 disaster declaration Governor Tom Wolf had renewed every 90 days since March 2020.
fix_example.result: The first use of the new power ended a declaration that had run about 15 months, and a Pennsylvania emergency now lapses after 21 days without a legislative vote.

source.title: Pa. legislature votes to immediately end Wolf's coronavirus disaster declaration

I066.title: Executive orders stand in for durable law
I066.summary: When Congress is gridlocked, presidents set more policy by executive order, and the next administration can reverse it. People and agencies then face rules that may change with each election.
I066.mechanism: Gridlock and broad delegation push policy into presidential directives that a later administration can reverse.
I066.evidence_note: Well supported. The American Presidency Project counts 281 executive orders in the first 1.58 years of President Trump's second term, through August 20, 2026, about 173 a year, compared with about 41 a year under President Biden. Howell (2003), combining a formal model with data from 1945 to 1998, found that unilateral presidential action rises when Congress is divided or gridlocked.
I066.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Writing purposes and limits into statutes is the direct response. No study has evaluated whether reporting requirements change how many orders are issued.
I066.response: Congress would state statutory purposes and limits, require reporting of significant executive actions and legislate durable policy through working committees. Executive agencies would file the reports.
I066.tradeoff: Many orders are lawful and necessary, so counting them alone is misleading.
I066.success_measure: Policy reversals between administrations, and clarity of statutory authority.

aimed_reforms.why: Lets a Senate majority pass statutes, so less policy has to move through executive orders.

problem_example.headline: The Mexico City Policy flips with each new party
problem_example.text: The Reagan administration announced the Mexico City Policy in 1984, requiring foreign groups that get U.S. family planning aid to agree not to perform or actively promote abortion. Each Democratic president since has rescinded it, and each Republican has restored it. Biden rescinded it in 2021, and Trump reinstated it in January 2025.

source.title: The Mexico City Policy: An Explainer

fix_example.headline: A 1973 aid limit written into law has held
fix_example.text: Congress wrote the Helms Amendment into the Foreign Assistance Act in 1973. It bars U.S. aid from paying for abortion as a method of family planning, and it is still law today. Presidents of both parties have had to follow it, while the Mexico City Policy has flipped six times.
fix_example.result: The statutory rule has stayed in force for more than 50 years under presidents of both parties, while the executive policy on the same subject was reversed six times.

source.title: The Mexico City Policy: An Explainer

I067.title: Presidential immunity narrows criminal accountability
I067.summary: In 2024 the Supreme Court held that former presidents are immune from criminal prosecution for official acts, absolutely so for core constitutional powers. A statute cannot reverse a constitutional holding, so the remaining checks are oversight, impeachment and amendment.
I067.mechanism: Immunity for official acts reduces the legal consequences for abuse of presidential authority.
I067.evidence_note: Documented. In Trump v. United States (July 1, 2024), the Supreme Court held that a former president has absolute immunity for core constitutional acts, presumptive immunity for other official acts and no immunity for unofficial acts. A statute cannot reverse a constitutional holding.
I067.remedy_note: Hypothesis. A constitutional amendment is the only route to change the holding, and there is no evidence of a path to one.
I067.response: Congress would use records preservation, impeachment and oversight through appropriations. Congress and the states would pursue a carefully drafted constitutional amendment for broader criminal accountability.
I067.tradeoff: Ordinary statutes cannot override constitutional holdings, and a president's lawful decisions still need independence.
I067.success_measure: Congress's access to records for oversight, and clarity in how courts apply the immunity.

problem_example.headline: Immunity ruling pared back the federal election case
problem_example.text: In August 2024, special counsel Jack Smith filed a slimmed-down indictment against Donald Trump in the federal 2020 election case. Prosecutors removed allegations about Trump's late-2020 effort to get the Justice Department to back his false voter fraud claims. The Supreme Court's immunity ruling had held that a president's dealings with that department are immune official acts.

source.title: New federal indictment filed against Trump in federal Jan. 6 case
source.publisher: The Washington Post, via Anchorage Daily News

fix_example.headline: A 1974 law kept Nixon's tapes in public hands
fix_example.text: In December 1974, four months after Richard Nixon resigned, President Gerald Ford signed a law directing the government to take custody of Nixon's presidential papers and tapes. The materials included about 42 million pages and 880 tape recordings. In 1977 the Supreme Court upheld the law in Nixon v. Administrator of General Services.
fix_example.result: The Court rejected Nixon's separation-of-powers and privilege challenges, so the records stayed in government custody for archivists to screen.

source.title: Nixon v. Administrator of General Services, 433 U.S. 425 (1977)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Supreme Court opinion text)

I068.title: Withholding appropriated money weakens Congress's spending decisions
I068.summary: A president can delay or withhold money Congress has appropriated, which stalls programs even when the withholding is later found unlawful. In 2025 the Government Accountability Office found several violations, and the Supreme Court let a $4 billion pocket rescission stand.
I068.mechanism: Executive withholding of appropriated funds frustrates programs Congress enacted.
I068.evidence_note: Documented. On June 16, 2025, the Government Accountability Office found that the Institute of Museum and Library Services violated the Impoundment Control Act by withholding about $78.5 million without the required message to Congress, one of several such findings in 2025. On September 26, 2025, in Department of State v. AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, a Supreme Court stay order allowed a $4 billion pocket rescission, a request to cancel funds sent so late in the fiscal year that the money expires before Congress acts. The order concluded at that stage that the private plaintiffs could not enforce the appropriation through the Administrative Procedure Act.
I068.remedy_note: Hypothesis. GAO's findings had no enforcement effect in 2025, and the Court's stay order limited private enforcement, so the proposed court remedies would need new statutory standing.
I068.response: Congress, the Government Accountability Office and the courts would enforce reporting on appropriations and provide timely court remedies. Congress would clarify agencies' spending duties and the procedure for rescissions.
I068.tradeoff: Some spending discretion is lawful and has to be distinguished from unlawful withholding.
I068.success_measure: Unlawful withholding resolved, and how quickly appropriated money is spent.

aimed_reforms.why: Enforces impoundment law so withheld money reaches the programs Congress funded.

status.text: The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 remains in force. The Government Accountability Office, which audits for Congress, found violations in several 2025 decisions, including withheld NIH grant funds (August 5, 2025) and FEMA assistance funds (September 29, 2025), and found two more on October 7, 2026, involving EPA's Community Change Grants and grants from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. On September 26, 2025 the Supreme Court, acting on an emergency application, let about $4 billion in foreign aid expire after the President proposed rescinding it so late in the fiscal year that the money lapsed before Congress acted, a move called a pocket rescission. The Court's preliminary view was that the Act likely bars grant recipients from suing under the Administrative Procedure Act to enforce the appropriation.

problem_example.headline: Library grants withheld in violation of budget law
problem_example.text: In 2025, the Institute of Museum and Library Services withheld grant funds Congress had appropriated, including terminated competitive grants its acting director put at about $78.5 million. On June 16, 2025, the Government Accountability Office concluded that the agency had violated the Impoundment Control Act by withholding the money.

source.title: Institute of Museum and Library Services: Applicability of the Impoundment Control Act (B-337375)

fix_example.headline: The 1974 budget law gave Congress the final say
fix_example.text: The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 requires a president who wants to cancel appropriated funds to send Congress a formal request. From 1974 through 2008, presidents proposed 1,178 such rescissions totaling $76 billion. Congress approved 461 of them, worth about $25 billion, or a third of the money requested.
fix_example.result: Congress enacted 39% of proposed rescissions, covering 33% of the dollars presidents asked to cancel.

source.title: Impoundment Control Act: Use and Impact of Rescission Procedures (GAO-10-320T)

I069.title: Old war authorizations support new military action
I069.summary: Congress's 2001 authorization for the use of military force still supports operations a quarter-century later without a fresh vote. In December 2025 Congress repealed the 1991 and 2002 authorizations, the first such repeal since 1971.
I069.mechanism: Outdated authorizations allow prolonged use of military force without fresh consent from Congress.
I069.evidence_note: Documented. Roll Call reported that the defense authorization law for fiscal year 2026, signed December 18, 2025, repealed the 1991 and 2002 authorizations for the use of military force. The 2001 authorization remains in effect, and war-powers resolutions on military strikes against boats failed.
I069.remedy_note: Plausible. The 1991 and 2002 repeals were the first since 1971. The 2001 authorization and strikes ordered under the President's own Article II power remain unaddressed.
I069.response: Congress would set expiry dates for obsolete authorizations, require specific votes on missions and their funding, and strengthen timely reporting.
I069.tradeoff: Operational secrecy and urgent defense require limited exceptions.
I069.success_measure: Active authorizations reviewed, and compliance with the missions Congress approved.

problem_example.headline: A 2001 war vote covered a 2014 air campaign
problem_example.text: In September 2014, the Obama administration cited the 2001 authorization for use of military force, along with the 2002 Iraq authorization, as legal authority for strikes on the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria. The 2001 law names no group, and the administration argued that the Islamic State was a successor to the al Qaeda behind the September 11 attacks.

source.title: U.S. Military Action Against the Islamic State: Answers to Frequently Asked Legal Questions (R43720)

fix_example.headline: Congress repealed two old Iraq war authorizations
fix_example.text: The defense law President Trump signed on December 18, 2025, repealed the 1991 Gulf War and 2002 Iraq War authorizations. Roll Call reported it was the first time Congress had taken back a war authorization since it repealed the Gulf of Tonkin resolution in 1971. The 2001 authorization still underpins counterterrorism operations.
fix_example.result: Two dormant authorizations are gone, while the 2001 law that covers most current operations remains in force.

source.title: Congress inches toward reclaiming war powers with AUMF repeals

I070.title: Firing and emptying watchdog offices weakens oversight
I070.summary: On January 24, 2025, at least 17 inspectors general were removed without the 30 days' notice to Congress that the law requires. A federal judge said the President almost undoubtedly broke the law but declined to reinstate them, which shows how much oversight depends on remedies.
I070.mechanism: Removals, vacancies and budget cuts impair offices that investigate the officials who appoint them.
I070.evidence_note: Documented. At least 17 inspectors general were removed on January 24, 2025 without the 30 days' advance notice to Congress that the Inspector General Act requires. In Storch v. Hegseth (D.D.C., September 24, 2025), the judge said the President 'almost undoubtedly' violated the Act and denied reinstatement; the case was stayed pending Slaughter, and no ruling on the merits had been found as of October 14, 2026. The statute requires notice to Congress and gives inspectors general no fixed tenure.
I070.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The notice requirement was violated and the court declined reinstatement. The proposed remedies, covering records, acting succession and budget transparency, are untested.
I070.response: Congress, the courts and the Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency would enforce notice and stated reasons for removal, protect records and acting succession, make watchdog budgets transparent and provide fast remedies.
I070.tradeoff: Trump v. Slaughter (2026) ended tenure protection for FTC commissioners, so safeguards for inspectors general need their own legal analysis; notice duties and budget protections give no equivalent of tenure.
I070.success_measure: How long watchdog posts stay vacant, and recommendations acted on.

aimed_reforms.why: Gives inspectors general working remedies (reinstatement, records, budget, subpoena enforcement) when oversight is resisted.

status.text: On January 24, 2025 at least 17 inspectors general were removed by email without the 30 days' notice to Congress that the Inspector General Act requires. Eight of them sued (Storch v. Hegseth, U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia). On September 24, 2025 the court said the President almost undoubtedly violated the Act, but it denied reinstatement, because the President could remove them again after giving notice, and it paused the case until the Supreme Court decided Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026). In July 2026 the court set a process for summary-judgment motions, with a conference planned for the week of August 24, 2026. The latest docket entry listed, a July 20, 2026 minute order, shows no ruling on the merits.

problem_example.headline: State Department went years without a confirmed watchdog
problem_example.text: The State Department had no Senate-confirmed inspector general for about five and a half years before Steve Linick took the job in 2013. Foreign Policy reported it was the longest such gap in any federal department at the time. A senior department official served as interim watchdog throughout, a period spanning Hillary Clinton's entire tenure as secretary.

source.title: Stopping the Rot at Foggy Bottom, From Benghazi to Afghanistan's Missing Millions

fix_example.headline: A 2022 law demanded reasons for removing watchdogs
fix_example.text: A law signed in December 2022 requires a president to give Congress 30 days' notice and detailed, case-specific reasons before removing an inspector general. President Biden's two 2024 notices cited outside investigations as reasons. In January 2025, more than a dozen inspectors general were removed without that notice, and a federal judge later said the law was almost undoubtedly violated but declined to reinstate them.
fix_example.result: The rule shaped the 2024 removals; after the January 2025 removals it produced a court finding of a likely violation with no reinstatement.

source.title: Removal of Inspectors General: The First Tests of New Statutory Requirements (IN12363)

I071.title: Fear of retaliation keeps government insiders silent
I071.summary: Government employees who see wrongdoing may stay quiet when reporting it could cost them their careers. Protected channels work only if retaliation gets a timely remedy.
I071.mechanism: Insiders stay silent when lawful reporting threatens their careers. No source measures how often retaliation happens.
I071.evidence_note: Plausible. The U.S. Office of Special Counsel's annual reports give caseloads for prohibited personnel practices and whistleblower disclosures, with no estimate of how common retaliation is. The grade rests on institutional consensus.
I071.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Interim relief and access to counsel have been proposed. Caseload data exist, with no estimate of prevalence or deterrence.
I071.response: Congress, inspectors general and the courts would strengthen protected reporting channels, interim relief while a case proceeds, access to counsel and enforceable remedies against retaliation.
I071.tradeoff: Disclosures involving classified information need secure, lawful channels.
I071.success_measure: Retaliation cases resolved, and follow-up on disclosures found to be substantiated.

aimed_reforms.why: Inspectors general are a main channel for protected disclosures, and remedies that work make the channel usable.

problem_example.headline: An air marshal's whistleblower case took nine years
problem_example.text: In 2003, federal air marshal Robert MacLean told an MSNBC reporter that the TSA had canceled overnight missions from Las Vegas soon after a hijacking threat briefing. The TSA fired him in April 2006 for disclosing sensitive security information. In January 2015, the Supreme Court ruled that his disclosure was not excluded from whistleblower protection.

source.title: Department of Homeland Security v. MacLean, 574 U.S. 383 (2015)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Supreme Court opinion text)

I072.title: Unpredictable Supreme Court vacancies raise the stakes of each appointment
I072.summary: Justices serve for life, so the timing of deaths and retirements decides how many appointments each president gets. Recent confirmations have passed by near party-line votes.
I072.mechanism: Lifetime appointments make vacancies unpredictable, so each one becomes a high-stakes contest.
I072.evidence_note: Well supported. U.S. Senate records show recent Supreme Court confirmations passing by margins of 52 to 48, 50 to 48 and 53 to 47, close to party lines. The 2021 Presidential Commission on the Supreme Court reviewed proposals for term limits and for adding seats.
I072.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Eighteen-year terms are widely proposed and untested. The 2021 Presidential Commission found that putting them in place by statute is constitutionally uncertain.
I072.response: Congress and the states would compare regular 18-year Supreme Court terms, with transition rules, against amendment options, and publish standards for selecting nominees.
I072.tradeoff: Term limits set by statute are constitutionally disputed, and adding seats to the Court can set off escalation.
I072.success_measure: Predictable appointments, and the Court's legitimacy and independence.

aimed_reforms.why: Regular 18-year terms give each presidential term two appointments, removing the role of chance vacancies.

problem_example.headline: One president got no picks, another got three
problem_example.text: The Senate's list of Supreme Court nominations since 1789 shows none from President Jimmy Carter. Donald Trump's three nominees were confirmed in 2017, 2018 and 2020 by margins of two to nine votes. Barack Obama's 2016 nominee, Merrick Garland, received no Senate action and no vote.

source.title: Supreme Court Nominations (1789-present)

fix_example.headline: Germany's top court judges serve one 12-year term
fix_example.text: Germany's Federal Constitutional Court has 16 justices, and each one leaves after a single 12-year term or at age 68, with no second term allowed. Half are elected by the Bundestag and half by the Bundesrat, and every pick needs a two-thirds majority in the electing body.
fix_example.result: Terms end on a fixed schedule and each pick needs a two-thirds vote; the source does not measure any effect on how contested appointments are.

source.title: Organisation (The Federal Constitutional Court)

I073.title: Supreme Court ethics complaints have no independent review
I073.summary: The Supreme Court adopted a code of conduct in 2023, and no outside body enforces it for the justices. When a court polices itself, complaints and conflicts can go unresolved.
I073.mechanism: Self-policing leaves judicial conflicts and complaints unresolved.
I073.evidence_note: Documented. The Supreme Court adopted a Code of Conduct on November 13, 2023; it creates no independent process to decide complaints or enforce the code. Fix the Court, an advocacy group, reported in 2025 that the code remains unenforced, that the Judicial Conference dropped a referral concerning Justice Thomas, and that the Supreme Court Ethics, Recusal and Transparency Act had not been enacted.
I073.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Independent complaint processes exist for the lower federal courts. Extending one to the Supreme Court has been proposed and not enacted.
I073.response: The Supreme Court, or Congress, would publish reasons for recusals, review disclosures and create an independent complaint process consistent with judicial independence.
I073.tradeoff: A 2023 code already exists, and enforcement procedures have to avoid giving either party control over cases.
I073.success_measure: Completeness of disclosures, and how complaints are resolved.

aimed_reforms.why: Adds an enforceable ethics process for the justices.

problem_example.headline: A justice took undisclosed luxury trips for two decades
problem_example.text: In April 2023, ProPublica reported that Justice Clarence Thomas had accepted luxury trips from Dallas businessman Harlan Crow virtually every year for more than two decades without reporting them on his annual financial disclosures. Experts told ProPublica the law required disclosure of private jet flights. The article said the Supreme Court is left almost entirely to police itself, and Thomas publicly defended the trips.

source.title: Clarence Thomas and the Billionaire

fix_example.headline: Lower federal judges face a formal complaint process
fix_example.text: The federal courts' Table S-22 counts misconduct complaints against judges under 28 U.S.C. 351-364. In the year ending September 30, 2025, people filed 1,857 complaints. Chief circuit judges dismissed 1,700 in whole or in part, and three complaints were referred to special committees.
fix_example.result: In the same year, four complaints ended with voluntary corrective action, and none led to censure, reprimand, suspension of assignments or any other remedial action.
fix_example.where: U.S. federal courts below the Supreme Court

source.title: Table S-22: Complaints Filed and Action Taken Under 28 U.S.C. 351-364 (12 months ending September 30, 2025)
source.publisher: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts

I074.title: Litigants can pick their judge by filing in one-judge divisions
I074.summary: In federal divisions with a single judge, a party filing a case knows who will hear it, even in cases with national effects. Random assignment across a whole district removes that choice.
I074.mechanism: Single-judge divisions let litigants predict who will hear cases with national consequences.
I074.evidence_note: Documented. On March 12, 2024, the Judicial Conference issued guidance calling for district-wide random assignment of cases seeking statewide or nationwide relief. The guidance is not binding; districts kept discretion and some declined.
I074.remedy_note: Plausible. The 2024 guidance calls for district-wide assignment. It binds no district, and some declined to follow it.
I074.response: The federal judiciary, or Congress by statute, would require district-wide random assignment for broad challenges to public law and publish audits of assignments.
I074.tradeoff: Rural residents' access to court and legitimate specialized case management need protection.
I074.success_measure: Rate of predictable assignments, and exceptions found in audits.

problem_example.headline: A one-judge Waco court drew patent suits
problem_example.text: In Waco, Texas, the only judge in a single-judge federal division began drawing patent lawsuits, which the Brennan Center says he courted. Because one judge sat there, filers knew who would hear their cases. Senators Thom Tillis, a Republican, and Patrick Leahy, a Democrat, complained to the Judicial Conference that such judge shopping creates an appearance of impropriety.

source.title: Judge Shopping, Explained

fix_example.headline: Judges urged district-wide assignment, and some districts agreed
fix_example.text: In March 2024, the Judicial Conference issued nonbinding guidance that district courts should use district-wide assignment for civil cases seeking statewide or national relief. Federal districts in six states, including Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, changed their case-assignment rules to comply. The Northern District of Texas, which includes the one-judge Amarillo division, quickly said it would not follow the guidance.
fix_example.result: Because the guidance is not binding, it changed practice only in districts that chose to adopt it.

source.title: Judge Shopping, Explained

I075.title: Some major emergency orders come without written reasons
I075.summary: The Supreme Court decides emergency applications quickly, before full briefing, and some of those orders have large effects. Of 30 applications on Trump administration actions decided since January 2025, 7 came without a majority's written reasoning.
I075.mechanism: Interim rulings with large consequences are decided without full briefing, and a minority of them carry no majority reasoning.
I075.evidence_note: Documented. The Brennan Center's tracker counts 30 emergency applications concerning Trump administration actions decided from January 20, 2025 through September 8, 2026; 23 favored the administration and 7 lacked majority reasoning. Vladeck's The Shadow Docket (2023) traces the growth of emergency orders and unexplained rulings; it is scholarly and argues a position.
I075.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Written reasons by default are a choice the Court can make for itself. Majority reasoning appeared in 23 of 30 cases, so the gap is partial and shrinking.
I075.response: The Supreme Court and the federal appellate courts would give written reasons by default, publish standards for emergency relief and expedite full review where feasible.
I075.tradeoff: A real emergency may need an immediate short order, with the explanation to follow.
I075.success_measure: Share of emergency orders with reasons, and time to full review on the merits.

problem_example.headline: An unexplained order paused a ruling against Alabama's map
problem_example.text: On February 7, 2022, the Supreme Court stayed a lower court's preliminary injunctions against Alabama's congressional map in a brief order with no majority reasoning. A concurrence said the stay was not a decision on the merits and that, if the lower court were upheld, its order could take effect for elections after 2022. Four justices dissented.

source.title: Merrill v. Milligan, No. 21A375 (stay order and separate opinions)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Supreme Court text)

fix_example.headline: The Court heard argument before ruling on a vaccine rule
fix_example.text: In January 2022, the Supreme Court heard expedited oral argument on emergency applications against the Biden administration's workplace vaccine-or-test rule. Six days after the January 7 argument, it issued an unsigned opinion explaining why it stayed the rule, along with a written concurrence and dissent.
fix_example.result: The ruling came with the majority's reasoning in writing six days after argument.

source.title: National Federation of Independent Business v. Department of Labor, OSHA, No. 21A244
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Supreme Court text)

I076.title: Enforcing your rights depends on what you can pay
I076.summary: Court fees and a shortage of legal help keep many people from pursuing valid claims. Low-income Americans get no or inadequate help for 92% of their civil legal problems.
I076.mechanism: Fees, shortages of lawyers and delay keep people from enforcing their rights.
I076.evidence_note: Documented. The Legal Services Corporation's 2022 survey found that low-income Americans received no or inadequate legal help for 92% of their civil legal problems.
I076.remedy_note: Plausible. Randomized evidence on the value of a lawyer is mixed: Greiner and Pattanayak (2012) found that offers of counsel did not change outcomes in one setting, and effects vary by forum. Funding legal aid is supported for eviction and some benefit cases.
I076.response: Congress, the states and the courts would fund public defense and civil legal aid, simplify procedures and provide fee waivers and remote access.
I076.tradeoff: Simpler procedures still have to deliver fair process and reliable decisions.
I076.success_measure: Litigants without representation, delays, and rights enforced.

problem_example.headline: Most civil legal problems of low-income people go unaided
problem_example.text: In 2022, the Legal Services Corporation and NORC at the University of Chicago surveyed about 5,000 adults about civil legal problems. Low-income Americans got no legal help, or not enough, for 92% of the civil legal problems they faced.

source.title: The Justice Gap: The Unmet Civil Legal Needs of Low-income Americans

I077.title: Vague laws shift policy disputes to the courts
I077.summary: When a statute leaves an agency's authority unclear, courts now decide what it means without deferring to the agency. Clear purposes and limits written into law make responsibility easier to see.
I077.mechanism: Ambiguous statutes, combined with changed judicial doctrine, make agencies' authority to carry out laws unstable.
I077.evidence_note: Documented. Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (June 28, 2024) overruled Chevron deference: courts interpret statutes independently, while lawful delegations and agency expertise still count. The Congressional Research Service has analyzed the ruling's implications for agency rules and pending cases.
I077.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Explicit delegations are the direct response, and there is no evidence yet on whether drafting has changed since Loper Bright.
I077.response: Congress would draft explicit delegations, standards and review clauses and invest in legislative counsel. Agencies would build stronger evidentiary records for their rules.
I077.tradeoff: Loper Bright leaves room for agency discretion that Congress grants clearly.
I077.success_measure: Rules upheld in court, time taken to clarify disputed authority, and certainty in implementation.

problem_example.headline: Broadband rules flipped three times before a court decided
problem_example.text: The Federal Communications Commission classified broadband as a telecommunications service in 2015 under President Obama, then reversed course in 2018 under President Trump.
