It switched back in 2024 under President Biden. On January 2, 2025, the Sixth Circuit set aside the 2024 rule, reading the Communications Act for itself and giving the agency no deference.

source.title: Ohio Telecom Association v. FCC (In re MCP No. 185), Nos. 24-7000 et al.
source.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit

fix_example.headline: Congress settled tobacco authority with an explicit law
fix_example.text: In 2000, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 that Congress had not given the Food and Drug Administration authority to regulate tobacco. Nine years later, Congress passed the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act, signed June 22, 2009, which expressly gives the FDA authority to regulate how tobacco products are made and marketed.
fix_example.result: The FDA has regulated tobacco under the explicit grant since 2009, including a ban on cigarettes with flavors other than menthol and tobacco.

source.title: Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act - An Overview

I078.title: Policing and court fees impose unequal burdens
I078.summary: When local governments rely on fines and fees for revenue, enforcement can fall hardest on residents least able to pay. Debts, arrests and convictions then cost people wealth and, after a felony, the right to vote.
I078.mechanism: Policing, punishment and financial penalties impose unequal costs on wealth and civic participation.
I078.evidence_note: Documented. The Justice Department's 2015 investigation of the Ferguson, Missouri police department found that enforcement driven by revenue fell disproportionately on Black residents; the findings cover one jurisdiction. The Brennan Center found in 2019 that fees and fines in three states cost more to collect than expected and burdened poor residents. The Sentencing Project, an advocacy group, estimated that about 4.0 million people were barred from voting by a felony conviction in 2024.
I078.remedy_note: Plausible. Reforms of fines and fees have descriptive support, since collection costs exceed revenue in some places. Review of a person's ability to pay has no outcome evaluation.
I078.response: States, the Justice Department and local governments would reform fines and fees, review ability to pay, address discriminatory enforcement through independent accountability and fund public defense.
I078.tradeoff: Public safety and individual rights both have to be measured.
I078.success_measure: Disparities in enforcement, victimization rates, and wrongful detention.

problem_example.headline: Ferguson leaned on fines that fell hardest on Black people
problem_example.text: The Justice Department's 2015 investigation found that Ferguson, Missouri, expected fines and fees to bring in $3.09 million of its projected $13.26 million in general fund revenue, and that leaders pressed officers to write citations. From 2012 to 2014, Black people, about two-thirds of the population, made up 93% of arrests.

source.title: Investigation of the Ferguson Police Department
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division

fix_example.headline: Texas moved to restore licenses lost over unpaid fines
fix_example.text: In 2019, Texas lawmakers passed H.B. 2048, which the Brennan Center said would reinstate hundreds of thousands of driver's licenses suspended over unpaid fees and fines. In the Texas and New Mexico counties Brennan studied, the counties spent more than 41 cents of every fee and fine dollar on court hearings and jailing alone.
fix_example.result: The law was projected to restore hundreds of thousands of licenses; the source does not report a final count.

source.title: The Steep Costs of Criminal Justice Fees and Fines

I079.title: Discrimination still limits equal rights and opportunity
I079.summary: Unequal treatment by race, sex or disability still keeps people from jobs and other opportunities. Field experiments show that hiring discrimination against Black applicants has not declined since 1989.
I079.mechanism: Unequal treatment by race, sex and disability limits rights and opportunity.
I079.evidence_note: Well supported. A meta-analysis of 28 field experiments (Quillian and colleagues, 2017) found that the gap in employer callbacks between white and Black applicants with matched resumes has not changed since 1989. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission received 88,531 charges in fiscal year 2024; charges are allegations.
I079.remedy_note: Plausible. Civil-rights enforcement is established. Audit studies show hiring discrimination unchanged over three decades, so enforcement alone has not moved the baseline.
I079.response: Congress, the Justice Department, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the states would enforce civil-rights law, audit access and outcomes, and fund remedies that work, with due process.
I079.tradeoff: Unlawful discrimination has to be distinguished from every observed disparity.
I079.success_measure: Discrimination findings that hold up on review, and gaps in access.

problem_example.headline: Boston and Chicago employers favored white-sounding names
problem_example.text: In Boston and Chicago, economists Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan answered newspaper help-wanted ads with fictitious resumes, publishing the results in 2003. Resumes with white-sounding names got 50 percent more callbacks than otherwise similar ones with Black-sounding names. Federal contractors and employers advertising as equal opportunity employers discriminated as much as others.

source.title: Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination (NBER Working Paper 9873)

fix_example.headline: Black economic gains followed the 1964 civil rights law
fix_example.text: In a 1991 study, economists John Donohue and James Heckman found that from 1920 to 1990, Black Americans saw only two periods of relative economic improvement. The second came in the years after the 1964 Civil Rights Act and federal enforcement on government contractors began. Gains in schooling could not explain how large that progress was.
fix_example.result: The authors tie the mid-1960s gains to federal civil rights policy in general and do not isolate the effect of any single provision.

source.title: Continuous Versus Episodic Change: The Impact of Civil Rights Policy on the Economic Status of Blacks (NBER Working Paper 3894)

I080.title: Surveillance and coercive powers can deter lawful speech and protest
I080.summary: People may avoid speaking, searching online or protesting when they fear being watched or targeted by intelligence, immigration or police powers. The size of the effect depends on the power and the setting.
I080.mechanism: Broad intelligence, immigration or policing authority deters lawful speech and assembly.
I080.evidence_note: Plausible. Using an interrupted time series, Penney (2016) found that traffic to terrorism-related Wikipedia articles fell after the 2013 disclosures about government surveillance. The Brennan Center summarizes Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court findings of about 278,000 improper queries of Section 702 data in 2020 and 2021. Section 702 expired on June 12, 2026.
I080.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Warrant and minimization requirements were debated during the 2026 reauthorization, which ended with Section 702 lapsing on June 12, 2026. No evidence shows whether reforms reverse a chilling effect.
I080.response: Congress, the courts and agencies would require warrants where the Constitution calls for them, limit retention and use of collected data, provide independent review and offer accessible remedies for abuse.
I080.tradeoff: Real security needs require narrow exceptions that courts can review.
I080.success_measure: Unlawful surveillance found, access to protest, and use of remedies.

problem_example.headline: FBI searched surveillance data for protesters and donors
problem_example.text: The Brennan Center reports that the FBI ran warrantless searches of data gathered under Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act to reach communications of Black Lives Matter protesters. Other searches reached U.S. government officials and 19,000 donors to a single congressional campaign.

source.title: Section 702 of FISA: 2026 Resource Page

fix_example.headline: FBI query limits cut searches of Americans sharply
fix_example.text: In 2021, the FBI began requiring agents to opt in before searching Section 702 data and to get attorney approval for batch jobs of 100 or more queries. In 2022 it added approvals for sensitive searches. Estimated FBI searches for U.S. persons fell from about 3.4 million in the year to November 2021 to about 204,000 a year later.
fix_example.result: Under the original counting method, estimated U.S. person queries dropped about 94% in one year, though ODNI does not say the changes alone caused the decline.

source.title: Annual Statistical Transparency Report Regarding the Intelligence Community's Use of National Security Surveillance Authorities, Calendar Year 2022
source.publisher: Office of the Director of National Intelligence

I081.title: Fewer real competitors let firms raise prices
I081.summary: When a market has few credible sellers, firms gain room to raise prices or cut quality. How much power concentration creates depends on the market and on how easily new rivals can enter.
I081.mechanism: Markets with fewer effective sellers let firms raise prices and reduce quality or innovation.
I081.evidence_note: Well supported. De Loecker, Eeckhout and Unger (2020) found average markups over cost rising from about 21% in 1980 to 61% in 2016, using firm-level data; markups are a different measure from concentration, and their method is debated. Kwoka's 2015 review of merger retrospectives found price increases after most studied mergers, in a sample weighted toward industries with usable price data. Berry, Gaynor and Scott Morton (2019) explain why national trends alone fall short of proving market power and support analysis market by market.
I081.remedy_note: Well supported. Retrospective studies show price increases after mergers the agencies cleared, which supports stronger review. The 2023 Merger Guidelines lower the thresholds at which a merger is presumed harmful; they are nonbinding. No study evaluates better-funded litigation as a package.
I081.response: Congress, the Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission and the states would fund merger review and monopolization cases that examine relevant markets, barriers to entry and actual conduct.
I081.tradeoff: Concentration is a warning sign; on its own it proves neither illegality nor inefficiency.
I081.success_measure: Prices, new entry, quality, and remedies that can be enforced.

aimed_reforms.why: Blocks or unwinds mergers that raise prices, keeping a second seller in the market.

problem_example.headline: Beer prices jumped after the MillerCoors deal
problem_example.text: In June 2008, SABMiller and Molson Coors combined their U.S. beer operations into a joint venture called MillerCoors. A 2017 study in Econometrica found retail beer prices rose sharply soon after at both MillerCoors and its main rival, Anheuser-Busch. The authors estimated prices ran 6 to 8% above what ordinary competition between the brewers would produce.

source.title: Understanding the Price Effects of the MillerCoors Joint Venture (Miller and Weinberg)

fix_example.headline: Courts blocked the Kroger and Albertsons grocery merger
fix_example.text: In December 2024, a federal judge in Oregon blocked Kroger's $24.6 billion purchase of Albertsons after the Federal Trade Commission, seven states and the District of Columbia sued. Judge Adrienne Nelson wrote that "the proposed merger would remove that competition," and a Washington state judge separately blocked the deal. Albertsons ended the merger agreement the next day and sued Kroger.
fix_example.result: Albertsons terminated the deal, so the two chains stayed separate rivals.

source.title: Oregon judge blocks merger of Kroger and Albertsons

I082.title: Strings of small acquisitions build local dominance
I082.summary: A company can buy competitors one at a time in deals too small to require reporting to antitrust agencies. Together the purchases can leave a local market with few alternatives.
I082.mechanism: Firms build local dominance through many acquisitions that each fall below federal reporting thresholds.
I082.evidence_note: Well supported. Wollmann (2019) found that when Congress raised the premerger reporting threshold in 2001, unreported mergers between competitors rose sharply, using a nationwide quasi-experimental design. Since February 10, 2025, the revised federal premerger notification form has required firms to disclose prior acquisitions in the same lines of business.
I082.remedy_note: Plausible. The 2024 notification form change and section 2.8 of the 2023 Merger Guidelines provide for reviewing a series of acquisitions together, and no outcome evaluation exists yet. Wollmann's research on dialysis found that unreported roll-ups raised patient mortality, which supports the case for review.
I082.response: Congress and the antitrust agencies would add related acquisitions together for reporting and review, and monitor roll-up strategies and their local effects.
I082.tradeoff: Review should not swamp small, legitimate transactions.
I082.success_measure: Combined market shares after serial deals, roll-ups reviewed, and new entry.

aimed_reforms.why: Merger enforcement that counts related deals together reaches roll-ups below reporting thresholds.

problem_example.headline: A Texas anesthesia roll-up drew a federal lawsuit
problem_example.text: In 2023, the Federal Trade Commission sued U.S. Anesthesia Partners, alleging the group spent a decade buying up nearly every large anesthesia practice in Texas. The agency alleged the strategy cost Texans tens of millions of dollars more each year for anesthesia care. In April 2026, the FTC announced a preliminary settlement that it says will restore a competitive market if carried out.

source.title: FTC Charts Path to Restore Competition in Texas Anesthesia Markets in USAP Litigation

fix_example.headline: A wider merger filing form was struck down
fix_example.text: The FTC's expanded merger filing form, in effect since February 2025, required companies being bought, not only buyers, to describe their relevant earlier acquisitions. On February 12, 2026, Judge Jeremy Kernodle in the Eastern District of Texas vacated the rule, agreeing the agency had not shown its benefits outweighed its "significant and widespread costs."
fix_example.result: The judge delayed the rollback seven days to allow an emergency appeal to the Fifth Circuit, and the FTC said it was reviewing the ruling and weighing its options.
fix_example.where: Federal (U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Texas)

source.title: Federal judge vacates FTC's expanded premerger notification requirements

I083.title: A firm that controls one stage can block rivals at the next
I083.summary: A company that owns an essential supplier or distribution route can favor its own operations and deny rivals access. Integration can also cut costs, so the net effect depends on the case.
I083.mechanism: A firm that controls an adjacent stage of production can favor itself or block rivals' access.
I083.evidence_note: Well supported. In April 2025 a federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia found that Google unlawfully tied its publisher ad server to its ad exchange and monopolized both; the remedies ordered on September 2, 2026 regulate conduct and require no divestiture. Crawford and colleagues (2018) found that vertical integration in cable television both lowered costs and foreclosed rival networks, with the net effect varying by case. Salop (2018) argues for stronger vertical enforcement in a legal and economic essay that offers no new empirical evidence.
I083.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Structural separation has one large precedent, the 1984 breakup of AT&T, and no modern platform test. In both Google cases in 2025 and 2026, courts chose conduct remedies, so evidence on when separation should replace conduct rules is limited.
I083.response: Congress, the agencies and the courts would apply nondiscrimination and access rules where justified, and separate the businesses structurally when conduct remedies fall short.
I083.tradeoff: Integration can reduce costs, so harm has to be established and the costs of each remedy compared.
I083.success_measure: Rivals' access to the integrated stage, and costs to patients or customers.

aimed_reforms.why: Merger enforcement covers vertical deals that would give one firm control of a rival's supplier or outlet.

problem_example.headline: Google tied its ad tools together, a court found
problem_example.text: A federal court found that Google unlawfully tied its ad server for website publishers, DFP, to its own ad exchange, AdX, where online ads are bought and sold. In September 2026, Judge Leonie Brinkema ordered six years of conduct rules, including making DFP work with rival exchanges, and rejected a request to make Google sell AdX and DFP.

source.title: A Deep Dive Into the Antitrust Remedies That Spared Google's Ad Tech Business

fix_example.headline: The AT&T breakup split local lines from long distance
fix_example.text: Under a 1982 antitrust decree, AT&T split off its local telephone monopolies, which held 80 to 85% of U.S. access lines, from its long-distance business. Long-distance rates fell afterward, though Brookings economist Robert Crandall argued in 2007 that federal cuts in the access charges carriers paid drove most of the decline.
fix_example.result: Rates fell and long-distance competition grew, but the breakup's own role is debated; Crandall cited an analysis suggesting that adjusting to the decree cost $5 billion in lost productivity in 1984 and 1985.

source.title: The AT&T Divestiture: Was It Necessary? Was It a Success? (Crandall, presentation at the Justice Department)
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Antitrust Division (archive)

I084.title: Drug middlemen can profit from high list prices and their own pharmacies
I084.summary: Pharmacy benefit managers negotiate drug coverage for insurers and employers, and their rebates and fees can reward high list prices and steer patients to pharmacies they own. A 2026 federal law sets new rules that take effect starting in 2028.
I084.mechanism: Pharmacy benefit managers' fee, rebate and steering arrangements can set their own interests, and those of their affiliated pharmacies, against the interests of patients and of the employers and plans that pay for drugs.
I084.evidence_note: Documented. The Federal Trade Commission's second interim staff report (January 2025) found that, for 51 specialty generic drugs from 2017 to 2022, pharmacies affiliated with the three largest pharmacy benefit managers took in $7.3 billion above estimated acquisition cost; the figure is revenue before other costs, reported by agency staff without a court ruling. The first interim report (July 2024) documented steering to affiliates and spread pricing. In a 2024 administrative complaint, the FTC alleged that the companies inflated insulin costs, citing Humalog's list price rising from about $21 in 1999 to over $274 in 2017; the case moved to settlement in 2026.
I084.remedy_note: Plausible. In Rutledge v. Pharmaceutical Care Management Association (December 2020), the Supreme Court ruled that the federal law governing employer benefit plans does not stop Arkansas from regulating the rates pharmacy benefit managers pay pharmacies. The federal provisions are enacted and not yet in effect, so no evidence on their effects exists. As of October 15, 2026 the FTC's insulin case against the largest pharmacy benefit managers has produced no final order, so there are no outcome data.
I084.response: Congress, the states, the Federal Trade Commission and plan sponsors would carry out and audit the pharmacy benefit provisions of Public Law 119-75 as they phase in: Medicare Part D fee and pass-through rules from January 1, 2028, an any-willing-pharmacy rule from 2029, and pass-through for employer plans in plan years beginning on or after August 3, 2028. Remaining conflicts over affiliate steering and reimbursement would be handled through purchasing rules and enforcement, with structural separation considered only on a developed record.
I084.tradeoff: Federal authority differs between employer plans under ERISA and Medicare, and removing rebates alone may raise premiums.
I084.success_measure: Net drug cost, patients' out-of-pocket cost, and access to pharmacies.

aimed_reforms.why: Targets the rebate, fee and steering conflicts of pharmacy benefit managers directly.

status.text: Partly enacted. Public Law 119-75 (February 3, 2026) sets Medicare drug-plan fee and rebate pass-through rules from January 1, 2028, Medicare pharmacy contract standards from January 1, 2029, and rebate pass-through for employer plans for plan years beginning on or after August 3, 2028. In the Federal Trade Commission's insulin case, the docket showed no final order as of October 15, 2026. Express Scripts' proposed consent order dates from February 4, 2026 and Caremark's from July 14, 2026 (public comments closed September 4). The Optum Rx case was withdrawn from adjudication on June 12, 2026 so the Commission could consider a proposed settlement, which had not been published.

problem_example.headline: Middlemen's own pharmacies earned billions on specialty generics
problem_example.text: In January 2025, Federal Trade Commission staff reported that pharmacies tied to the three largest pharmacy benefit managers took in $7.3 billion more than the drugs' estimated acquisition cost on specialty generic drugs from 2017 to 2022. The drugs included treatments for cancer and HIV, with markups of hundreds and thousands of percent.

source.title: FTC Releases Second Interim Staff Report on Prescription Drug Middlemen

fix_example.headline: Two drug middlemen settled the FTC insulin case
fix_example.text: In July 2026, the drug middleman Caremark agreed to a proposed Federal Trade Commission order resolving the agency's insulin case, after Express Scripts reached a similar deal in February. Caremark must offer plans a standard option that passes rebates to patients at the pharmacy counter and keep programs that cap members' out-of-pocket insulin costs.
fix_example.result: The FTC estimates the deal locks in up to $8.5 billion in consumer savings over 10 years; the order was proposed for public comment and no results have been measured.

source.title: FTC Secures Major Settlement with Caremark Resolving Antitrust Case Against Second Drug Middleman

I085.title: Hospital mergers raise the prices insurers and employers pay
I085.summary: When nearby hospitals merge, they gain bargaining power over insurers and charge more. Employer plans paid hospitals about 254% of Medicare rates in 2022.
I085.mechanism: Hospital and insurer consolidation raises negotiated prices through local bargaining power.
I085.evidence_note: Well supported. Using insurer claims data, Cooper and colleagues (2019) found that mergers of nearby hospitals raised prices by more than 6%, and that hospitals with no local rival charged about 12% more than those in markets with four or more. A 2015 review by Gaynor, Ho and Town found that consolidation raises prices with little gain in quality. RAND found that employer plans paid hospitals about 254% of Medicare rates in 2022; the figure is descriptive and drawn from a limited sample.
I085.remedy_note: Plausible. The Federal Trade Commission has won hospital merger challenges in court since 2011. Site-neutral payment, which pays the same for a service wherever it is delivered, and price caps have state evidence, such as Oregon's cap for its state employee plan, along with Congressional Budget Office cost estimates. Evidence on rate regulation outside Maryland is thin.
I085.response: Congress, the states and the antitrust agencies would review mergers and contract clauses that restrict competition, and compare rate regulation or public purchasing where competition cannot work.
I085.tradeoff: Rural hospitals need to stay open, and some integration brings real benefits to patients.
I085.success_measure: Prices adjusted for patient risk, access to care, and clinical quality.

aimed_reforms.why: Blocks mergers of nearby hospitals that would raise negotiated prices.

problem_example.headline: An Illinois hospital merger raised prices, regulators found
problem_example.text: In 2000, the Illinois hospital system Evanston Northwestern Healthcare bought a competitor, Highland Park Hospital. In 2007, the Federal Trade Commission ruled the deal illegal, finding the merged system raised prices "immediately and substantially." The agency stopped short of ordering a sale and required separate negotiating teams, so insurers could again bargain with the hospitals apart.

source.title: Commission Rules That Evanston Northwestern Healthcare Corp.'s Acquisition of Highland Park Hospital Violated Federal Antitrust Law

fix_example.headline: Oregon capped hospital prices for state workers' plans
fix_example.text: Oregon lawmakers in 2017 capped what hospitals could charge the state's employee and educator health plans at 200% of Medicare rates for in-network care, starting in late 2019. A study published by the Milbank Memorial Fund estimated the cap saved about $107.5 million in its first 27 months, roughly 4% of plan spending.
fix_example.result: Researchers estimated about $107.5 million in savings over the first 27 months, about 4% of plan spending.

source.title: How Payment Caps Can Reduce Hospital Prices and Spending: Lessons from the Oregon State Employee Plan (Murray, Whaley, Fuse Brown, Ryan)

I086.title: Dominant platforms can favor their own products
I086.summary: A platform that controls access to customers can rank its own services first or charge dependent businesses steep fees. Courts have found Google acted unlawfully in search and ad tech, while the FTC lost its case against Meta in 2025.
I086.mechanism: Dominant platforms use control of a gateway to favor their own products and extract high fees from dependent sellers and developers. Courts have found unlawful conduct by Google in search and ad tech; the FTC lost its monopolization case against Meta.
I086.evidence_note: Documented for Google. In August 2024 a federal court in Washington, DC held that Google unlawfully maintained search monopolies through exclusive default agreements; the final judgment of December 5, 2025 requires data sharing and limits exclusivity without divestiture. In April 2025 a federal court in Virginia found that Google unlawfully tied its ad server to its ad exchange. A 2020 House Judiciary subcommittee staff report documented self-preferencing at Amazon, Apple, Google and Facebook, with the parties divided over remedies. On November 18, 2025, a federal court ruled for Meta in the FTC's case, and the FTC appealed.
I086.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Rules for designated gatekeepers proposed in the American Innovation and Choice Online Act were not enacted. The European Union's Digital Markets Act, in force since 2024, is the only operating example and has no completed independent evaluation.
I086.response: Congress and the competition agencies would define which platforms are covered gatekeepers, prohibit specified self-preferencing, and require interoperable access with enforceable dispute resolution.
I086.tradeoff: These rules can reduce the benefits of integration and create security risks.
I086.success_measure: Fees paid by sellers, users' ability to switch, innovation, and user welfare.

problem_example.headline: Europe's top court upheld Google's shopping fine
problem_example.text: In June 2017, the European Commission fined Google €2.4 billion for putting results from its own shopping comparison service at the top of search pages, while rival services showed up as plain results prone to demotion. In September 2024, the EU Court of Justice dismissed Google's final appeal and let the fine stand.

source.title: Judgment of the Court of Justice in Case C-48/22 P, Google and Alphabet v Commission (Google Shopping), press release
source.publisher: Court of Justice of the European Union

fix_example.headline: The EU fined Google under its new platform law
fix_example.text: In July 2026, the European Commission fined Google €460 million under the Digital Markets Act, the EU's rulebook for gatekeeper platforms, for ranking its own services, such as shopping and hotel results, above rivals' in search. Google must treat rival services fairly within 60 days or face further penalties.
fix_example.result: The Commission is still assessing changes Google proposed, and no independent study has measured the law's effect on competition.

source.title: Commission fines Google €890 million for breaches of the Digital Markets Act

I087.title: Exclusive data makes dominant platforms hard to challenge
I087.summary: Large stores of user data and the difficulty of switching services keep new competitors out. Rules on data portability and interoperability have to protect privacy as well.
I087.mechanism: Exclusive data and switching costs deter entry against incumbent platforms.
I087.evidence_note: Well supported. The court in the federal Google search case found in 2024 that exclusive default agreements maintained Google's monopoly, and its December 2025 judgment ordered data sharing. The Stigler Center's 2019 expert report synthesizes theory and evidence on data-driven network effects and switching costs, without causal estimates. The 2020 House Judiciary subcommittee staff report documented related practices at the largest platforms.
I087.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The European Union requires data portability and interoperability under the GDPR and the Digital Markets Act, and no evaluation shows an effect on entry. The data-sharing remedy in the 2025 Google search judgment is the first U.S. test and has no results yet.
I087.response: Congress and the agencies would require data portability that protects privacy, interoperable interfaces, and scrutiny of data agreements that exclude rivals.
I087.tradeoff: Sharing data without users' consent can harm them.
I087.success_measure: Users who switch services, privacy breaches, and new entry.

problem_example.headline: Google's default deals fed it more search data
problem_example.text: In August 2024, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., ruled that Google illegally kept its search monopoly through exclusive deals that made it the default search engine. In a December 2025 opinion, Judge Amit Mehta wrote that those deals let Google see far more queries than any rival, "reinforcing the flywheel of network effects that entrenched Google's monopoly."
problem_example.where: Federal (U.S. District Court, District of Columbia)

source.title: United States v. Google LLC (search), Memorandum Opinion, Dec. 5, 2025
source.publisher: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (via DOJ Antitrust Division case page)

fix_example.headline: A court ordered Google to share search data
fix_example.text: Google's December 2025 final judgment requires it to license some search index and user data to qualified competitors, with privacy and security safeguards worked out by a court-appointed technical committee. In September 2026, the plaintiffs reported that the license terms were still being drafted and that Google was withholding some user-data information pending a source code agreement.
fix_example.result: The plaintiffs' report describes no data shared so far, so the remedy's effect on competition is unmeasured.
fix_example.where: Federal (U.S. District Court, District of Columbia)

source.title: United States v. Google LLC (search), Plaintiffs' Second Status Report on Enforcement and Compliance, Sept. 17, 2026
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice Antitrust Division (court filing)

I088.title: Debt-heavy ownership can put essential services at risk
I088.summary: Private-equity owners can load a nursing home or hospital with debt and payments to related companies. Studies of acquired nursing homes and hospitals found worse outcomes for patients.
I088.mechanism: Private-equity ownership that relies on borrowed money and payments to related parties can degrade or endanger essential services.
I088.evidence_note: Well supported. Using Medicare data and a quasi-experimental design, Gupta and colleagues (2021) found that private-equity acquisition of nursing homes raised short-term patient mortality by about 11% and reduced staffing. A 2023 JAMA study found a 25% rise in hospital-acquired conditions at private-equity-acquired hospitals compared with similar hospitals. A 2025 bipartisan Senate Budget Committee report documented sale-leasebacks and dividend recapitalizations before the failure of Steward Health Care and other systems; it is case evidence.
I088.remedy_note: Hypothesis. State laws requiring review and disclosure of these transactions, in Massachusetts (2025), Oregon and Indiana, are new and unevaluated. The evidence supports disclosure and gives no estimate of the effect of solvency duties.
I088.response: Congress, the states and sector regulators would require disclosure of ownership and of payments to related parties, and impose solvency and continuity duties when an essential-service provider is acquired.
I088.tradeoff: Ownership form alone does not prove poor performance.
I088.success_measure: Closures, debt levels, service quality, and fees paid out to owners.

problem_example.headline: Patient deaths rose after private equity bought nursing homes
problem_example.text: A study released by the National Bureau of Economic Research in 2021 found that when private-equity firms bought nursing homes, patient mortality rose by about 11%. The authors traced the rise in part to declines in patient well-being and nurse staffing at the homes they studied.

source.title: Owner Incentives and Performance in Healthcare: Private Equity Investment in Nursing Homes (Gupta, Howell, Yannelis, Gupta), NBER Working Paper 28474

fix_example.headline: Massachusetts widened review of private-equity health deals
fix_example.text: In January 2025, Massachusetts enacted a law requiring 60 days' notice to the state's Health Policy Commission and attorney general before deals that shift control of a health care provider to a private-equity or other major investor. It also bars new hospital licenses when the main campus is leased from a health care real estate investment trust.
fix_example.result: The law is too new to evaluate, and no study has measured its effect on patient care or provider finances.

source.title: An Act enhancing the market review process, Chapter 343 of the Acts of 2024

I089.title: Short-term pay incentives can crowd out long-term investment
I089.summary: Executives paid on quarterly targets may cut investment or staff to hit them. Whether this adds up to too little investment across the economy is contested, and share buybacks alone are no evidence of harm.
I089.mechanism: Executive pay tied to short-term measures can lead firms to favor payouts over investment, resilience and workforce development. Aggregate evidence of underinvestment is contested, and share buybacks alone are no evidence of harm.
I089.evidence_note: Plausible. In a survey of 401 executives (Graham, Harvey and Rajgopal, 2005), most said they would give up long-term value to smooth reported earnings; these are stated intentions. Almeida, Fos and Kronlund (2016) found that firms that would just miss earnings-per-share targets cut investment and jobs to fund buybacks, using a regression-discontinuity design. Kaplan (2017) argues that aggregate evidence of harmful short-termism is weak.
I089.remedy_note: Hypothesis. No evaluation of rules tying executive pay to long-term outcomes exists. The SEC's rule on buyback disclosure was vacated in 2023. A study of a 1994 German reform found that worker seats on company supervisory boards had no effect on wages and came with more capital invested per worker.
I089.response: The Securities and Exchange Commission within its authority, Congress and shareholders would tie executive pay to long-term audited outcomes, strengthen board accountability and give workers more voice in governance.
I089.tradeoff: Long-term metrics can also be gamed, and buybacks are not harmful in themselves.
I089.success_measure: Investment, workplace safety, employee retention, and long-term returns.

problem_example.headline: Executives said they would skip good projects to hit targets
problem_example.text: In a survey of 401 financial executives released in 2004, 55% said they would pass up a project expected to add considerable value if taking it on meant missing that quarter's consensus earnings estimate. Most said earnings per share is the number outside investors watch most closely.

source.title: The Economic Implications of Corporate Financial Reporting (Graham, Harvey, Rajgopal), NBER Working Paper 10550

fix_example.headline: German worker board seats came with more investment
fix_example.text: German law gives worker representatives one-third of board seats at many stock corporations, but a 1994 reform dropped that rule for firms incorporated after August 1994. Comparing companies set up just before and after the cutoff, economists found worker seats had no effect on wages and, if anything, increased capital formation.
fix_example.result: Firms with worker board seats paid similar wages and built more capital; an NBER summary reports long-run capital stocks 40 to 50% larger.

source.title: Labor in the Boardroom (Jäger, Schoefer, Heining), NBER Working Paper 26519
source.publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2021)

I090.title: Hidden fees and manipulative design inflate what people pay
I090.summary: A low advertised price that grows at checkout, or a subscription that is hard to cancel, hides the true cost of a purchase. In one field experiment, hiding fees until checkout raised what buyers spent by about 21%.
I090.mechanism: Hidden fees, complex contracts and manipulative interface defaults weaken informed consumer choice.
I090.evidence_note: Well supported. In a field experiment on StubHub, Blake, Moshary, Sweeney and Tadelis (2021) found that showing fees only at checkout raised spending by about 21% and made purchases more likely; the result is causal and comes from one platform. A 2022 Federal Trade Commission staff report catalogs manipulative design practices, known as dark patterns, and enforcement actions against them.
I090.remedy_note: Well supported for all-in pricing, which has direct experimental support. The FTC's fee rule, effective May 12, 2025, requires all-in prices for live-event tickets and lodging, and California's SB 478 (2024) reaches more sectors; both are too new to evaluate. The Eighth Circuit vacated the FTC's click-to-cancel rule in July 2025.
I090.response: Congress, the Federal Trade Commission and the states would require all-in prices, simple cancellation and clear consent, and enforce the law against unfair and deceptive practices.
I090.tradeoff: Detailed design rules can become outdated as technology changes.
I090.success_measure: Unexpected fees, time needed to cancel, and complaints.

problem_example.headline: Hiding ticket fees until checkout led buyers to spend more
problem_example.text: StubHub shared its data with economists who compared ticket buyers shown the full price, fees included, from the start with buyers who saw fees only at checkout. Their study, released in 2018, found that hidden fees made prices hard to compare, and buyers spent more and chose pricier seats than when the full price was clear.

source.title: Price Salience and Product Choice (Blake, Moshary, Sweeney, Tadelis), NBER Working Paper 25186
source.publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (published in Marketing Science, 2021)

fix_example.headline: Amazon agreed to pay $2.5 billion over Prime sign-ups and cancellations
fix_example.text: In September 2025, Amazon agreed to pay a $1 billion civil penalty and $1.5 billion in refunds to settle Federal Trade Commission charges that it enrolled people in Prime without clear consent and made canceling hard. The order requires a clear button for declining Prime and a simple way to cancel.
fix_example.result: Refunds go to an estimated 35 million consumers; no study has yet measured how sign-ups and cancellations changed.

source.title: FTC Secures Historic $2.5 Billion Settlement Against Amazon

I091.title: Forced arbitration blocks joint claims over widespread harms
I091.summary: Many contracts require customers and workers to settle disputes privately, and to give up class actions, before any problem arises. People with small claims then rarely pursue them.
I091.mechanism: Mandatory arbitration agreements signed before any dispute suppress enforcement of small, widespread consumer and employment harms.
I091.evidence_note: Well supported. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 2015 study found arbitration clauses across most of the credit-card and checking-account markets; consumers filed about 600 arbitrations a year, while class settlements paid $2.7 billion over five years. The Economic Policy Institute, a labor-oriented research group, estimated from a survey that about 56% of nonunion private-sector workers were covered by mandatory arbitration by 2017. In Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis (2018), the Supreme Court upheld class-action waivers in employment arbitration agreements.
I091.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The CFPB's 2017 arbitration rule was repealed under the Congressional Review Act before it took effect. The 2022 law ending forced arbitration of sexual assault and harassment claims is in force and unevaluated. No U.S. study measures the outcomes of a broad limit.
I091.response: Congress would limit mandatory arbitration agreements signed before a dispute for covered consumer and employment claims, while keeping voluntary settlement after a dispute arises.
I091.tradeoff: Litigation costs may rise, so access to remedies and the fairness of outcomes need to be measured.
I091.success_measure: Claims resolved, compensation paid, and procedural fairness.

problem_example.headline: The Supreme Court upheld waivers of workers' group claims
problem_example.text: In 2018, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 in Epic Systems v. Lewis that employers can enforce contracts requiring workers to settle disputes in one-on-one arbitration. The employees in the combined cases had tried to bring class or collective lawsuits over federal wage-and-hour claims, and the ruling held their individual arbitration agreements must be enforced.

source.title: Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 584 U.S. ___ (2018)
source.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States (text via Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)

fix_example.headline: A 2022 law ended forced arbitration of harassment claims
fix_example.text: In March 2022, Congress amended the Federal Arbitration Act so that people alleging sexual harassment or sexual assault can take their cases to court. Arbitration agreements and class-action waivers signed before the dispute arose cannot be enforced in those cases if the person bringing the claim chooses court.
fix_example.result: The law is in force, and no study has yet measured how many claims have moved from arbitration to court.

source.title: 9 U.S. Code § 402 (Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act, Pub. L. 117-90)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (U.S. Code text)

I092.title: Patent tactics delay cheaper drug competition
I092.summary: Drug makers can stack new patents on existing drugs and pay generic rivals to delay entry, stretching exclusivity past the reward for the original invention. Patients wait longer for cheaper generic and biosimilar versions.
I092.mechanism: Thickets of overlapping patents, evergreening (new patents on existing drugs) and settlements that pay rivals to stay out extend drug exclusivity beyond the reward for innovation.
I092.evidence_note: Well supported. Feldman (2018) found that 78% of drugs associated with new patents from 2005 to 2015 were existing drugs, in a descriptive analysis of FDA Orange Book data. In FTC v. Actavis (2013), the Supreme Court held that settlements in which a brand-name maker pays a generic rival to delay entry are subject to antitrust scrutiny. A 2010 FTC staff study, from before that ruling, estimated that such deals cost consumers $3.5 billion a year.
I092.remedy_note: Well supported. The FTC's annual reports under the Medicare Modernization Act show that pay-for-delay settlements fell sharply after Actavis. Reforms to patent quality lack outcome evaluation.
I092.response: Congress, the Patent and Trademark Office, the Food and Drug Administration and the antitrust agencies would tighten patent quality, review settlements that exclude rivals and ease entry for generics and biosimilars.
I092.tradeoff: Valuable research and development still needs returns.
I092.success_measure: Time until a competitor enters, quality of patents granted, and treatment costs.

problem_example.headline: A drugmaker paid generic rivals to wait
problem_example.text: According to a Federal Trade Commission complaint described by the Supreme Court, Solvay, maker of the brand-name drug AndroGel, paid generic makers to settle patent suits. Actavis agreed to keep its generic off the market until August 31, 2015, for an estimated $19 million to $30 million a year for nine years. That date fell 65 months before Solvay's patent expired.

source.title: FTC v. Actavis, Inc., 570 U.S. 136 (2013)
source.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States (text via Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)

fix_example.headline: Pay-for-delay deals fell after a 2013 ruling
fix_example.text: In June 2013, the Supreme Court ruled in FTC v. Actavis that payments from brand-name drugmakers to generic rivals to settle patent fights can face antitrust challenge. The Federal Trade Commission later reported that possible pay-for-delay deals filed with it fell from 40 in fiscal 2012, before the ruling, to 21 in fiscal 2014.
fix_example.result: Possible pay-for-delay deals filed with the FTC dropped by nearly half in two years, from 40 to 21.

source.title: FTC Report on Drug Patent Settlements Shows Potential Pay-for-Delay Deals Decreased Substantially in the First Year Since Supreme Court's Actavis Decision

I093.title: Utility networks need accountable rules for a single provider
I093.summary: Building a second power grid or water system rarely makes sense, so customers usually have one practical provider. Regulation or public ownership then has to keep prices and service in check.
I093.mechanism: Where duplicating a network is inefficient, a private monopoly needs regulation or public provision to avoid harm to customers.
I093.evidence_note: Well supported. Joskow's 2007 handbook chapter sets out the standard economic treatment of natural monopolies and the incentive problems in regulating them. Borenstein and Bushnell's 2015 review of 20 years of electricity restructuring found mixed efficiency gains and costs shifted to consumers in some states.
I093.remedy_note: Plausible. Rate regulation, restructuring and municipal provision each have mixed records, so no design clearly outperforms the others, and the proposed options are reasonable without being ranked by evidence.
I093.response: States, local authorities and Congress would use accountable rate regulation, public options or municipal provision, each with published service obligations.
I093.tradeoff: Public ownership also needs competence and discipline in spending capital.

problem_example.headline: California's power market let suppliers push prices up
problem_example.text: After California restructured its electricity market, retail prices were frozen and state regulators generally prohibited or discouraged long-term contracts between utilities and wholesale suppliers. A 2002 GAO report found evidence that wholesale suppliers raised prices above competitive levels in summer 2000, and once prices rose, the market's design did not bring them back down.

source.title: Restructured Electricity Markets: California Market Design Enabled Exercise of Market Power (GAO-02-828)
source.publisher: U.S. General Accounting Office (now Government Accountability Office)

I094.title: Licensing rules keep new businesses and workers out
I094.summary: About 29% of U.S. workers needed a government license to do their jobs in 2008, and licensing raises pay for license holders while reducing employment. Reviewing each license separates real safety protections from unneeded barriers.
I094.mechanism: Occupational licensing blocks productive new entrants. The record's further claims about procurement and financing rules are asserted without evidence.
I094.evidence_note: Well supported for licensing. Kleiner and Krueger (2013) estimated that about 29% of U.S. workers held a license in 2008. Kleiner and Soltas (2023) found that licensing raises wages by about 15% and reduces employment, with a large estimated welfare cost, using variation across states. A 2015 framework from the White House, the Treasury and the Council of Economic Advisers synthesized the evidence for state reviewers.
I094.remedy_note: Plausible. Workers move between states less often in occupations with state-specific licenses. Arizona's 2019 universal recognition law, which accepts licenses issued by other states, is unevaluated, and splitting large contracts so small suppliers can bid has no outcome study.
I094.response: States, cities and procurement bodies would review licenses for whether safety requires them, simplify permits and divide large contracts so qualified small suppliers can bid.
I094.tradeoff: Some standards protect health and public trust.
I094.success_measure: Business starts, cost of compliance, and safety outcomes.

problem_example.headline: A dentist-run board shut down teeth-whitening shops
problem_example.text: In North Carolina, the state dental board, where six of eight members must be practicing dentists, sent at least 47 cease-and-desist letters to teeth-whitening providers who were not dentists, and they stopped offering the service. In 2015, the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the board could face antitrust law because the state did not actively supervise it.

source.title: North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC, 574 U.S. 494 (2015)
source.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States (text via Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)

fix_example.headline: Arizona accepts licenses earned in other states
fix_example.text: Arizona law lets a person licensed in good standing in another state for at least a year receive an Arizona license in the same field and at the same level, after discipline and criminal-history checks. Since July 2022, licensing agencies must track application data and report it to the governor each year.
fix_example.result: No independent study of the law's effect on jobs or migration was found, and the atlas lists it as unevaluated.

source.title: Arizona Revised Statutes § 32-4302

I095.title: Lean supply chains can turn one disruption into a shortage
I095.summary: When an industry depends on a few suppliers, a disaster or shutdown at one of them can spread across the economy. Buyers also have less bargaining room when alternatives are scarce.
I095.mechanism: Concentrated supply chains transmit shocks across the economy and leave buyers dependent on single suppliers.
I095.evidence_note: Well supported. Using firm network data, Carvalho and colleagues (2021) found that the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake spread through supply chains to distant firms. Elliott, Golub and Leduc (2022) show in a formal model that efficient supply networks can sit near a threshold of fragility. The White House's 2021 supply-chain review documented U.S. dependencies in semiconductors, batteries and pharmaceuticals.
I095.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Subsidies under the CHIPS Act and the Inflation Reduction Act are being paid out without a completed evaluation of whether they add investment that would not otherwise happen. Tying support to performance is standard advice without outcome evidence.
I095.response: Congress and agencies would map critical dependencies, spread purchasing across suppliers and tie targeted industrial support to performance and review.
I095.tradeoff: Protection can harden into a permanent subsidy or a trade conflict.
I095.success_measure: Number of suppliers, recovery time after disruptions, and whether subsidies add investment.

problem_example.headline: One chip plant fire rippled through car production
problem_example.text: In 2021, a fire at a Renesas chip plant in Japan, which the White House said supplied 30% of the microcontrollers used in cars, deepened a global chip shortage. A White House review that June estimated the shortage would cost the global auto industry about $110 billion in 2021 and nearly four million vehicles.

source.title: Building Resilient Supply Chains, Revitalizing American Manufacturing, and Fostering Broad-Based Growth (100-day supply chain review)

I096.title: Antitrust agencies lack the resources for complex cases
I096.summary: Antitrust agency budgets fell relative to the economy and to merger activity through the 2010s, while the firms they investigate can spend far more. Thin staffing, and staff leaving for the firms they oversee, lower the expected cost of breaking competition law.
I096.mechanism: Gaps in resources, and movement of staff to the firms they regulate, weaken deterrence at enforcement agencies.
I096.evidence_note: Plausible. A 2019 analysis by Kades for the Washington Center for Equitable Growth documented that antitrust agency budgets fell relative to GDP and to merger activity through the 2010s. Tabakovic and Wollmann (2018) found that patent examiners who later joined law firms granted more patents to those firms, causal evidence of revolving-door effects in one agency.
I096.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The Merger Filing Fee Modernization Act of 2022 raised filing fees to fund the agencies and has not been evaluated. No study measures the effect of staffing on case outcomes.
I096.response: Congress, the states and the agencies would provide stable enforcement budgets and competitive pay for technical staff, and monitor remedies in public.
I096.tradeoff: More cases do not automatically mean better enforcement.
I096.success_measure: Compliance with remedies, case quality, and outcomes for consumers.

aimed_reforms.why: Merger enforcement depends on agencies with the staff to investigate and litigate complex deals.

problem_example.headline: A merger wave strained the FTC in 2021
problem_example.text: In August 2021, the Federal Trade Commission said a "tidal wave of merger filings" was straining its capacity to investigate deals. Because federal law generally gives the agencies 30 days for an initial review, the FTC began sending form letters telling companies that investigations of deals it could not fully review remained open.

source.title: Adjusting merger review to deal with the surge in merger filings (Holly Vedova, Bureau of Competition)

fix_example.headline: Bigger mergers now pay bigger filing fees
fix_example.text: A 2022 federal law reset merger filing fees by deal size to give the antitrust agencies more money. For 2026, the Federal Trade Commission charges $35,000 to file on deals under $189.6 million and $2.46 million on deals of $5.869 billion or more.
fix_example.result: The fees go to the agencies, and no study has measured whether the added money changed case outcomes.

source.title: Filing Fee Information (Premerger Notification Program)

I097.title: Weak penalties let employers retaliate against organizing
I097.summary: When an employer illegally fires union supporters, federal labor law allows only back pay and reinstatement, with no civil penalties. Employers were charged with unfair labor practices in about 42% of union election campaigns in 2016 and 2017.
I097.mechanism: Penalties for unlawful interference with organizing are too small to deter it.
I097.evidence_note: Well supported. The National Labor Relations Act limits remedies to reinstatement and back pay, with no civil penalties. The Economic Policy Institute, a labor-oriented research group, found that employers were charged with unfair labor practices in 41.5% of union election campaigns in 2016 and 2017, and with illegal firings in about 20%; charges are allegations until the Board rules on them. Ferguson (2008), modeling National Labor Relations Board data from 1999 to 2004, found that only a minority of organizing drives reach a first contract.
I097.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The penalties in the PRO Act have not been enacted. The Third and Fifth Circuits rejected the Board's expanded-remedy doctrine from Thryv (2022) in 2024 and 2025, so no U.S. evidence on the effect of penalties exists.
I097.response: Congress, through legislation, and the National Labor Relations Board would strengthen prompt reinstatement, add meaningful civil penalties and speed up decisions in organizing cases.
I097.tradeoff: Remedies require due process and authority that courts will sustain.
I097.success_measure: Time to resolve retaliation cases, and first contracts reached.

aimed_reforms.why: Adds penalties that deter illegal firings during organizing drives.

problem_example.headline: Starbucks fired Memphis organizers, and rehiring orders got harder
problem_example.text: In 2022, Starbucks fired seven workers at a Memphis cafe, several of them union organizers, saying they broke policy by letting a TV crew in after hours. The labor board said the firings illegally undercut the union drive, and a federal judge ordered the workers rehired. In 2024, the Supreme Court ruled the lower courts had used the wrong test and sent the case back under a stricter one.

source.title: Supreme Court backs Starbucks over fired pro-union workers (Andrew Chung, Reuters, republished by KSL.com)

fix_example.headline: Labor board's wider remedy for illegal firings hits court limits
fix_example.text: In 2022, the National Labor Relations Board began ordering employers to repay workers for direct and foreseeable money losses from illegal acts, beyond back pay. In December 2024, the Third Circuit threw out that order in a case over two fired Philadelphia Starbucks baristas, ruling the board can restore only what the employer withheld, such as back pay. Other appeals courts have split on the question.
fix_example.result: Federal appeals courts disagree on whether the wider remedy is lawful, and its effect on retaliation has not been measured.

source.title: NLRB v. Starbucks Corp., Nos. 23-1953 and 23-2241 (precedential opinion)
source.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit

I098.title: Workers win a union and then wait for a first contract
I098.summary: Workers can vote for a union and still go without a contract while bargaining stalls. Only a minority of organizing drives end with a first contract, so a formal win can bring little change in pay or conditions.
I098.mechanism: Union recognition without a first contract delivers little practical bargaining power.
I098.evidence_note: Well supported. Ferguson (2008), modeling National Labor Relations Board data from 1999 to 2004, found that only a minority of organizing drives reach a first contract.
I098.remedy_note: Plausible. Johnson (2010) found that Canadian provinces with first-contract arbitration, in which a neutral arbitrator sets terms when bargaining stalls, had more settlements and fewer strikes over first contracts. There is no U.S. federal test.
I098.response: Congress would set bargaining deadlines with mediation, and make carefully designed first-contract arbitration a statutory option.
I098.tradeoff: Arbitrators need legitimacy and knowledge of the industry.
I098.success_measure: Time to a first contract, and worker satisfaction.

aimed_reforms.why: First-contract arbitration produces an agreement when bargaining stalls.

problem_example.headline: Starbucks union stores still lack a contract after four years
problem_example.text: In December 2021, baristas at a Buffalo, New York, Starbucks voted for the chain's first U.S. union. By March 2026, Workers United represented about 600 of roughly 10,000 company-run stores, and Bloomberg reported the two sides had yet to reach a contract. Talks that broke down in late 2024 were being revived that spring.
problem_example.where: Buffalo, New York, and Starbucks stores nationwide

source.title: Starbucks, Union Working to Revive Long-Stalled Contract Talks (Josh Eidelson)

fix_example.headline: Canada's first-contract arbitration cut strikes over first deals
fix_example.text: Several parts of Canada let a neutral arbitrator set the terms of a first contract when bargaining stalls. A 2010 study by Susan Johnson in the ILR Review found the option cut strikes and lockouts over first contracts by at least half. Unions rarely used it and arbitrators seldom imposed terms, and the author concluded its availability alone pushed both sides toward agreement.
fix_example.result: Where first-contract arbitration was available, strikes and lockouts over first contracts fell by at least half, with no significant change in their length.

source.title: First Contract Arbitration: Effects on Bargaining and Work Stoppages (Susan J. T. Johnson)

I099.title: Firm-by-firm bargaining lets competitors undercut standards
I099.summary: A contract that covers one employer can be undercut by competitors and contractors outside it. Sector-wide boards try to set basic pay and conditions across a whole industry.
I099.mechanism: Firm-by-firm bargaining leaves contractors and competitors outside agreements, so standards erode under competition.
I099.evidence_note: Well supported. The OECD's 2019 Employment Outlook found across countries that coordinated bargaining at the sector level goes with higher coverage and less wage dispersion; the evidence is associational.
I099.remedy_note: Plausible. California's AB 1228 (2023) created a Fast Food Council and a $20 minimum wage in 2024, the one live U.S. sectoral board. An early evaluation by UC Berkeley's labor research institute found no detectable employment loss; other studies disagree, and the findings are preliminary.
I099.response: States, and Congress, would pilot sectoral wage boards with worker and employer representatives, legal authority and independent evaluation.
I099.tradeoff: Federal labor-law preemption and antitrust law limit how such boards can be designed.
I099.success_measure: Workers covered, pay, employment, and new firms entering the sector.

aimed_reforms.why: Industry boards set floors across a sector, so competitors cannot undercut a single contract.

problem_example.headline: Grocery strike ends with fewer benefits for new hires
problem_example.text: In October 2003, about 70,000 Southern California grocery workers began a strike and lockout over health insurance costs at three big chains. The fight played out as Wal-Mart, which paid lower wages and offered fewer benefits, planned 40 superstores in the region. After 139 days, the union accepted a deal giving new workers fewer benefits than veteran clerks.

source.title: Tentative Settlement Reached in Long-Running California Supermarket Strike

fix_example.headline: California sets fast-food pay through an industry council
fix_example.text: California's 2023 law created a Fast Food Council with power to raise the industry's wage each year and set a $20 minimum at large fast-food chains in April 2024. UC Berkeley researchers found average pay rose 18% while employment held steady and menu prices rose 3.7%. A 2025 working paper by other economists estimated about 18,000 fewer fast-food jobs.
fix_example.result: Average pay rose about 18%, and studies disagree on whether the policy cost jobs.

source.title: New study analyzes impact of California's $20 minimum wage for fast food workers
source.publisher: UC Berkeley Institute for Research on Labor and Employment

I100.title: Farmworkers and domestic workers are left out of federal bargaining law
I100.summary: The National Labor Relations Act excludes agricultural laborers and domestic workers from its definition of employee. Whether they can bargain collectively depends on state law.
I100.mechanism: Agricultural, domestic and some other workers are excluded from federal collective-bargaining protection.
I100.evidence_note: Documented. The National Labor Relations Act's definition of employee excludes agricultural laborers and domestic workers. Legal scholarship in the Ohio State Law Journal (2011) traces these exclusions to the racial politics of the 1930s; it is historical analysis by legal scholars.
I100.remedy_note: Hypothesis. California's Agricultural Labor Relations Act (1975) and domestic-worker bills of rights in 11 states exist. No rigorous evaluation of extending coverage was found.
I100.response: Congress would extend statutory bargaining rights, or states would create parallel protections, with clear coverage and enforcement.
I100.tradeoff: Coverage boundaries and small household employers need workable rules.
I100.success_measure: Share of the workforce protected, and access to remedies.

problem_example.headline: New York farmworker fired for organizing sues for bargaining rights
problem_example.text: Crispin Hernandez was fired from a farm in Lowville, New York, after trying to organize his coworkers. Federal labor law excludes farmworkers, and a 1937 state law did too, so he filed suit in 2016 with a Syracuse workers' center. In 2019, a state appeals court struck down the state exclusion, calling bargaining a fundamental right of all employees.

source.title: Workers Center Of Central New York Wins Lawsuit Allowing Farm Workers To Organize

fix_example.headline: Few California farmworkers have a union under state law
fix_example.text: California's 1975 Agricultural Labor Relations Act gave farmworkers the bargaining rights that federal law leaves out, with a state board to run union elections. By 2022, CalMatters reported, representation had dwindled so low that UC Merced researchers could not confidently measure it. That year, the state added a card-check option meant to make organizing easier.
fix_example.result: Union representation stayed very low under the state law, and the 2022 card-check change has not been evaluated.

source.title: Newsom relents, signs farmworker union bill after pressure from Biden and labor

I101.title: Falling union membership weakens workers' voice at work and in politics
I101.summary: Union membership fell from 20.1% of U.S. wage and salary workers in 1983 to 10.0% in 2025. With fewer members, workers have less power to bargain and less organized political voice.
I101.mechanism: Declining union membership reduces countervailing power in workplaces and in politics.
I101.evidence_note: Well supported. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports union membership at 10.0% of wage and salary workers in 2025, down from 20.1% in 1983; the 2025 figure excludes October and is not strictly comparable with other years. Farber, Herbst, Kuziemko and Naidu (2021) trace how union density moved with inequality over the twentieth century. Feigenbaum, Hertel-Fernandez and Williamson (2018) found that right-to-work laws reduced turnout and the Democratic share of the vote, consistent with unions' political role.
I101.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Modernized access for organizing has not been enacted, and no U.S. evaluation links specific access rules to membership.
I101.response: Congress, unions and the states would modernize access for organizing, protect lawful collective action and fund worker-rights education that employers do not control.
I101.tradeoff: Worker choice and union accountability both need to be measured.
I101.success_measure: Membership, workers represented, and member participation.

aimed_reforms.why: Makes organizing pay off by deterring illegal firings and producing first contracts.

problem_example.headline: Union membership falls to half its 1983 rate
problem_example.text: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in February 2026 that 10.0% of U.S. wage and salary workers belonged to a union in 2025, about 14.7 million people. That is about half the 20.1% rate of 1983. In private companies the rate was 5.9%, while public-sector workers were more than five times as likely to belong.

source.title: Union Members, 2025

fix_example.headline: British Columbia's card-check rules raised union win rates
fix_example.text: British Columbia required union certification elections from 1984 to 1993, then restored card check, which certifies a union once enough workers sign cards. A 2004 study by Chris Riddell found union win rates fell about 19 percentage points under mandatory elections and rose by about as much when card check returned. Employer opposition was about twice as effective under elections.
fix_example.result: Union certification success rose about 19 percentage points after card check replaced mandatory elections in 1993.

source.title: Union Certification Success under Voting versus Card-Check Procedures: Evidence from British Columbia, 1978-1998 (Chris Riddell)

I102.title: Calling employees contractors shifts costs onto workers
I102.summary: When an employer labels employees as independent contractors, they lose minimum-wage, overtime and insurance protections and pay more of their own taxes. State audits find that 10% to 20% of employers misclassify some workers.
I102.mechanism: Labeling employees as contractors removes wage, insurance and tax protections and shifts costs to workers.
I102.evidence_note: Well supported. A 2015 Economic Policy Institute review of state audit studies found that 10% to 20% of employers misclassify workers. New Jersey's 2019 task force reported that audits of 1% of employers in 2018 found about 12,300 misclassified workers. Katz and Krueger (2019) show that the population in alternative work arrangements can be measured, though its size is disputed.
I102.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Functional tests of employment status exist, including California's AB 5 and a 2024 Labor Department rule that is now being rescinded. No evaluation of classification tests on worker income was found.
I102.response: Congress, the Labor Department and the states would use clear functional tests of employment status, enforce them jointly and penalize deliberate evasion.
I102.tradeoff: Independent businesses need to remain free to work as contractors.
I102.success_measure: Wages recovered, correct classification, and workers' own preferences.

problem_example.headline: New Jersey audits find thousands of misclassified workers
problem_example.text: In 2018, New Jersey's Labor Department found 12,315 misclassified workers through its required audits of just 1% of the state's employers. The audits turned up $462 million in underreported wages and $13.9 million in underreported contributions to unemployment, disability, family leave and workforce funds. A 2019 state task force named construction and trucking among the industries where the practice is common.

source.title: Report of the Task Force on Employee Misclassification
source.publisher: State of New Jersey, Department of Labor and Workforce Development

fix_example.headline: Labor Department proposes new contractor rule after 2024 test
fix_example.text: In January 2024, the Labor Department published a rule on who counts as an employee or an independent contractor under federal wage law, replacing a 2021 rule, and it took effect that March. A compliance guide describes its six-factor economic reality test. In February 2026, the department announced a new proposed rule on the same question.
fix_example.result: The 2024 test took effect in March 2024, and about two years later the department opened new rulemaking on contractor status.

source.title: Employee or Independent Contractor Classification Under the FLSA: rulemaking
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

I103.title: Subcontracting lets lead firms control work without legal responsibility
I103.summary: A large company can set the pace and pay of work done by a contractor's employees while pointing to the contractor as the employer. Outsourced janitors and security guards earn 4% to 7% less than in-house workers doing the same jobs.
I103.mechanism: Lead firms control working conditions through subcontracting while denying legal responsibility.
I103.evidence_note: Well supported. Using Current Population Survey data, Dube and Kaplan (2010) found that outsourced janitors and security guards earned 4% to 7% less than in-house peers. In Germany, Goldschmidt and Schmieder (2017) found from administrative data that domestic outsourcing cut wages by 10% to 15% in affected occupations. Weil's The Fissured Workplace (2014) synthesizes the pattern across industries with enforcement case evidence; Weil later led the Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division.
I103.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The National Labor Relations Board's 2023 joint-employer rule was vacated in March 2024. No evaluation of joint-liability rules on wage recovery exists.
I103.response: Congress, the Labor Department and procurement agencies would tie joint-employer liability to actual control and require labor compliance through supply chains in public contracts.
I103.tradeoff: Rules drawn too broadly can burden independent franchise owners.
I103.success_measure: Wages recovered, safety compliance, and accountability of the firm in control.

problem_example.headline: German outsourcing cut pay for cleaning and security jobs
problem_example.text: In Germany, when employers moved jobs such as cleaning and security to outside service firms, pay in those jobs fell about 10% to 15% compared with similar jobs kept in-house. That is the finding of a 2015 study by Deborah Goldschmidt and Johannes Schmieder. They estimate that outsourcing these services explains about a tenth of the rise in German wage inequality since the 1980s.

source.title: The Rise of Domestic Outsourcing and the Evolution of the German Wage Structure (Goldschmidt, Schmieder), NBER Working Paper 21366; published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2017

fix_example.headline: Labor board's broader joint-employer test keeps changing
fix_example.text: In its 2015 Browning-Ferris decision, the National Labor Relations Board said it would consider a company's reserved or indirect control over another firm's workers when deciding joint-employer status. A federal appeals court upheld that idea in 2018, but a 2020 rule counted such control only when it reinforced direct control. A 2023 rule rescinded the 2020 rule and restored the broader test.
fix_example.result: The standard shifted three times between 2015 and 2023, ending with a rule set to take effect December 26, 2023 that again counts reserved and indirect control.

source.title: Standard for Determining Joint Employer Status (final rule), 88 FR 73946

I104.title: A fixed minimum wage buys less every year
I104.summary: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 2009, so inflation has steadily cut what it buys. Thirty states set a higher floor, and about 19 adjust theirs automatically.
I104.mechanism: A wage floor fixed in dollars loses purchasing power over time.
I104.evidence_note: Documented. The Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division lists the federal minimum wage at $7.25 since July 2009; the fall in its real value follows arithmetically from inflation. Thirty states set a higher floor.
I104.remedy_note: Contested. About 19 states index their minimum wage to prices or wages. Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer (2019) found no detectable job loss from state increases through 2016, a result that studies using other methods contest. The Congressional Budget Office's 2019 median estimate for a $15 federal minimum by 2025 was 1.3 million jobs lost and 1.3 million people lifted out of poverty, with wide uncertainty.
I104.response: Congress and the states would set a phased wage floor with published indexing to inflation or wages, and evaluate employment effects region by region.
I104.tradeoff: The level and pace of increases affect employment, prices and small firms.
I104.success_measure: Real pay for low-wage workers, hours, and employment.

aimed_reforms.why: An indexed floor keeps its value without a new vote every few years.

status.text: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009. As of July 1, 2026, 30 states and the District of Columbia set a higher state minimum.

problem_example.headline: Twenty states still rely on the $7.25 federal floor
problem_example.text: The Labor Department's list of state minimum wages, updated July 1, 2026, shows 30 states with rates above the federal $7.25 an hour. The other 20, including Texas and Pennsylvania, set no floor above $7.25: 13 match it, 5 have no minimum wage law, and Georgia and Wyoming list $5.15, though covered employers must pay $7.25.
problem_example.where: United States; 20 states including Texas and Pennsylvania

source.title: State Minimum Wage Laws (updated July 1, 2026)
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

fix_example.headline: Ohio raises its minimum wage automatically each year
fix_example.text: Ohio adjusts its minimum wage every year by a set formula, the Labor Department reports, and its rate for employers with annual gross receipts of $405,000 or more is $11.00 an hour. Washington also adjusts yearly and now stands at $17.13. The federal minimum is $7.25.
fix_example.result: Ohio's wage floor rises each year by formula and stands at $11.00 for larger employers, while the federal floor is $7.25.

source.title: State Minimum Wage Laws (updated July 1, 2026)
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

I105.title: Workers cannot reliably recover stolen wages
I105.summary: Unpaid overtime and pay below the minimum wage cost low-wage workers billions of dollars a year, and federal recoveries cover a small fraction. Missing records, weak enforcement and fear of retaliation keep many claims from being filed.
I105.mechanism: Wage theft persists because workers lack records, legal help and effective enforcement.
I105.evidence_note: Well supported. The Economic Policy Institute estimated in 2017 that minimum-wage violations alone cost workers $15 billion a year, extrapolating from the Current Population Survey. In a 2008 survey of 4,387 low-wage workers in three large cities, 26% had been paid below the minimum wage in the prior week. The Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division recovered $259 million for 176,957 workers in fiscal year 2025, small relative to the estimated losses.
I105.remedy_note: Plausible. States with stronger penalties and enforcement show higher compliance, in observational comparisons across states.
I105.response: The Labor Department and the states would fund wage investigators, require electronic pay records, protect workers from retaliation and enforce in partnership with community groups.
I105.tradeoff: Audits should be proportionate and open to appeal.
I105.success_measure: Pay recovered, repeat violations, and time to resolve claims.

problem_example.headline: Low-wage workers in three cities lost 15% of pay
