I135.success_measure: Child-care places, costs to families, staff retention, and quality.

aimed_reforms.why: Funds child-care supply with decent workforce pay, which lowers prices and keeps centers open.

problem_example.headline: Child care workers earn near the bottom of all jobs
problem_example.text: The Treasury Department's 2021 report on child care found that workers in the field averaged $24,230 a year, placing them in the second percentile of all occupations. Families with children under 5 who paid for care spent an average of 13% of family income on it in 2017.

source.title: The Economics of Child Care Supply in the United States

fix_example.headline: Washington, D.C. raised early educator pay through a public fund
fix_example.text: Washington, D.C.'s Early Childhood Educator Pay Equity Fund paid supplements of $10,000 to $14,000 a year to more than 4,000 educators in licensed child care during its first two years. A 2024 Mathematica study found the fund added 219 educators to the city's child care workforce, about 7% more than expected without it.
fix_example.result: Early educator employment in the city rose by about 7% relative to the estimate without the program, while the change in the number of child care businesses was not statistically significant.

source.title: Jobs in the Balance: The Two-Year Labor Market Impacts of Washington, DC's Early Childhood Educator Pay Equity Fund (Schochet)

I136.title: Long-term care drains family earnings and savings
I136.summary: Unpaid family caregiving was valued at $600 billion in 2021, and more than 710,000 people were on waiting lists for Medicaid home care in 2024. Caregiving reduces women's employment and wages.
I136.mechanism: Unpaid care and fragmented coverage deplete families' earnings and assets.
I136.evidence_note: Well supported. AARP's Public Policy Institute, part of an advocacy organization, valued unpaid family caregiving at $600 billion in 2021. KFF counted more than 710,000 people on waiting lists for Medicaid home and community-based services in 2024, an incomplete measure of unmet need. Using panel data, Van Houtven, Coe and Skira (2013) found that caregiving reduces women's employment and wages.
I136.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Expanding home and community-based services reduces use of institutions in observational studies. Washington's public long-term care insurance begins paying benefits in 2026 and has no evaluation yet.
I136.response: Congress and the states would expand home and community services, support family caregivers and put long-term care financing on a sustainable footing.
I136.tradeoff: Limits on the care workforce and on budgets require phasing in.
I136.success_measure: Unmet care needs, caregivers' earnings, and moves into institutions.

aimed_reforms.why: Paid leave insurance lets family caregivers take time without losing their jobs.

problem_example.headline: Over 710,000 people waited for Medicaid home care
problem_example.text: KFF's 2024 survey of states counted more than 710,000 people on waiting or interest lists for Medicaid home and community-based services. Those who eventually got services had waited an average of 40 months. Some states put people on lists without screening for eligibility, so the count can overstate need in places.

source.title: A Look at Waiting Lists for Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services from 2016 to 2024

fix_example.headline: Washington began paying public long-term care benefits in 2026
fix_example.text: Washington state workers have paid 0.58% of their wages into the WA Cares Fund since July 2023. On July 1, 2026, benefits became available in what the state calls the first public long-term care insurance program in the country. Approved beneficiaries can draw up to $36,500 over their lifetime, an amount that rises with inflation.
fix_example.result: Benefits became available in July 2026, too recently for any evaluation of effects on family caregivers or household savings.

source.title: WA Cares Fund benefits now available
source.publisher: Washington State Department of Social and Health Services, WA Cares Fund

I137.title: School resources follow neighborhood wealth
I137.summary: Where school funding depends on local property wealth and neighborhoods are separated by income and race, children get unequal preparation. More spending per pupil raises completed schooling and adult earnings.
I137.mechanism: Unequal school funding and segregation reproduce unequal preparation for children.
I137.evidence_note: Well supported. Jackson, Johnson and Persico (2016) found that 10% more spending per pupil over 12 years raised completed education and adult earnings, using court-ordered finance reforms. A 2024 meta-analysis of U.S. evaluations found that spending increases improve outcomes on average.
I137.remedy_note: Well supported. School finance reforms that sent more money to low-income districts raised achievement there (Lafortune, Rothstein and Schanzenbach, 2018), and court-ordered increases raised adult earnings. Tools for integrating schools rest on older desegregation evidence with fewer recent tests.
I137.response: States, school districts and Congress would use weighted state funding formulas, equitable facilities, effective early learning and integration tools with local participation.
I137.tradeoff: Money has to turn into better teaching and supportive conditions to make a difference.
I137.success_measure: Resource gaps between districts, learning, and completion.

problem_example.headline: Pennsylvania court ruled school funding system unconstitutional
problem_example.text: In 2023, Pennsylvania's Commonwealth Court ruled that the state's school funding system violates the state constitution. Judge Renée Cohn Jubelirer wrote that students in districts with low property values and incomes are deprived of the same opportunities as others. At the time, the state leaned heavily on local property taxes and had some of the nation's widest spending gaps between wealthy and low-income districts.

source.title: Pennsylvania's school funding system violates state constitution, judge rules

fix_example.headline: California's weighted school funding raised scores in high-need districts
fix_example.text: California's Local Control Funding Formula, enacted in 2013, sends extra money to districts with many high-need students. A 2021 Public Policy Institute of California study found that each additional $1,000 in concentration grant funding raised the share of students meeting state standards by about 5.1 percentage points. Effects on graduation rates were less clear.
fix_example.result: Each extra $1,000 in targeted funding raised the share of students meeting standards by about 5.1 points, and the highest-need districts narrowed their gap in college-prep course completion by 9 points.

source.title: Targeted K-12 Funding and Student Outcomes: Evaluating the Local Control Funding Formula (Lafortune)

I138.title: Students borrow without finishing a credential that pays
I138.summary: Six-year completion rates at four-year colleges sit around 60% to 65%, and loan defaults concentrate among students who did not finish or attended for-profit schools. Support to finish, and accountability for schools, address the risk before repayment begins.
I138.mechanism: Students take on debt without earning credentials that raise their earnings.
I138.evidence_note: Well supported. Using administrative data, Looney and Yannelis (2015) found that student-loan defaults concentrate among borrowers who did not complete and those who attended for-profit schools. The National Center for Education Statistics reports six-year completion around 60% to 65% at four-year institutions. A 2019 study found that for-profit certificate students earned no more, and often less, after enrolling.
I138.remedy_note: Well supported. In a randomized trial, CUNY's ASAP program raised three-year graduation rates by 18 percentage points and six-year rates by 10 points. An early guarantee of free tuition at a flagship university, tested by random assignment, raised enrollment among high-achieving low-income students from 12% to 27%. Federal accountability rules for colleges were adopted and then revised, with no stable evaluation.
I138.response: Congress, the states and colleges would increase need-based aid, completion support and accountability for institutions, simplify repayment and evaluate targeted relief.
I138.tradeoff: Debt relief alone leaves future pricing and low-value programs unchanged.
I138.success_measure: Completion, debt burden, earnings, and repayment.

problem_example.headline: Corinthian Colleges collapse left 560,000 borrowers needing relief
problem_example.text: Corinthian Colleges, a for-profit chain, closed in April 2015. The Education Department found it had misrepresented job placement rates in programs across the country. In 2022 the department canceled $5.8 billion in remaining federal loans for 560,000 former students.

source.title: Education Department Approves $5.8 Billion Group Discharge to Cancel All Remaining Loans for 560,000 Borrowers who Attended Corinthian Colleges

fix_example.headline: CUNY's ASAP program nearly doubled community college graduation
fix_example.text: At three City University of New York community colleges, the ASAP program paired students with advisers who carry small caseloads and covered costs such as transit fares and textbooks. In MDRC's randomized trial, 40% of ASAP students had earned a degree after three years, compared with 22% of the control group.
fix_example.result: After three years, 40% of ASAP students had earned a degree versus 22% of the control group.

source.title: Doubling Graduation Rates: Three-Year Effects of CUNY's Accelerated Study in Associate Programs (ASAP) for Developmental Education Students

I139.title: The neighborhood where a child grows up shapes later earnings
I139.summary: Children whose families moved to lower-poverty neighborhoods before age 13 earned about 31% more as adults. Help finding homes in high-opportunity areas, and investment in existing neighborhoods, offer two routes to better outcomes.
I139.mechanism: Neighborhood conditions in childhood shape later earnings and access to opportunity.
I139.evidence_note: Well supported. In the Moving to Opportunity randomized trial, Chetty, Hendren and Katz (2016) found that children who moved to lower-poverty areas before age 13 earned about 31% more as adults. Chetty and colleagues (2020) document large gaps in mobility by race and place using tax data.
I139.remedy_note: Well supported. In a randomized trial in Seattle, mobility counseling raised the share of voucher families moving to high-opportunity areas from 15% to 53%.
I139.response: The Department of Housing and Urban Development, the states and cities would combine affordable housing in high-opportunity areas with mobility counseling and investment in existing communities.
I139.tradeoff: Moving can break community ties, and families need a real choice.
I139.success_measure: Children's time in high-opportunity areas, later outcomes, and residents who stay.

aimed_reforms.why: Allowing more homes by right in high-demand areas opens high-opportunity neighborhoods to more families.

problem_example.headline: Moving young children to lower-poverty areas raised adult earnings
problem_example.text: Between 1994 and 1998, the Moving to Opportunity experiment offered randomly chosen families in high-poverty public housing in five large cities vouchers to move. Children whose families used a voucher to move to a lower-poverty area before age 13 earned 31% more in their mid-twenties, about $3,477 a year. Moves in the teen years showed no such gain.

source.title: The Effects of Exposure to Better Neighborhoods on Children: New Evidence from the Moving to Opportunity Experiment (Chetty, Hendren, Katz)
source.publisher: NBER Working Paper 21156; published in the American Economic Review, 2016

fix_example.headline: Seattle-area search help moved more voucher families to opportunity
fix_example.text: In Seattle and King County, a randomized trial offered housing voucher families customized help with the housing search and short-term financial aid. The share moving to neighborhoods with high upward mobility rose from 15% to 53%. A second trial traced most of that effect to the customized search assistance.
fix_example.result: Moves to high-upward-mobility neighborhoods rose from 15% of families in the comparison group to 53% of families offered the help.

source.title: Creating Moves to Opportunity: Experimental Evidence on Barriers to Neighborhood Choice
source.publisher: NBER Working Paper 26164; published in the American Economic Review, 2024

I140.title: Past exclusion and present barriers sustain racial wealth gaps
I140.summary: White households hold about six times the wealth of Black households, and the gap stopped narrowing around 1980. Redlining maps drawn in the 1930s still show up in lower homeownership and home values decades later.
I140.mechanism: Historic exclusion and current barriers compound unequal assets across racial groups.
I140.evidence_note: Well supported. Derenoncourt and colleagues (2024), using data back to 1860, found the white-to-Black wealth ratio at about 6 to 1, with convergence stalled since 1980. Comparing areas on either side of map boundaries, Aaronson, Hartley and Mazumder (2021) found that the Home Owners' Loan Corporation's 1930s redlining maps reduced homeownership and home values for decades. The Federal Reserve's 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances shows median family wealth differing widely by race.
I140.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Fair-lending enforcement has case evidence. Asset-building programs have simulations and one randomized trial, Oklahoma's SEED child accounts, with modest early effects. Targeted repair programs are small and unevaluated.
I140.response: Congress, the states and the courts would enforce fair lending, widen access to asset building and evaluate targeted repair for documented public harms.
I140.tradeoff: Legal design and accurate attribution of harm matter.
I140.success_measure: Wealth gaps, access to credit, and whether remedies work.

problem_example.headline: 1930s redlining maps left lasting gaps in homeownership
problem_example.text: In the 1930s, the federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation drew maps grading neighborhoods in 239 cities. Comparing areas on either side of map boundaries in 149 cities, Chicago Fed economists found that the lowest-graded side had homeownership rates 3 to 4 percentage points lower through 1980. Its gap in house values peaked around 1980 and narrowed by 2010.

source.title: The Effects of the 1930s HOLC 'Redlining' Maps (Aaronson, Hartley, Mazumder)
source.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Working Paper 2017-12; published in AEJ: Economic Policy, 2021

I141.title: Rural and former industrial regions lose jobs and people
I141.summary: Regions hit by import competition from China had not recovered their lost employment by 2019. Weak services and people moving away can make the decline harder to reverse.
I141.mechanism: Trade and technology shocks, weak services and outmigration reinforce local decline.
I141.evidence_note: Well supported. Autor, Dorn and Hanson (2021) found that regions exposed to the China trade shock had not recovered employment by 2019. Austin, Glaeser and Summers (2018) argue for targeted place-based policy in an analytical paper.
I141.remedy_note: Plausible. The Tennessee Valley Authority raised long-run regional incomes, while many enterprise zones did not, according to Bartik's 2020 review of place-based policy. Design matters, and whether subsidized jobs would have appeared anyway is hard to verify.
I141.response: Congress, the states and regional bodies would invest in broadband, transport and health access, and use place-based grants that show they add jobs, with support for workers changing jobs.
I141.tradeoff: Subsidies can chase firms without helping residents.
I141.success_measure: Residents' earnings, access to services, and jobs that would not otherwise exist.

problem_example.headline: Job losses from Chinese imports persisted for years
problem_example.text: A 2021 Brookings paper tracked U.S. labor markets that faced rising import competition from China in goods such as furniture and textiles. Those places saw more plant closures and larger declines in manufacturing employment. The damage grew until 2013 and persisted through at least 2018, when the data end.

source.title: On the Persistence of the China Shock (Autor, Dorn, Hanson)

fix_example.headline: Tennessee Valley Authority left lasting manufacturing gains
fix_example.text: The Tennessee Valley Authority was one of the most ambitious regional development programs in U.S. history. Comparing its region with areas where similar authorities were proposed but never approved by Congress, economists Patrick Kline and Enrico Moretti found farm job gains reversed when subsidies ended. Manufacturing gains kept growing long after federal transfers stopped, raising regional income.
fix_example.result: Manufacturing employment gains in the TVA region kept growing after subsidies lapsed and raised regional income, though the authors found those regional gains were offset by losses elsewhere in the country.

source.title: Local Economic Development, Agglomeration Economies, and the Big Push: 100 Years of Evidence from the Tennessee Valley Authority (Kline, Moretti)
source.publisher: NBER Working Paper 19293; published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2014

I142.title: Poor transport and utility connections raise the cost of living
I142.summary: U.S. infrastructure earns a C grade from civil engineers, and drinking-water systems need $625 billion over 20 years. Unreliable connections make it harder to reach work or care and raise household costs.
I142.mechanism: Poor transport and utility connections restrict access to jobs, school and care and raise household costs.
I142.evidence_note: Well supported. In the Moving to Opportunity study, access to a car predicted employment gains (Blumenberg and Pierce, 2014). The Environmental Protection Agency's 2023 survey estimates $625 billion in drinking-water infrastructure needs over 20 years. The American Society of Civil Engineers gave U.S. infrastructure an overall C in 2025, a needs assessment by a professional association.
I142.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Evaluations find modest employment effects from transit investment. Plans that put maintenance first have engineering support and few outcome studies.
I142.response: Congress, the states and local utilities would put maintenance first and fund reliable transit, safe streets, water and affordable energy through accountable capital plans.
I142.tradeoff: Projects need funding for their whole life and credible cost estimates.
I142.success_measure: Travel time to jobs and services, reliability, and household costs.

problem_example.headline: EPA puts drinking-water repair needs at $625 billion
problem_example.text: In 2023, the Environmental Protection Agency estimated that U.S. drinking-water systems need $625 billion over 20 years. About $423 billion of that is for replacing or rehabilitating aging pipes, and the agency counts roughly four million lead service lines still in the ground.

source.title: EPA's 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey and Assessment

fix_example.headline: Newark says it replaced lead pipes in under three years
fix_example.text: Newark, New Jersey, began replacing lead water lines in 2018, backed by a $75 million city bond and a $120 million Essex County bond. The city says it replaced all of its roughly 23,000 known lead service lines in under three years, at no charge to residents. It also reported four straight monitoring periods with lead below 15 parts per billion.
fix_example.result: The city reported lead below 15 parts per billion for four consecutive monitoring periods, and its water director credited a new corrosion control system for the drop.

source.title: Mayor Baraka and Governor Murphy welcome Vice President Harris and U.S. EPA Administrator Regan to city to highlight success of lead line replacement program

I143.title: Pollution and disaster losses fall hardest on low-income communities
I143.summary: Fine-particle pollution falls disproportionately on people of color, and climate damage hits poorer counties hardest. In the riskiest ZIP codes, home insurance premiums ran 82% higher and nonrenewals about 80% higher from 2018 to 2022.
I143.mechanism: Low-income communities face more pollution, larger disaster losses and insurers pulling back from coverage.
I143.evidence_note: Documented. A Treasury Department report of January 2025 found that from 2018 to 2022 homeowners insurance premiums were 82% higher, and nonrenewal rates about 80% higher, in the riskiest ZIP codes. Using modeled exposure, Tessum and colleagues (2021) found that fine-particle pollution falls disproportionately on people of color across income levels. Hsiang and colleagues (2017) project that climate damages fall hardest on poorer counties in the South.
I143.remedy_note: Well supported. The benefits of the Clean Air Act exceed its costs by about 30 to 1, and the law narrowed racial gaps in exposure. Managed relocation away from high-risk areas has no U.S. evaluation.
I143.response: Congress, the Environmental Protection Agency, the states and cities would reduce emissions and local pollution, fund resilience and fair relocation, and reform how risk is priced, with targeted help on affordability.
I143.tradeoff: Pricing risk without alternatives can hit low-income households hardest, and relocation must guard against forced displacement.
I143.success_measure: Pollution exposure, losses avoided, and access to insurance.

aimed_reforms.why: Building codes and mitigation cut disaster losses, which keeps insurance available and protects owners' equity.

problem_example.headline: Homeowners in high-risk ZIP codes paid 82% more
problem_example.text: The Treasury Department's Federal Insurance Office studied more than 246 million homeowners policies from 2018 to 2022. Homeowners in the 20% of ZIP codes with the highest climate risk paid $2,321 in premiums on average, 82% more than those in the lowest-risk fifth. Their nonrenewal rates ran about 80% higher.

source.title: Treasury release on homeowners insurance costs and availability (Federal Insurance Office analysis)

fix_example.headline: Clean Air Act rules narrowed racial gaps in pollution exposure
fix_example.text: Federal Clean Air Act rules have cut fine-particle pollution, with larger declines in areas with bigger Black populations. A 2023 study in the American Economic Review found the law can account for over 60% of the narrowing in the Black-white gap in exposure since 2000.
fix_example.result: The study attributes over 60% of the racial convergence in fine-particle exposure since 2000 to the Clean Air Act.

source.title: What Caused Racial Disparities in Particulate Exposure to Fall? New Evidence from the Clean Air Act and Satellite-Based Measures of Air Quality (Currie, Voorheis, Walker)

I144.title: National averages hide barriers to getting ahead
I144.summary: About 90% of children born in 1940 grew up to earn more than their parents, compared with about 50% of those born in the 1980s. Results differ sharply by race and place, so a single national figure hides where pathways are blocked.
I144.mechanism: Absolute mobility, relative mobility and mobility by group move differently, so averages hide blocked pathways.
I144.evidence_note: Well supported. Chetty and colleagues (2017) found that absolute mobility, the chance of earning more than one's parents at age 30 after inflation, was about 90% for children born in 1940 and about 50% for those born in the 1980s. Using tax data, Chetty and colleagues (2020) showed large gaps by race and place in relative mobility, the chance of moving up the income ranking.
I144.remedy_note: Documented. The Opportunity Atlas, built with the Census Bureau, already publishes mobility measures for small areas, so the proposal is feasible.
I144.response: The Census Bureau, research institutions and agencies would publish mobility measures by birth cohort, race, gender, disability and place, with privacy protection and consistent definitions.
I144.tradeoff: Estimates for small areas carry uncertainty and arrive years after the fact.
I144.success_measure: Mobility by birth cohort, data quality, and groups missing from the data.

problem_example.headline: Black boys earn less than white peers almost everywhere
problem_example.text: Opportunity Insights researchers used de-identified records covering nearly the whole U.S. population from 1989 to 2015 to compare children raised at the same parental income. Black boys went on to earn less than white boys in 99% of Census tracts. The researchers found no comparable gap between Black and white women.

source.title: Race and Economic Opportunity in the United States: An Intergenerational Perspective (Chetty, Hendren, Jones, Porter)
source.publisher: Opportunity Insights; published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2020

fix_example.headline: Census Bureau published neighborhood-level mobility data in 2018
fix_example.text: In 2018, the Census Bureau and Opportunity Insights released the Opportunity Atlas, a Census tract-level dataset of children's outcomes in adulthood. It shows results such as earnings and incarceration for children born from 1978 to 1983, split by race and by parents' income, using data covering nearly the entire U.S. population.
fix_example.result: Tract-level mobility estimates are now public for the whole country, though the cited source does not measure how agencies have used them.

source.title: The Opportunity Atlas

I145.title: Work and care leave some people little time for civic life
I145.summary: People holding several jobs or caring for family can struggle to attend meetings and stay involved. Money and civic skills predict participation more strongly than free time, so time pressure is one barrier among several.
I145.mechanism: Multiple jobs and care duties can reduce civic participation outside elections, though money and civic skills predict participation more strongly than free time does.
I145.evidence_note: Plausible. In their civic voluntarism model, Verba, Schlozman and Brady (1995) found that money and civic skills predict participation more strongly than free time. AmeriCorps and the Census Bureau report that 28.3% of people volunteered through an organization in 2023.
I145.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Paying participants in intensive deliberative panels is standard practice, according to the OECD's 2020 review of close to 300 such processes. There is no causal evidence on how payment changes participation by income.
I145.response: Local governments, employers and civic groups would offer evening and hybrid meetings, child care and interpretation, and pay participants in intensive civic panels.
I145.success_measure: Participation by income, and people who come back to take part again.

problem_example.headline: Busy schedules kept millions of 2022 voters home
problem_example.text: In the 2022 midterm elections, 37.2 million registered voters did not cast a ballot. The most common reason they gave the Census Bureau was being too busy or having a conflicting schedule, cited by 9.9 million of them.

source.title: Census Bureau Releases 2022 Congressional Election Voting Report

fix_example.headline: Washington paid lottery-picked residents to join a climate assembly
fix_example.text: The Washington Climate Assembly, which first met in January 2021 and was described as a first-of-its-kind experiment in the U.S., chose 80 residents and 10 alternates by random-digit phone dialing. Each member was offered a $500 honorarium, and consultants set up computers and Wi-Fi for members who had not owned a personal computer.
fix_example.result: Crosscut reported that members roughly matched the state's racial diversity, gender breakdown and income levels, but it did not report whether the honorarium changed who agreed to serve.

source.title: Washington hosts first climate assembly in the United States

I146.title: Public meetings hear mostly from organized insiders
I146.summary: People who speak at local public meetings are older, more often male, more likely to own homes and more opposed to new housing than the voters around them. Officials can come away with a distorted picture of what residents want.
I146.mechanism: Self-selection into public meetings distorts whose preferences officials hear.
I146.evidence_note: Well supported. Matching meeting minutes to voter files, Einstein, Palmer and Glick (2019) found that commenters were older, more often male, more likely to own homes and more opposed to housing than voters overall. Using a regression discontinuity, Yoder (2020) found that owning property causally raises participation in local politics.
I146.remedy_note: Plausible. Assemblies selected by lottery produce bodies that match the population, according to the OECD's 2020 review. Evidence that governments act on their recommendations comes from individual cases.
I146.response: Legislatures and cities would combine open public comment with civic lotteries stratified to match the population, and publish their responses to panel recommendations.
I146.tradeoff: A randomly selected panel cannot replace the accountability of elected officials.
I146.success_measure: How representative participants are, public responses, and policy follow-up.

aimed_reforms.why: Lottery-selected assemblies with a duty to respond bring in residents who would not self-select.
Allowing homes by right moves housing decisions out of the meetings that owners dominate.

problem_example.headline: Massachusetts zoning meetings heard mostly from older opponents
problem_example.text: In 97 Massachusetts cities and towns outside Boston, researchers read planning and zoning board minutes from 2015 to 2017. The average commenter was 58, compared with 50 among all voters, and 63% of comments opposed proposed housing while about 15% supported it.

source.title: 'Troubling' Findings on Who Speaks Up About Housing Development

fix_example.headline: Ireland's lottery-picked assembly shaped a national referendum
fix_example.text: In 2016, Ireland drew 99 citizens at random to broadly represent the public and study the Eighth Amendment, the constitutional provision restricting abortion. A parliamentary committee considered the assembly's report and in December 2017 recommended a referendum on removing it.
fix_example.result: Voters removed the amendment on May 25, 2018, with 66.4% in favor.

source.title: Ireland - Public debate concerning abortion and the repeal of the eighth amendment to the constitution (2016)

I147.title: Civic associations are losing members and support
I147.summary: Membership in local associations and congregations has fallen for decades, and church membership dropped below half of U.S. adults in 2020. Fewer places for recurring shared work mean fewer chances to build local trust.
I147.mechanism: Civic associations struggle to sustain shared work and local trust.
I147.evidence_note: Well supported. Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000) documents a long decline in membership associations, though some of its measures are contested. Skocpol (2003) traces a shift from membership federations to professionally managed advocacy groups. Gallup found that church membership fell to 47% of U.S. adults in 2020, the first time below half.
I147.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Neutral grants for libraries and associations have no evaluation of their effect on civic trust.
I147.response: States, cities and philanthropies would support libraries, community spaces and independent associations through neutral grants and affordable access.
I147.tradeoff: Funding has to avoid favoring any party.
I147.success_measure: Active associations, and the diversity of people taking part.

aimed_reforms.why: Builds membership organizations where people of different parties do shared work.

problem_example.headline: Church membership fell below half of Americans
problem_example.text: In 2020, Gallup found that 47% of U.S. adults belonged to a religious congregation, the first time in its polling that the share fell below half. Membership had stood at 70% in 1999 and 73% when Gallup first measured it in 1937.

source.title: U.S. Church Membership Falls Below Majority for First Time

fix_example.headline: Akron park upgrades raised neighbor contact but not trust
fix_example.text: Starting in 2016, a group of national foundations funded upgrades to parks and public spaces in several cities through Reimagining the Civic Commons. In Akron's Summit Lake neighborhood, the share of residents socializing with neighbors in a given week rose to 53% from 31%.
fix_example.result: Residents who said most people can be trusted fell from 18% in 2017 to 10% in 2022, so the results are mixed.

source.title: How 59 data points helped foundations spark elusive change

I148.title: Residents cannot see how to influence a decision
I148.summary: When people cannot tell when a decision will be made or who makes it, taking part feels futile and insiders gain. Belief that government responds to people like oneself is at or near record lows.
I148.mechanism: Opaque processes produce a sense of futility and dependence on insiders.
I148.evidence_note: Plausible. The American National Election Studies series shows external political efficacy, the belief that government responds to people like oneself, at or near record lows. Michener (2018) found that experiences with Medicaid administration shape later political participation, and Soss (1999) found that the design of welfare programs teaches recipients lessons about government.
I148.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Publishing decision calendars and explanations has no causal evaluation, and transparency experiments show mixed effects on trust.
I148.response: Governments at every level would publish decision calendars, the officials responsible, the ways to take part and plain-language explanations of final choices.
I148.tradeoff: Information without real influence can deepen cynicism.
I148.success_measure: Understanding of the process, official responses, and participation.

aimed_reforms.why: Requires officials to answer recommendations in public, showing residents what their input changed.
Gives residents a defined budget decision they can see and affect.

problem_example.headline: New York's Amazon deal skipped the city's land-use review
problem_example.text: In November 2018, Amazon chose Long Island City, Queens, for a new headquarters under a deal with New York's governor and mayor. The state planned to approve it through a process that bypassed the city's land-use review, where the City Council plays a key role, and local Councilman Jimmy Van Bramer said he learned of the deal through the news.

source.title: New York State bypassed City Council on Amazon

fix_example.headline: New York City puts land-use decisions on a public clock
fix_example.text: New York City sends major land-use changes through a fixed public review. The local community board gets 60 days, then the borough president 30, the City Planning Commission 60 and the City Council 50, so residents can see who decides and when.
fix_example.result: The schedule makes each step and decision-maker public, but no study has measured whether it gives residents more influence or trust.

source.title: The Process: Siting New Jails

I149.title: Hostility toward the other party leads voters to excuse their own side
I149.summary: When partisans dislike or fear the other party, many will still vote for their own candidate after that candidate breaks democratic rules. That weakens the electoral cost of misconduct, though researchers dispute how much.
I149.mechanism: Hostility toward the other party leads partisans to excuse misconduct by their own side.
I149.evidence_note: Well supported. In Graham and Svolik's 2020 experiments, only about 3.5% of voters were willing to defect from their party's candidate over an undemocratic position in realistic matchups, although the average penalty in vote share was 11.7 points. Iyengar and colleagues (2019) review the causes and consequences of affective polarization, the dislike of the other party's supporters. Broockman, Kalla and Westwood (2023) found that affective polarization does not clearly reduce accountability, so the link is contested.
I149.remedy_note: Plausible. A megastudy testing 25 interventions reduced partisan animosity, and several also reduced support for undemocratic practices or partisan violence. Durability was measured over about two weeks, and effects on conduct outside the study are untested.
I149.response: Civic groups, parties and local institutions would organize structured cross-party work on concrete shared problems and apply equal standards to political conduct.
I149.tradeoff: Contact reduces hostility only under certain conditions, and surface civility cannot settle conflicts over rights.
I149.success_measure: Attitudes toward the other party, joint work across parties, and consistent application of conduct standards.

aimed_reforms.why: Cross-partisan membership and service is the structured contact this record proposes.

problem_example.headline: Fewer hardline Montana voters punished an attack on a reporter
problem_example.text: In 2017, Republican candidate Greg Gianforte body-slammed a reporter in his campaign office the night before Montana's congressional election, when more than half of voters had already cast absentee ballots. Yale researchers found that Election Day voters in politically moderate precincts punished him by voting across party lines, while significantly fewer did so in hardline Republican precincts.

source.title: Most U.S. Voters Value Party Over Democracy

fix_example.headline: Washington's climate assembly brought rival viewpoints to shared work
fix_example.text: In early 2021, 80 Washington residents chosen by lottery spent seven weeks online writing climate recommendations for the Legislature. Evaluators from the Clinton School of Public Service reported a decrease in sensitivity to polarization and a willingness to work together among people with different viewpoints and political identities.
fix_example.result: The findings were preliminary and covered only assembly members, so lasting or wider effects are unmeasured.

source.title: Park, Richards, Noori Present Evaluation Findings to Washington State Climate Assembly
source.publisher: Clinton School of Public Service, University of Arkansas

I150.title: Scapegoating divides people who could work together
I150.summary: Blaming racial or identity groups for hardship can pull attention away from the institutions that cause it. It also denies people equal standing and splits potential coalitions.
I150.mechanism: Scapegoating diverts grievances from institutional causes and denies equal standing.
I150.evidence_note: Plausible. Sides, Tesler and Vavreck's Identity Crisis (2018) found from surveys that identity attitudes predicted vote shifts in 2016 more than economic distress did. In a field experiment, Enos (2014) found that brief exposure to members of an outgroup increased exclusionary attitudes.
I150.remedy_note: Plausible. A review of 27 randomized studies that measured outcomes at least a day after contact between groups found that contact typically reduces prejudice. Effects were weaker for racial and ethnic prejudice, no study addressed adults' racial or ethnic prejudice, and long-term studies are scarce.
I150.response: Schools, civic groups and parties would protect equal participation and create local forums that connect material problems to evidence without blaming whole groups.
I150.tradeoff: Dialogue requires safety and equal status for those taking part.
I150.success_measure: Gaps in participation, and discriminatory incidents.

aimed_reforms.why: Repeated shared work across groups is the kind of contact this record's response relies on.

problem_example.headline: Boston commuters grew less welcoming after brief contact
problem_example.text: In July and August 2012, Harvard researcher Ryan Enos placed Spanish speakers working for his study on commuter rail platforms in largely Anglo-white Boston-area towns for 10 working days. Regular riders who saw them shifted toward wanting fewer immigrants from Mexico and opposing letting undocumented immigrants stay, though the effect may have weakened with repeated contact.

source.title: Causal effect of intergroup contact on exclusionary attitudes (Enos), PNAS 111(10), author copy
source.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

fix_example.headline: Door-to-door conversations eased hostility toward immigrants for months
fix_example.text: In field experiments published in 2020, political scientists Joshua Kalla and David Broockman tested door-to-door conversations in which canvassers and voters swapped personal stories without judgment. Across three experiments, 230 canvassers talked with 6,869 voters in seven U.S. locations, and the first experiment reduced exclusionary attitudes toward unauthorized immigrants for at least four months.
fix_example.result: The effect was small, about 0.08 of a standard deviation, and two later experiments on attitudes toward transgender people found similar results.

source.title: Reducing Exclusionary Attitudes through Interpersonal Conversation: Evidence from Three Field Experiments (Kalla, Broockman)

I151.title: Living apart reduces everyday contact across groups
I151.summary: Americans increasingly live in neighborhoods separated by income and, to a degree, by party. Fewer shared places mean less ordinary contact across groups, though the effect on cooperation has not been measured.
I151.mechanism: Residential and institutional separation narrows shared experience across groups. Its consequences for cooperation are plausible and unmeasured.
I151.evidence_note: Plausible. Brown and Enos (2021) measured partisan residential sorting for 180 million voters. Mummolo and Nall (2017) found that partisans rarely choose neighborhoods by politics, which limits how much of the sorting is deliberate. Income segregation rose along with income inequality, according to Reardon and Bischoff (2011).
I151.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Inclusive public spaces and service across communities have no causal evaluation of their effect on belonging.
I151.response: Cities, schools and civic organizations would expand inclusive public spaces, service projects across communities and access to housing, with evaluation.
I151.tradeoff: Forced contact or displacement can backfire.
I151.success_measure: Sustained contact across groups, and a sense of belonging.

aimed_reforms.why: Cross-community civic service creates the shared experience that separation removes.

problem_example.headline: Rich and poor Americans increasingly live apart
problem_example.text: In 2010, 18% of upper-income U.S. households lived in mostly upper-income neighborhoods, double the 9% of 1980, the Pew Research Center found. Income segregation rose in 27 of the 30 largest metro areas, with Houston and Dallas the most divided of the ten biggest.
problem_example.where: United States (Houston and Dallas highest among the 10 largest metros)

source.title: The Rise of Residential Segregation by Income

fix_example.headline: Housing vouchers helped young children who moved
fix_example.text: The Moving to Opportunity experiment gave randomly chosen families in high-poverty housing projects vouchers to move to lower-poverty neighborhoods. A 2015 study led by economist Raj Chetty found that children who moved before age 13 earned 31% more a year in their mid-twenties than children in the comparison group.
fix_example.result: Children who moved after 13 saw no gain and possibly harm, and the study did not measure contact across groups.

source.title: The Effects of Exposure to Better Neighborhoods on Children: New Evidence from the Moving to Opportunity Experiment (Chetty, Hendren, Katz)
source.publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research, Working Paper 21156

I152.title: Loneliness and distrust may make cooperation harder
I152.summary: Americans spend more time alone than they did two decades ago, and loneliness carries well-documented health risks. Whether it weakens communities' ability to solve problems together has not been measured.
I152.mechanism: Weak relationships and low trust make collective problem-solving harder. The health effects of loneliness are well supported; the step to weaker collective problem-solving is asserted without measurement.
I152.evidence_note: Plausible. The U.S. Surgeon General's 2023 advisory synthesizes evidence on loneliness and health. Using the American Time Use Survey, a 2023 study found that time alone rose and social engagement fell from 2003 to 2020. Neither source measures collective problem-solving.
I152.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Investment in community institutions has no evaluation of its effect on cooperation.
I152.response: States, cities and nonprofits would invest in accessible community institutions and repeated shared activities, in partnership with public health agencies.

aimed_reforms.why: Repeated shared work in membership organizations builds the relationships this record finds missing.

problem_example.headline: Americans' time with friends fell by two-thirds
problem_example.text: In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General warned that about half of American adults report experiencing loneliness. Drawing on time-use data, the advisory found that time spent with friends in person fell from 60 minutes a day in 2003 to 20 minutes in 2020.

source.title: Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation: The U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory
source.publisher: Office of the U.S. Surgeon General

fix_example.headline: England funded neighborhood projects to fight loneliness
fix_example.text: England's Know Your Neighbourhood Fund put up to £30 million into volunteering and loneliness projects in 27 disadvantaged areas, running until March 2025. When surveyed at the start, 15% of people in funded projects said they felt lonely often or always, compared with 7% of the general population.
fix_example.result: An independent interim evaluation published in August 2025 said it was not yet possible to assess the fund's impact.

source.title: Interim overarching evaluation on the Know Your Neighbourhood Fund
source.publisher: UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport (evaluation by RSM UK)

I153.title: Parties tolerate conduct that weakens democratic rules
I153.summary: When voters rarely punish their own side, parties pay little price for nominating or protecting members who deny election results or intimidate opponents. Party rules and discipline are one place this can be checked.
I153.mechanism: Electoral incentives reward parties that tolerate election denial, intimidation or abuse by their members.
I153.evidence_note: Well supported. Graham and Svolik (2020) found that only about 3.5% of voters would defect from their party's candidate over an undemocratic position in realistic matchups. Levitsky and Ziblatt's How Democracies Die (2018) argues from comparative history that party gatekeeping is a central safeguard. Bright Line Watch surveys of experts and the public track the erosion of democratic norms through 2026.
I153.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Party conduct standards have comparative examples abroad and no U.S. test.
I153.response: Political parties and civic organizations would adopt enforceable standards for nominations and conduct, with transparent disciplinary procedures.
I153.tradeoff: Gatekeeping needs internal democracy and due process.
I153.success_measure: Compliance with party rules, and consistent sanctions.

problem_example.headline: Each party mostly shielded its own member from censure
problem_example.text: In November 2021, the House censured Republican Paul Gosar for posting a cartoon that depicted violence against Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez; 207 Republicans voted no and 2 voted yes. In December 2023, it censured Democrat Jamaal Bowman, who had pleaded guilty to falsely pulling a fire alarm; 191 Democrats voted no and 3 voted yes.

source.title: Roll Call 379: H.Res. 789, Censuring Representative Paul Gosar
source.publisher: Office of the Clerk, U.S. House of Representatives

I154.title: Threats and violence raise the cost of public life
I154.summary: The U.S. Capitol Police opened 14,938 threat cases in 2025, the third straight annual rise, and 43% of state legislators surveyed reported threats. When serving in office or speaking up invites danger, fewer people take part.
I154.mechanism: Threats raise the personal cost of public service and of public disagreement.
I154.evidence_note: Documented. The U.S. Capitol Police opened 14,938 threat-assessment cases in 2025, the third straight annual increase. In a 2024 Brennan Center survey, 43% of state legislators reported threats.
I154.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Funding for threat prevention has no outcome evaluation; the case for it rests on official counts and surveys.
I154.response: The Justice Department, the states and local law enforcement would fund lawful threat prevention, protect people who are targeted and prosecute violence under viewpoint-neutral standards.
I154.tradeoff: Broad labels of extremism can chill lawful protest.
I154.success_measure: Threat cases resolved, safety of victims, and public participation.

problem_example.headline: Threats against Congress jumped to nearly 15,000 cases
problem_example.text: In 2025, the U.S. Capitol Police's threat assessment unit investigated 14,938 concerning statements aimed at members of Congress, up from 9,474 in 2024. It was the third straight yearly increase and the highest count in the five years the agency reported.

source.title: USCP Threat Assessment Cases for 2025

fix_example.headline: Capitol Police tripled local protection agreements in 2025
fix_example.text: In 2025, the U.S. Capitol Police tripled its formal agreements with local law enforcement agencies that help protect members of Congress in their home districts. It has also detailed its own attorneys to the Justice Department, where they have consulted with agents on 875 cases and worked on 1,705 subpoenas.
fix_example.result: Threat cases still rose sharply that year, and no evaluation has measured whether these steps prevented violence.

source.title: USCP Threat Assessment Cases for 2025

I155.title: Unsupported fraud claims weaken acceptance of defeat
I155.summary: After the 2020 election, claims of fraud large enough to change the outcome failed in court, and a review by conservative lawyers found no supporting evidence in any of 64 cases. Such claims still threaten the peaceful transfer of power when officials act on them.
I155.mechanism: Unsupported claims of election fraud weaken the peaceful transfer of power.
I155.evidence_note: Documented. The House Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack on the United States Capitol issued its final report in 2022 on the effort to overturn the 2020 result. Lost, Not Stolen (2022), an independent review by conservative lawyers and former officials, found no evidence of outcome-changing fraud in any of 64 court cases.
I155.remedy_note: Plausible. Experiments show mixed effects of audit evidence on belief. The Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022 clarified certification duties.
I155.response: Election offices, parties and courts would publish audit evidence people can understand, require officials to follow lawful certification and treat concession after a resolved contest as the norm.
I155.tradeoff: Legitimate challenges to results must remain available.
I155.success_measure: Public understanding of audit evidence, and lawful transfers of power.

problem_example.headline: Appeals court refused to block Pennsylvania's 2020 certified result
problem_example.text: In November 2020, the Trump campaign asked a federal appeals court to stop Pennsylvania's certified presidential totals, a margin of 80,555 votes, from taking effect. The Third Circuit refused, noting the campaign "never alleges that any ballot was fraudulent," and Judge Stephanos Bibas wrote that "calling an election unfair does not make it so."

source.title: Donald J. Trump for President, Inc. v. Secretary, Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, No. 20-3371
source.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit

fix_example.headline: Congress raised the bar for objecting to electoral votes
fix_example.text: In December 2022, Congress amended the federal law for counting presidential electoral votes. An objection to a state's votes now needs the signatures of at least one-fifth of each chamber's members, and the vice president's role in the count is limited to "solely ministerial duties."
fix_example.result: Congress counted the 2024 electoral votes under these rules on January 6, 2025; whether they raise public acceptance of results is unmeasured.

source.title: Provisions of the Constitution and United States Code (Electoral College)
source.publisher: National Archives, Office of the Federal Register

I156.title: A sense that nothing works keeps people from taking part
I156.summary: Trust in the federal government stood at 17% in September 2025, near historic lows. People who believe every institution is beyond repair may stop trying to influence decisions, leaving more room for organized insiders.
I156.mechanism: A belief that institutions cannot be repaired reduces participation and leaves more room for capture by organized interests.
I156.evidence_note: Plausible. A long-running survey series on trust in the federal government put it at 17% in September 2025, near historic lows; question wording, poll source and smoothing affect the series. Hetherington (2005) found from panel data that low trust reduces support for redistributive policy. The Pew Research Center found in 2023 that majorities describe politics as exhausting.
I156.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Pairing candor about failure with visible repair has no evaluation, and some transparency experiments backfire.
I156.response: Governments, civic educators and newsrooms would pair honest accounts of failure with visible institutional repair and verified local results.
I156.tradeoff: Claims of success that read as propaganda damage credibility.
I156.success_measure: Knowledge of outcomes, participation, and trust that matches performance.

aimed_reforms.why: Reliable delivery of benefits, refunds and permits is the visible repair most people would notice.

problem_example.headline: Trust in the federal government fell to 17%
problem_example.text: In September 2025, a Pew Research Center poll found that just 17% of Americans trust the government in Washington to do what is right. Pew's compiled series begins in 1958, and trust peaked at 77% in 1964.

source.title: Public Trust in Government: 1958 to 2025

I157.title: Civics classes teach facts more than practice
I157.summary: Eighth graders' national civics scores fell for the first time in 2022. Students learn the branches of government and get little practice taking part in a real public decision.
I157.mechanism: Civics instruction emphasizes recall over the skills of participation.
I157.evidence_note: Documented. The National Assessment of Educational Progress recorded its first decline in eighth-grade civics scores in 2022, leaving the average no different from 1998. Campbell's 2019 review found that an open classroom climate and applied practice predict later participation.
I157.remedy_note: Plausible. Campbell's 2019 review found that an open classroom climate and applied practice predict later participation. Those findings are associations from observational studies, and action civics programs have little rigorous evaluation.
I157.response: States, schools and libraries would teach budgeting, evaluating sources, rights and deliberation through nonpartisan local projects.
I157.tradeoff: Curriculum has to avoid party indoctrination and protect open discussion.
I157.success_measure: Civic skills applied in practice, and sustained engagement.

problem_example.headline: Eighth-grade civics scores fell for the first time
problem_example.text: In 2022, the average civics score of U.S. eighth graders on the National Assessment of Educational Progress fell 2 points from 2018, the test's first decline. The score was no different from 1998, and the share of students below the Basic level rose 3 percentage points.

source.title: NAEP 2022 Civics Highlights, Grade 8

fix_example.headline: Massachusetts requires a student-led civics project
fix_example.text: In November 2018, Massachusetts enacted a law requiring every public school serving eighth graders, and every public high school, to give each student at least one student-led, nonpartisan civics project. It also created a Civics Project Trust Fund, with private gifts reviewed so they do not undermine neutral teaching.
fix_example.result: The law requires yearly reports on the fund's money but not on student outcomes, so effects on later participation are unmeasured.

source.title: Acts of 2018, Chapter 296: An Act to Promote and Enhance Civic Engagement

I158.title: Selling reforms as cure-alls invites disappointment
I158.summary: Presenting a complicated reform as a complete fix sets expectations it cannot meet. Whether that disappointment turns into resistance is a hypothesis that has not been tested in reform campaigns.
I158.mechanism: Overpromising what a reform will do produces later disappointment and resistance. The claim is a hypothesis.
I158.evidence_note: Hypothesis. No study listed for this record measures disappointment or resistance after an overpromised reform. Ballotpedia records the 2026 initiative to repeal Alaska's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election, one case of a reform facing reversal; the record does not show why voters sought it.
I158.remedy_note: Hypothesis. In experiments, Fernbach and colleagues (2013) found that asking people to explain how a policy works reduced the extremity of their positions. Framing research from the FrameWorks Institute informs layered explanation. Neither has been evaluated in a reform campaign.
I158.response: Educators and reform organizations would explain one mechanism, one concrete policy and its tradeoff at a time, in layered materials with accessible sources.
I158.tradeoff: Simplifying can erase real uncertainty about causes.
I158.success_measure: Comprehension, the rate of misconceptions, and accurate recall.

problem_example.headline: A health law promise collided with cancellation notices
problem_example.text: President Obama, selling the 2010 health care law, said many times that "if you like your health care plan, you can keep it." By December 2013, analysts estimated about 4 million Americans had received cancellation notices, and PolitiFact named the promise its Lie of the Year.

source.title: Lie of the Year: 'If you like your health care plan, you can keep it'

I159.title: Public feedback rarely turns into better services
I159.summary: Congressional offices and agencies receive large volumes of messages and have little capacity to connect them to recurring service failures. A visible response process would show residents whether their experience led to a change.
I159.mechanism: Constituent messages arrive in high volume and are poorly connected to service improvement.
I159.evidence_note: Plausible. The Congressional Management Foundation's 2017 survey of offices found rising volumes of constituent contact and limited staff capacity. Bergan (2009) found in a field experiment that a constituent email campaign shifted state legislators' votes, which shows that some feedback registers.
I159.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Public issue tracking with required responses has no evaluation.
I159.response: Legislatures and agencies would create accessible feedback systems with public issue tracking and required responses, while protecting personal records.
I159.tradeoff: Automated summaries of feedback need audits and a human route for appeal.
I159.success_measure: Quality of responses, issues resolved, and privacy protection.

aimed_reforms.why: A public duty to respond is the element this record's feedback systems would require.

problem_example.headline: Flint residents' water complaints went unheeded for months
problem_example.text: In April 2014, Flint, Michigan, began treating Flint River water full time. Michigan's Flint Water Advisory Task Force later found that the state environmental agency "stubbornly worked to discredit and dismiss" people raising alarms, and that the governor's office relied on incorrect information despite "months of citizens' complaints." The city switched back in October 2015.

source.title: Flint Water Advisory Task Force Final Report
source.publisher: Flint Water Advisory Task Force, State of Michigan

fix_example.headline: UK petitions with 10,000 signatures get a government reply
fix_example.text: The UK Parliament's petition site promises a published government response to any petition that gathers 10,000 signatures. Petitions reaching 100,000 are considered for debate in Parliament and are usually debated, and each response appears on the petition's own page with its date.
fix_example.result: By October 2026 the site listed 406 petitions with government responses in the current Parliament, though no study has tied the system to better services.

source.title: How petitions work

I160.title: Future generations have little voice in current decisions
I160.summary: Voters reward disaster relief after the fact and give little credit for spending to prepare beforehand. People who will bear later costs, including today's children, have little organized voice in current decisions.
I160.mechanism: Short political horizons neglect prevention and future burdens.
I160.evidence_note: Well supported. Healy and Malhotra (2009) found that voters reward disaster relief spending and give no electoral credit for preparedness spending, a causal result. Jacobs (2011) gives a comparative account of when democracies invest for the long term. The Congressional Budget Office projects federal debt rising from 101% of GDP in 2026 to 120% in 2036.
I160.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Wales's Well-being of Future Generations Act is the main institutional example and has no rigorous evaluation.
I160.response: Congress, the states and audit institutions would require long-term impact statements, youth participation and independent review of future risks for major decisions.
I160.tradeoff: Forecasts are uncertain, and the authority of unelected reviewers needs limits.
I160.success_measure: Long-term risks addressed, and how costs and benefits are spread across generations.

problem_example.headline: Voters rewarded disaster relief over preparation
problem_example.text: In 2009, researchers Andrew Healy and Neil Malhotra found that U.S. voters reward the president's party for disaster relief spending and give it no credit for preparedness spending. They estimated that each $1 spent on preparedness is worth about $15 in future damage it prevents.

source.title: Myopic Voters and Natural Disaster Policy (Healy, Malhotra)

fix_example.headline: Wales wrote future generations into law
fix_example.text: In 2015, Wales passed the Well-being of Future Generations Act, which places a well-being duty on public bodies and lets the Auditor General examine how they apply the sustainable development principle. It also created a Commissioner for Future Generations to advise and assist public bodies.
fix_example.result: The Act builds in oversight through Auditor General examinations, Commissioner reviews and annual reports, but the law itself does not measure whether public bodies' long-term decisions changed.

source.title: Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015

I161.title: Presidential direction of prosecutions threatens equal enforcement
I161.summary: In 2025 the President publicly urged prosecutions of named critics, and a newly appointed prosecutor brought them days later. A judge dismissed those cases because the prosecutor was unlawfully appointed, and no court has found the prosecutions selective.
I161.mechanism: Political direction of law enforcement can be used to punish opponents or protect allies. The documented case shows public presidential direction followed by indictments; no court has found selective prosecution.
I161.evidence_note: Documented. On November 24, 2025, a federal judge dismissed without prejudice the indictments of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James, finding that the interim U.S. Attorney who brought them had been unlawfully appointed; NPR reported that the President had publicly urged the prosecutions days before her appointment. The Congressional Research Service has analyzed the appointment ruling. The dismissal rested on the appointment defect, and no court has made a finding about motive.
I161.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Policies governing contacts between the White House and the Justice Department, and recusal rules, have been proposed. The 2025 dismissals rested on appointment defects, with no finding of selective prosecution.
I161.response: Congress, the Justice Department and the courts would publish enforcement criteria and policies for White House contacts with the Justice Department, keep records of those contacts, require recusal for conflicts and provide oversight and court remedies where the law allows.
I161.tradeoff: Prosecutors keep discretion and presidents keep lawful supervision of the executive branch, so full independence cannot be assumed.
I161.success_measure: Consistent treatment of comparable cases, documented contacts, and conflicts resolved.

problem_example.headline: Charges the President urged were dismissed on appointment grounds
problem_example.text: In September 2025, days before Lindsey Halligan was sworn in as interim U.S. attorney in eastern Virginia, President Trump posted that the Justice Department should prosecute former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Halligan then obtained indictments of both. On November 24, 2025, a federal judge dismissed the cases without prejudice, ruling that Halligan had been unlawfully appointed.

source.title: Judge tosses Comey, James cases after finding prosecutor unlawfully appointed

I162.title: Pardons can remove consequences for conduct that served those in power
I162.summary: On January 20, 2025, the President granted about 1,500 pardons and commutations for offenses connected to the events at the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. A statute can require disclosure; narrowing the pardon power itself would take a constitutional amendment.
I162.mechanism: Pardons reduce accountability for conduct that benefited powerful officials.
I162.evidence_note: Documented. A White House proclamation of January 20, 2025 granted about 1,500 pardons and commutations for offenses related to the events at or near the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021.
I162.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Disclosure of reasons and contacts are statutory proposals. The pardon power itself cannot be narrowed by statute.
I162.response: The President would give prompt reasons for each grant and lawful disclosure of contacts, and Congress would require that disclosure and independent review of conflicts by law. Congress and the states would use a constitutional amendment for any restriction beyond what a statute can reach.
I162.tradeoff: Ordinary legislation cannot narrow the constitutional pardon power in any comprehensive way.
I162.success_measure: Timeliness of disclosure, and conflict reviews completed.

problem_example.headline: Clemency covered everyone convicted over January 6
problem_example.text: On January 20, 2025, President Trump commuted the sentences of 14 people and granted full pardons to all other individuals convicted of offenses tied to the events at or near the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. The proclamation gave no individual reasons and said it "ends a grave national injustice."

source.title: Granting Pardons and Commutation of Sentences for Certain Offenses Relating to the Events at or Near the United States Capitol on January 6, 2021

fix_example.headline: Georgia moved pardons from its governor to a board
fix_example.text: In 1943, after serious questions about how some governors' offices had handled pardons, Georgia created an independent State Board of Pardons and Paroles. Voters ratified a constitutional amendment that August giving the board power to grant pardons and commute sentences. Board members serve seven-year terms and cannot be removed before their terms end.
fix_example.result: Clemency in Georgia has been decided by an appointed board with fixed terms for more than 80 years; the source does not measure effects on pardon decisions.

source.title: About Us
source.publisher: Georgia State Board of Pardons and Paroles

I163.title: At-will removal of regulators narrows agency independence
I163.summary: In June 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that the President can remove FTC commissioners at will, and the same day left protection for Federal Reserve governors in place. Whether the change has altered enforcement priorities has not yet been measured.
I163.mechanism: Ending removal protection for commissioners narrows regulatory independence. The further claim, that at-will removal changes enforcement priorities, has no measured case yet.
I163.evidence_note: Documented for the legal change. In Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026), the Supreme Court held the FTC's for-cause removal protection unconstitutional and overruled what remained of Humphrey's Executor, leaving the Federal Reserve and non-Article III courts unresolved. In Trump v. Cook the same day, the Court left removal protection in place for a Federal Reserve governor. The Congressional Research Service explains the ruling's scope and open questions.
I163.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Protections built after Slaughter from records, reasons and oversight are untested. Trump v. Cook shows the Federal Reserve exception held at the stay stage.
I163.response: Congress, agencies and the courts would protect statutory duties, require published reasons, keep records, protect professional case development and maintain congressional oversight, and would analyze the remaining tenure arrangements separately.
I163.tradeoff: Slaughter leaves Federal Reserve tenure and ordinary career-service protections undecided.
I163.success_measure: Enforcement reversals made without explanation, vacancies, and compliance with review.

aimed_reforms.why: Builds independence from records, public reasons for removal and agency structure after Slaughter.

status.text: On June 29, 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in Trump v. Slaughter that the President may remove Federal Trade Commission members at will, and it overruled Humphrey's Executor (1935). The same day, in Trump v. Cook, the Court voted 5 to 4 to deny the government's request to let the President remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook while her case continues. Cook is an interim order: she stays in office for now, and the Court has not decided whether the Fed's for-cause protection is valid.

problem_example.headline: Two presidents removed FTC commissioners over policy
problem_example.text: In 1933, President Franklin Roosevelt removed FTC Commissioner William Humphrey, writing that their minds did not "go along together" on the commission's policies. The Supreme Court held in 1935 that the law allowed removal only for cause. In June 2026, ruling on President Trump's 2025 firing of Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter, the Court overruled that decision 6 to 3, so FTC commissioners can now be removed at will.

source.title: Trump v. Slaughter, No. 25-332
source.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States

I164.title: Empty seats and acting officials can stop agencies from acting
I164.summary: Commissions such as the Federal Election Commission and the National Labor Relations Board cannot decide cases without a quorum, and both lost one in 2025. Prolonged or unlawful acting appointments can also bypass Senate confirmation.
I164.mechanism: Unfilled seats block the quorums agencies need to act, and unlawful acting arrangements evade Senate confirmation.
I164.evidence_note: Documented. The National Labor Relations Board lacked a quorum from January 2025 until confirmations on January 7, 2026, according to a law-firm summary of the public record. The Federal Election Commission issued a notice of lack of quorum on April 6, 2026. The Congressional Research Service analyzed a 2025 court ruling that the appointment of an interim U.S. Attorney, Lindsey Halligan, was unlawful.
I164.remedy_note: Plausible. Published vacancy clocks and enforcement of limits on acting officials are procedural tools. Courts have voided actions by unlawfully appointed officials, which shows enforcement works case by case.
I164.response: Congress, executive agencies and the courts would publish how long each seat has been vacant and what that does to quorums, enforce lawful limits on acting service, keep professional lines of succession and schedule review of nominations.
I164.tradeoff: Rigid deadlines can create new paralysis, and succession must follow the statute.
I164.success_measure: Vacancy days, interruptions of quorum, and valid appointments.

aimed_reforms.why: Restores the Federal Election Commission's quorum, one of the vacancies this record names.
Builds quorum rules and staggered seats into agency design so vacancies do less damage.

problem_example.headline: Election regulator loses the votes it needs to act
problem_example.text: The Federal Election Commission lost its quorum on May 1, 2025, after Commissioner Allen Dickerson resigned and left three members, one short of the four votes needed to open investigations or defend lawsuits. Another resignation in October 2025 left two. In April 2026 the commission told a court it could not defend a lawsuit, with two nominations still pending.

source.title: FEC notice of lack of quorum

fix_example.headline: Supreme Court enforces the limit on acting officials
fix_example.text: In June 2010, Lafe Solomon became acting general counsel of the National Labor Relations Board, and in January 2011 President Barack Obama nominated him for the permanent job. In NLRB v. SW General (2017), the Supreme Court ruled that the Federal Vacancies Reform Act barred him from serving as acting officer once nominated, so his service violated the law.
fix_example.result: The ruling left an unfair labor practice complaint issued under Solomon's authority against SW General invalid.

source.title: NLRB v. SW General, Inc., No. 15-1251 (opinion text)
source.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)

I165.title: Small local governments lack money and expert staff
I165.summary: Towns with a small tax base often cannot afford the lawyers, engineers or procurement specialists their duties require. State grants and shared regional services are proposed ways to fill the gap.
I165.mechanism: Small governments lack the tax base and the legal and procurement capacity their duties require.
I165.evidence_note: Plausible. Government Accountability Office simulations show persistent operating gaps in state and local budgets; they do not measure staff capacity directly.
I165.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Equalizing grants and shared services are common in other federal countries, and no U.S. evaluation of shared-service programs on delivery exists.
I165.response: States and local governments, with federal grants from Congress, would provide equalizing grants, shared professional services and regional technical help, with public accountability for results.
I165.actor: States; local governments; Congress for grants
I165.tradeoff: Shared services can make government less responsive to each town, and recurring costs need steady funding.
I165.success_measure: Services completed, fiscal stress, and staffing gaps.

problem_example.headline: Thousands of rural communities lack staff to seek aid
problem_example.text: Headwaters Economics, an independent research group, counts 7,886 U.S. communities with very limited capacity, judged by measures such as local government staff and expertise. Its 2026 index finds 46% of them face high flood risk, and it warns that many lack the staff and tax base to apply for federal programs.

source.title: Rural Capacity Index

I166.title: State takeovers move local decisions away from local voters
I166.summary: States can override local governments or replace local boards, including county election boards. Power then shifts to officials whom local residents cannot vote out.
I166.mechanism: State preemption and restructuring of local boards move authority away from bodies that local voters elect.
I166.evidence_note: Plausible. Georgia's 2021 election law (SB 202) authorizes the State Election Board to take over county election administration; how often that power is used is the open empirical question. Grumbach's Laboratories Against Democracy (2022) documents declines in democratic performance at the state level and does not measure the effects of takeovers specifically.
I166.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Takeover criteria, due process and time limits are design proposals with no evaluation.
I166.response: State legislatures and state courts would require published criteria for any takeover, due process, a time limit and independent review, and would protect lawful local autonomy in state law. Residents would be able to invoke these protections.
I166.tradeoff: States hold broad constitutional authority over local governments, and its limits differ by state.
I166.success_measure: Stated reasons for takeovers, outcomes of review, and voting access in affected places.

problem_example.headline: Flint's state-appointed managers switched the city's water
problem_example.text: In 2014, state-appointed emergency managers running Flint, Michigan, switched the city's water source to the Flint River. A task force appointed by Governor Rick Snyder found in 2016 that the managers made that decision in place of locally elected officials. It said the structure made it extremely difficult for Flint residents to check decisions.

source.title: Flint Water Advisory Task Force Final Report
source.publisher: Flint Water Advisory Task Force (State of Michigan)

I167.title: Few local employers leave workers with few options
I167.summary: When a few employers dominate a local job market, and pay is hidden or jobs are hard to reach, workers have fewer alternatives. Hospital mergers that raised local concentration slowed wage growth for nurses and other staff.
I167.mechanism: Employer concentration, opaque pay and transport barriers weaken workers' outside options and bargaining power.
I167.evidence_note: Well supported. Prager and Schmitt (2021) found that hospital mergers that raised local concentration slowed wage growth for nurses and other staff. Local labor-market concentration goes with lower posted wages in observational data analyzed by Azar, Marinescu and Steinbaum (2022). The Treasury Department's 2022 review attributes roughly 15% to 25% wage suppression to imperfect competition, a range drawn from studies using different methods.
I167.remedy_note: Plausible.
