Cullen and Pakzad-Hurson estimate that wages fell about 2% after states passed laws protecting workers' right to discuss their pay, with smaller effects where workers had little individual bargaining power. The 2023 Merger Guidelines now cover effects on labor markets, with no outcome evidence yet.
I167.response: The Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission, Congress and the states would review mergers for labor-market effects, require usable pay ranges in job postings, support worker mobility and strengthen collective bargaining.
I167.tradeoff: Labor markets differ from product markets, and concentration alone is insufficient evidence of harm.
I167.success_measure: Job switching, wages offered, and the number of employers within reach.

aimed_reforms.why: Blocks mergers that would leave workers with fewer employers bidding for them.
Stronger bargaining remedies give workers power where they have few outside options.

problem_example.headline: Hospital mergers slowed raises for skilled health workers
problem_example.text: In U.S. hospital mergers that sharply raised local employer concentration, annual wage growth for workers with health-care skills fell by 1.0 to 1.7 percentage points, a 2021 study by economists Elena Prager and Matt Schmitt found. That is about a quarter of those workers' usual yearly raise. Mergers that did not sharply raise concentration showed no such slowdown.

source.title: The State of Labor Market Competition

fix_example.headline: State pay-talk protections led to slightly lower wages
fix_example.text: Several U.S. states have passed laws protecting private-sector workers' right to share salary information with coworkers. In a 2023 study, economists Zoë Cullen and Bobak Pakzad-Hurson found that wages fell about 2% after these laws took effect. The effect was muted where workers had little individual bargaining power.
fix_example.result: Wages fell about 2% after states protected pay discussions, so this form of transparency did not raise pay on its own.

source.title: Equilibrium Effects of Pay Transparency (Cullen, Pakzad-Hurson)

I168.title: Immigration-status threats deter workers from reporting abuse
I168.summary: Workers who fear deportation or loss of status are less likely to report unpaid wages or unsafe conditions. Employers who break the law then face less risk of being reported.
I168.mechanism: Threats tied to immigration status, and legal limbo, deter workers from reporting unlawful treatment.
I168.evidence_note: Well supported. A 2008 survey of 4,387 low-wage workers in three large cities found frequent wage violations, including 26% paid below the minimum wage in the prior week. In 2023 the Department of Homeland Security created a deferred-action process for workers involved in labor disputes; its status after 2025 needs checking.
I168.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Older studies found that legalization under the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 raised the wages of legalized workers. The 2023 deferred-action process has no evaluation, and the grade rests on plausibility.
I168.response: Congress, the Department of Homeland Security, the Labor Department and the states within their authority would protect labor complaints from retaliation, decide status applications promptly and enact workable pathways for migration and work authorization.
I168.actor: Congress; DHS; DOL; states within authority
I168.tradeoff: Citizens, lawful residents and undocumented people hold different rights, so policy needs precise eligibility rules.
I168.success_measure: Access to the complaint process, time to decide status applications, and wages recovered.

problem_example.headline: Supreme Court denied back pay to undocumented union supporter
problem_example.text: In 2002, the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in Hoffman Plastic Compounds v. NLRB that the labor board could not award back pay to Jose Castro, an undocumented worker laid off after supporting a union drive. The board had found the layoffs illegal. The Court said federal immigration law barred the award because Castro had never been authorized to work in the country.

source.title: Hoffman Plastic Compounds, Inc. v. NLRB, 535 U.S. 137 (2002), syllabus
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (U.S. Supreme Court opinion)

fix_example.headline: Homeland Security offered deferred action to workers in labor cases
fix_example.text: In 2023, the Department of Homeland Security began letting workers involved in labor investigations request deferred action, a temporary shield from deportation, backed by a statement from the labor agency. Initial grants generally last up to four years. The department's page, last updated in July 2024, gives no figures on use, and no evaluation has been published.
fix_example.result: Use of the process and its effect on workers' willingness to report abuse are unmeasured, and its status after 2025 could not be confirmed.

source.title: DHS Support of the Enforcement of Labor and Employment Laws

I169.title: Insurance cannot buy care that is not available nearby
I169.summary: At the end of 2025, 92.3 million people lived in areas short of primary-care clinicians, where only 48% of need was met. Rural hospital closures reduced access for the people they had served.
I169.mechanism: Shortages of clinicians and rural services block care that insurance would otherwise pay for.
I169.evidence_note: Documented. Health Resources and Services Administration data compiled by KFF show 92.3 million people living in primary-care shortage areas as of December 31, 2025, with 48% of need met. The Government Accountability Office found in 2020 that rural hospital closures reduced residents' access to care. The Association of American Medical Colleges projects a shortfall of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036, from a model.
I169.remedy_note: Hypothesis for access. Widening the scope of practice for nurse practitioners, midwives and other clinicians is a common proposal for raising access to care, and no evaluation of an access gain is cited for this record. Shortage-area counts and physician supply projections describe the gap the proposal targets.
I169.response: Congress, the states and health systems would expand training and retention in underserved areas, allow appropriate scope of practice, support telehealth and pay rural services sustainably.
I169.tradeoff: Training takes years, and remote care cannot replace every in-person service.
I169.success_measure: Waits for appointments, travel time, and preventable illness.

problem_example.headline: Rural hospital closures added miles to reach care
problem_example.text: The Government Accountability Office studied 64 rural hospitals that closed from 2013 to 2017. In the areas they had served, the median distance to general inpatient care rose from 3.4 miles in 2012 to 23.9 miles in 2018. In the areas of the 11 closed hospitals that had offered alcohol or drug abuse treatment, the median distance to that care grew by 39 miles.

source.title: Rural Hospital Closures: Affected Residents Had Reduced Access to Health Care Services (GAO-21-93)

I170.title: Unreliable access to food harms health and learning
I170.summary: In 2024, 13.7% of U.S. households had trouble getting enough food at some point in the year. Unstable income and poor access to food harm health and children's learning.
I170.mechanism: Unstable income and poor access to food reduce household health and children's learning.
I170.evidence_note: Well supported. The Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service found 13.7% of households food insecure in 2024. Gundersen and Ziliak's 2015 review links food insecurity to poorer health.
I170.remedy_note: Well supported for food assistance. Using the county-by-county rollout of food stamps, Hoynes, Schanzenbach and Almond (2016) found that access in childhood improved adult health and economic outcomes. The 2025 law, Public Law 119-21, narrowed eligibility for SNAP, an enacted reversal.
I170.response: Congress, the Department of Agriculture, the states and schools would improve automatic enrollment in nutrition benefits, school meals and accessible food distribution, with evaluated nutrition support.
I170.tradeoff: Eligibility and supply limits differ from place to place, and delivery has to respect people's dignity.
I170.success_measure: Food insecurity, benefit take-up, and child nutrition.

problem_example.headline: About one in seven households lacked reliable food in 2024
problem_example.text: The Agriculture Department's Economic Research Service found that 13.7% of U.S. households, or 18.3 million, were food insecure at some point in 2024. About 7.3 million children lived in homes where both children and adults were food insecure.

source.title: Food Security in the U.S.: Key Statistics & Graphics (Household Food Security in the United States in 2024)

fix_example.headline: Childhood access to food stamps improved adult health
fix_example.text: The Food Stamp Program rolled out across U.S. counties between 1961 and 1975, so some children gained access earlier than others. Using that rollout, economists found that childhood access led to a significant drop in metabolic syndrome, a cluster of conditions tied to obesity and diabetes, in adulthood. Women who had access as children also became more economically self-sufficient.
fix_example.result: Childhood access to food stamps still showed up decades later in lower rates of metabolic syndrome and, for women, greater economic self-sufficiency.

source.title: Long Run Impacts of Childhood Access to the Safety Net (Hoynes, Schanzenbach, Almond)
source.publisher: NBER Working Paper 18535; published in the American Economic Review, 2016

I171.title: Inaccessible places and rigid benefit rules limit disabled people's choices
I171.summary: In 2025, 22.8% of people with a disability were employed, compared with 65.2% of people without one. Supplemental Security Income still caps a recipient's savings at $2,000, a limit unchanged since 1989.
I171.mechanism: Inaccessible housing, services and workplaces, along with rigid benefit rules, restrict choice and income for disabled people.
I171.evidence_note: Documented. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported an employment-to-population ratio of 22.8% for people with a disability in 2025, against 65.2% for people without one. Federal rules cap Supplemental Security Income recipients' resources at $2,000 for an individual, unchanged since 1989. Deshpande and Li (2019) found that closing Social Security field offices cut disability applications most among the most vulnerable applicants, a causal result.
I171.remedy_note: Plausible. Maestas, Mullen and Strand found that for applicants near the eligibility line, receiving Social Security Disability Insurance reduced employment by about 28 percentage points. Which redesign of benefit rules would raise earnings remains untested in the studies cited here.
I171.response: Congress, the states and agencies would enforce accessibility, fund supports for independent living, improve administration of disability benefits and smooth the disincentives to work.
I171.tradeoff: Support needs vary, and basic dignity should not depend on employment.
I171.success_measure: Unmet support needs, accessibility, and successful appeals.

problem_example.headline: SSI savings cap has stayed at $2,000 since 1989
problem_example.text: Federal rules for Supplemental Security Income cap an individual recipient's countable resources at $2,000, or $3,000 for a couple. The cap rose in steps from $1,600 in 1985 and reached $2,000 on January 1, 1989, with no increase listed since.

source.title: 20 CFR 416.1205, Limitation on resources
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute (Code of Federal Regulations)

fix_example.headline: ABLE accounts let disabled savers keep more without losing SSI
fix_example.text: The ABLE Act, which became law on December 19, 2014, lets people whose disabilities began before a set age save in special accounts. The Social Security Administration disregards the first $100,000 in an ABLE account when applying the SSI resource limit. On January 1, 2026, eligibility widened from disability onset before age 26 to onset before age 46.
fix_example.result: SSA disregards up to $100,000 in an ABLE account for SSI, but the cited source reports no measured effect on work or earnings.

source.title: Spotlight on Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) Accounts

I172.title: A few large funders can steer civic and research agendas
I172.summary: Civic groups, school systems and researchers that depend on a few big foundations may follow those funders' priorities. Those choices affect the public without any election to check them.
I172.mechanism: Dependence on a few large funders steers research and civic agendas, outside electoral accountability.
I172.evidence_note: Plausible. Reckhow (2013) documented, through case studies of urban school districts, how concentrated foundation giving steered district agendas; the evidence covers education only. Reich (2018) analyzes foundation power and its tax subsidy as a normative and institutional argument, without an estimate of effects.
I172.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Disclosure of donors' interests and more diverse boards are governance norms without evaluation.
I172.response: Nonprofits, universities and funders would publish donors' material interests where lawful, protect research independence and diversify boards and funding sources. Legislatures would set narrow disclosure duties.
I172.actor: Nonprofits; universities; funders; legislatures for narrow disclosure duties
I172.tradeoff: Freedom of association, small donors' privacy and an independent civil society need protection.
I172.success_measure: Concentration of funding, conflicts disclosed, and editorial independence.

problem_example.headline: Gates-designed teacher plan missed its goals in public schools
problem_example.text: In 2009, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation designed and funded a teacher-effectiveness initiative that three public school districts, including Hillsborough County in Florida, adopted along with four charter networks. It tied teacher ratings to pay and staffing. A 2018 RAND evaluation found the initiative did not achieve its goals for student achievement or graduation.

source.title: Improving Teaching Effectiveness: Final Report (RR-2242)

I173.title: Federal obligations to tribal nations remain unmet
I173.summary: The federal government owes treaty and trust duties to tribal nations, and its funding for those duties has fallen persistently short. Remedies need to honor the duties and support decisions made by tribal nations themselves.
I173.mechanism: Dispossession and fragmented federal responsibilities constrain tribal assets and services.
I173.evidence_note: Documented. The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights found in 2018 that federal funding for trust obligations to Native Americans remains persistently short. The Government Accountability Office's 2025 High Risk List includes federal management of programs serving tribes among its 38 areas. A 2014 databook by the Taylor Policy Group documents reservation income and poverty across the 1990 to 2010 censuses.
I173.remedy_note: Plausible. Researchers at the Harvard Project on American Indian Economic Development conclude that self-determination, under which tribes run federally funded programs themselves, is the federal policy that has made the most progress against distressed conditions in Native communities. Consultation based on consent has no outcome evaluation.
I173.response: Congress, federal agencies and tribal governments would honor treaty and trust obligations, strengthen consultation based on consent, fund tribal infrastructure and support economic development that tribes direct.
I173.tradeoff: Tribal nations are sovereign political communities, so remedies cannot be reduced to generic racial inclusion.
I173.success_measure: Obligations fulfilled, access to services, and the scope of tribal decision authority.

status.text: Treaty and trust obligations to tribal nations are set by Congress and carried out by federal agencies. Voting rules show where state law meets those obligations. In Brakebill v. Jaeger (July 31, 2019) a divided panel of the Eighth Circuit let North Dakota enforce a voter-ID rule requiring a residential street address, which many homes on reservations lack. The state settled with tribal plaintiffs in February 2020, and a consent decree entered April 24, 2020 lets tribal voters without a street address vote by identifying their home's location on a map.

problem_example.headline: Civil rights commission found Native programs grossly underfunded
problem_example.text: In 2018, the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights found that federal funding for Native American programs remained grossly inadequate and had mostly stayed flat since 2003. The Indian Health Service budget met just over half of Native Americans' health care needs. Native Americans had 1.6 times the infant mortality rate of non-Hispanic whites.

source.title: Broken Promises: Continuing Federal Funding Shortfall for Native Americans

fix_example.headline: Self-determination let tribes run federal programs
fix_example.text: Since the 1970s, federal policy has let tribal governments run federally funded programs themselves. Harvard researchers Stephen Cornell and Joseph Kalt concluded in 2010 that this self-determination policy is the only one that has made significant progress against distressed conditions in Native communities. They found it has held for four decades through changes in party control of Congress and the White House.
fix_example.result: The researchers judge it the most effective federal approach, though the paper's abstract gives no single measured outcome.

source.title: American Indian Self-Determination: The Political Economy of a Policy that Works (RWP10-043)
source.publisher: Harvard Kennedy School Faculty Research Working Paper Series

I174.title: A fixed-size House makes districts larger as the population grows
I174.summary: The House has stayed at 435 seats for more than a century while the population grew, so each member now represents about 761,000 people. Larger districts go with less contact between residents and their representative.
I174.mechanism: Keeping the House at a fixed size while the population grows raises the number of constituents each member serves.
I174.evidence_note: Plausible. After the 2020 Census the average House district held 761,169 residents. Frederick (2010) found that larger districts go with less constituent contact and lower approval of the member; the evidence is observational and the effects modest.
I174.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The House has not grown since 1913, so expansion is untested, and evidence linking district size to contact is observational with modest effects.
I174.response: Congress would evaluate expanding the House with a published apportionment rule, a plan for staff and facilities, and coordination with any change to how districts elect members.
I174.tradeoff: More seats alone would leave disproportionality, gerrymandering and responsiveness unchanged.
I174.success_measure: Residents per member, constituents' access to their member's office, and the cost of the transition.

aimed_reforms.why: Adds seats so each member represents fewer people.

problem_example.headline: House districts have more than tripled in size since 1911
problem_example.text: Congress capped the House at 435 seats in the Apportionment Act of 1911, when the average member represented roughly 212,000 people. After the 2010 Census the average was about 710,000, and the Census Bureau put it at 761,169 after 2020.

source.title: Proportional Representation
source.publisher: U.S. House of Representatives, History, Art and Archives

I175.title: An annual wealth tax faces hard design problems
I175.summary: Much of the largest fortunes consists of gains that are never taxed because the assets are never sold, which has prompted proposals to tax wealth itself. A wealth tax runs into problems valuing assets, preventing avoidance and settling its constitutionality.
I175.mechanism: Untaxed appreciation and avoidance motivate taxes on the stock of wealth, which face obstacles in valuation, avoidance and constitutional law.
I175.evidence_note: Well supported. Scheuer and Slemrod (2021) review the design problems of wealth taxes: valuation, liquidity, avoidance and uncertain revenue. Jakobsen and colleagues (2020) found in Denmark that wealth taxes reduced measured wealth accumulation among the wealthiest households through avoidance and changed behavior. In Moore v. United States (2024), the Supreme Court upheld the mandatory repatriation tax and left open whether income must be realized before it can be taxed.
I175.remedy_note: Plausible. Most OECD countries that once had annual net wealth taxes have abandoned them. The alternatives, taxing gains at death or taxing tradable assets on their yearly change in value, have cost estimates and no U.S. test.
I175.response: Congress, the Treasury and the IRS would compare an annual wealth tax with a high threshold against inheritance reform, taxing gains at death and yearly taxation of gains on tradable assets, and would specify rules for valuation, deferral and avoidance.
I175.tradeoff: Constitutionality, valuation, capital flight and revenue are uncertain, and these proposals are alternatives whose revenues cannot simply be added together.
I175.success_measure: Net revenue after behavioral responses, measured avoidance, and administrative cost.

aimed_reforms.why: Taxing inherited gains and capital income is one of the alternatives this record compares.

problem_example.headline: Denmark cut, then abolished, its steep wealth tax
problem_example.text: Denmark once had one of the world's highest marginal wealth tax rates, then drastically cut and abolished it between 1989 and 1997. A 2018 study found the tax had clear effects on how much wealth people built up, with larger effects on the very wealthy than on the moderately wealthy.

source.title: Wealth Taxation and Wealth Accumulation: Theory and Evidence from Denmark (Jakobsen, Jakobsen, Kleven, Zucman), NBER Working Paper 24371; published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2020

I176.title: Income-support programs leave people with irregular earnings uncovered
I176.summary: Means tests and separate programs can leave people with irregular earnings without a dependable income floor. A basic income, a negative income tax and targeted credits need comparing on the same budget.
I176.mechanism: Means tests, fragmented programs and irregular earnings leave people without a reliable income floor.
I176.evidence_note: Well supported. Hoynes and Rothstein's 2019 review sets out the evidence on, and costs of, a universal basic income in the United States and other high-income countries.
I176.remedy_note: Well supported for responses in work. In a randomized trial in two U.S. states, recipients of $1,000 a month worked about 1.3 fewer hours a week (2024). Alaska's universal Permanent Fund Dividend produced no drop in overall employment, while part-time work rose (2022). A same-budget comparison of a basic income, a negative income tax and targeted credits is a modeling exercise and has not been tested as policy.
I176.response: Congress, and states running pilots, would compare a universal basic income, a negative income tax and targeted refundable benefits using the same budget and household distribution model.
I176.tradeoff: Gross cost, taxes, the inflation context and which existing services cash replaces all shape the effects, and cash cannot create care or housing that is scarce.
I176.success_measure: Poverty, take-up, changes in work, and net gains for households.

aimed_reforms.why: A fully refundable child credit is one of the targeted benefits the comparison covers.
Benefits that expand automatically make the floor more dependable when earnings fall.

problem_example.headline: Gig workers needed a special pandemic program for benefits
problem_example.text: In March 2020, Congress created Pandemic Unemployment Assistance in the CARES Act for people who did not qualify for regular unemployment pay. The Labor Department said this group included self-employed and gig workers. Without that law, such workers were not eligible for regular state unemployment insurance.

source.title: U.S. Department of Labor news release on Pandemic Unemployment Assistance guidance

fix_example.headline: $1,000-a-month trial found modest cuts in paid work
fix_example.text: In a randomized trial in two U.S. states, 1,000 low-income people received $1,000 a month with no strings for three years, while 2,000 others got $50 a month. Recipients cut paid work by 1 to 2 hours a week, and their income apart from the payments fell about $1,900 a year compared with the other group.
fix_example.result: Recipients worked 1 to 2 fewer hours a week, and their labor force participation fell 4.2 percentage points relative to the comparison group.

source.title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States (Vivalt, Rhodes, Bartik, Broockman, Krause, Miller), NBER Working Paper 32719

X01.title: In safe seats, a small primary electorate picks the winner
X01.summary: In most House districts one party is sure to win in November, so its primary decides who takes office. Turnout in those primaries is a small fraction of eligible voters.
X01.mechanism: Most House seats are effectively decided in low-turnout primaries, which leaves the general election little chance of changing the outcome. Unite America, an advocacy group, puts the 2024 share at about 87% of seats decided by roughly 7% of eligible voters; the exact figures depend on how a safe seat is defined.
X01.evidence_note: Well supported in direction. Unite America, which advocates primary reform, calculated that about 87% of U.S. House seats were effectively decided in 2024 primaries in which roughly 7% of eligible voters took part; the numbers depend on its threshold for a safe seat. Ballotpedia's 2024 competitiveness report separately counted 38 House races without major-party competition and found that 52% of incumbents faced no contested primary.
X01.remedy_note: Plausible. Alaska's top-four primary with a ranked general election and the top-two primaries of California and Washington have short records. Effects on legislators' moderation are contested, and Alaska voters decide on November 3, 2026 whether to repeal their system.
X01.response: States, and voters by initiative where allowed, would adopt top-four or all-party primaries with ranked general elections, citizen redistricting commissions or multi-member districts. Massachusetts Question 3, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would replace party primaries with a single primary in which the top two finishers advance.
X01.tradeoff: Parties lose control of nominations, and some voters lose a ballot line they value. Ranked counts take longer, and a primary that advances two candidates of one party leaves some voters without their party in November.
X01.success_measure: Share of seats with a competitive general election, turnout in the round that decides the seat, and share of incumbents facing a credible challenger in November.

aimed_reforms.why: Moves the deciding contest to a general election that all voters take part in.
Commission-drawn maps reduce the number of seats made safe by design.
Multi-member proportional districts make most seats contestable even where geography sorts voters.

status.text: Alaska uses a top-four primary with a ranked-choice general election, and Ballot Measure 2 on its November 3, 2026 ballot would repeal it. California and Washington use top-two primaries. Maine uses ranked-choice voting in party primaries and in general elections for federal office. Massachusetts Question 3, a top-two primary listing every candidate on one ballot with no ranked ballots, is on the November 3, 2026 ballot.

problem_example.headline: Primaries with 7% of eligible voters settled most House seats
problem_example.text: Unite America, a group that advocates primary reform, calculated that 380 U.S. House seats, about 87%, were effectively decided in 2024 primaries. It found those primaries drew 18.1 million voters, about 7% of those eligible, and that 169 members ran unopposed in their primary for a safe seat.

source.title: Analysis: 87% of U.S. House elections already determined in primaries by just 7% of Americans

fix_example.headline: Alaska sends four finishers of any party to November
fix_example.text: Since 2022, Alaska has used one primary open to every voter in place of party primaries, and the top four finishers in each race advance to a ranked-choice general election. Voters approved the change in 2020. Alaskans decide on November 3, 2026 whether to repeal it.
fix_example.result: The record is short, effects on legislators' moderation are contested, and the system faces a repeal vote on November 3, 2026.

source.title: Ranked Choice Voting (information page)

X02.title: States ban local voting methods and raise the bar for initiatives
X02.summary: Nineteen states now bar ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, including city elections. Some legislatures have also tried to make citizen initiatives harder to pass after voters used them.
X02.mechanism: States are banning local use of ranked-choice voting and trying to raise initiative thresholds after voters use them, closing routes residents have used to change election rules.
X02.evidence_note: Documented. As of March 2026, 19 states prohibit ranked-choice voting by statute; Ohio's ban, signed March 17, 2026, followed Indiana's in February. Ballotpedia reports that 17 of the 19 bans were enacted where Republicans held the governorship and both legislative chambers. In August 2023, Ohio voters rejected, 57% to 43%, a legislature-referred amendment that would have raised the vote needed to approve constitutional amendments to 60%.
X02.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Protecting home rule over local election methods is a legal design with no outcome evidence. Ohio's 2023 attempt to raise the initiative threshold was defeated by voters.
X02.response: State legislatures, or voters by initiative, would protect cities' authority to choose their own election method and shield the initiative process from rule changes in the middle of a cycle.
X02.tradeoff: When cities choose their own methods, neighboring places can use different rules, which adds work for county election offices and for voters who move between them.
X02.success_measure: States that ban local election methods, and initiative rules changed in the middle of a cycle.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, 19 states prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, which keeps their cities and counties from adopting it; Indiana and Ohio added prohibitions in 2026. Protections for a city's or county's choice of election method remain proposals.

problem_example.headline: Ohio banned ranked ballots in every election, including cities
problem_example.text: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed a bill on March 17, 2026, barring any election in the state from using ranked-choice voting. Cities that adopt it lose state local-government fund payments. Ohio became the 19th state with such a ban, weeks after Indiana enacted one in February.

source.title: Ohio becomes second state this year to ban ranked-choice voting

fix_example.headline: Ohio voters kept the majority rule for amendments
fix_example.text: Ohio's legislature put a measure on an August 2023 special ballot that would have raised the vote needed to approve constitutional amendments from a simple majority to 60%. Voters rejected it, 57% to 43%, keeping the existing rule.
fix_example.result: Constitutional amendments in Ohio, including those proposed by citizen initiative, still pass with a simple majority of voters.

source.title: Ohio Issue 1, 60% Vote Requirement to Approve Constitutional Amendments Measure (August 2023)

X03.title: Off-cycle local elections draw fewer and different voters
X03.summary: Cities and school districts that vote in odd years or in spring draw a fraction of November turnout. The smaller electorate is older and more organized, and local decisions answer more to it.
X03.mechanism: Holding local elections in odd years or in spring cuts turnout and gives organized interests a larger say over local government.
X03.evidence_note: Well supported. Using California voter files, Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian (2022) found that moving city elections to the November ballot roughly doubles turnout and makes the electorate more representative of residents. Kogan, Lavertu and Peskowitz (2018) found that off-cycle school-district elections shifted the electorate and went with higher teacher pay than in on-cycle districts. Anzia's Timing and Turnout (2014) documents the turnout gap and the larger role of organized groups in off-cycle contests.
X03.remedy_note: Well supported. California voter-file evidence shows that moving elections on-cycle roughly doubles turnout and changes who votes; policy effects are shown for school districts. California, through SB 415, and Nevada now require on-cycle local elections.
X03.response: States by mandate, and cities through their charters, would move local elections onto the November ballot.
X03.tradeoff: Ballots get longer, and some voters skip local races listed below national ones.
X03.success_measure: Local turnout, the mix of ages and of renters and owners among local voters, and housing approvals.

aimed_reforms.why: Moves local elections to the November ballot, which is this record's response.

status.text: California's SB 415 (2015), in effect since January 1, 2018, requires a city or other local body to move its elections onto the statewide election calendar when off-cycle elections have produced turnout at least 25% below its average in the previous four statewide general elections. Nevada and other states have also moved local elections on cycle.

problem_example.headline: Stand-alone city elections draw about half the voters
problem_example.text: Research reviewed by political scientists Zoltan Hajnal, Vladimir Kogan and G. Agustin Markarian finds that local elections held on the November ballot generally draw double the turnout of stand-alone local contests. In California cities, they found the off-cycle electorate was less representative of residents, especially by race and age.

source.title: Who Votes: City Election Timing and Voter Composition
source.publisher: Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian, American Political Science Review

fix_example.headline: California cities moved votes to November and widened the electorate
fix_example.text: California cities that moved their elections onto the statewide November ballot drew a broader set of voters. Using voter files, Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian found the on-cycle electorate was considerably more representative of residents, especially when local races coincided with a presidential election.
fix_example.result: Moving on-cycle produced a considerably more representative electorate, and the authors conclude that on-cycle elections can improve local democracy.

source.title: Who Votes: City Election Timing and Voter Composition
source.publisher: Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian, American Political Science Review

X04.title: Removing job protections shifts agencies from career to political control
X04.summary: A 2026 personnel rule removes standard firing protections from career jobs that influence policy, and about 8,000 positions were converted in June 2026. With more than a tenth of the federal workforce gone in 2025, agencies are losing expertise and continuity.
X04.mechanism: Removing tenure protections and large departures shift the federal workforce from career service toward political control.
X04.evidence_note: Documented. The Office of Personnel Management's Schedule Policy/Career rule, final in February 2026, removes standard removal protections from career positions that influence policy; about 8,000 positions were converted on June 3, 2026, and two lawsuits are pending without a ruling. Across 22 major agencies, the Government Accountability Office found that nearly 378,000 employees left in 2025 and about 127,000 were hired, leaving headcount down nearly 256,000, more than 11%, by January 2026. OPM's own data show a net decrease of 271,363 federal employees from January 20, 2025 through July 2026.
X04.remedy_note: Plausible. Statutory protection for career positions has been proposed. The case that it improves performance rests on evidence comparing programs run by appointees and by career managers (Lewis, 2008).
X04.response: Congress, the Office of Personnel Management and the courts would protect career positions in statute, publish clear rules for reductions in force and oversee large restructurings such as those led by the Department of Government Efficiency.
X04.tradeoff: Protection from political firing makes it harder to remove poor performers, so performance management has to work alongside it.
X04.success_measure: Vacancy rates, and service measures such as the IRS phone answer rate and Social Security wait times.

aimed_reforms.why: Merit hiring and protection from political firing are the statutory protections this record proposes.

status.text: The Office of Personnel Management's Schedule Policy/Career rule was published February 6, 2026 and took effect March 9, 2026. An executive order of June 3, 2026 moved about 8,000 positions, nearly all at grade GS-15 or above, into the schedule, and further presidential orders can add more. At least two lawsuits challenge the rule and the order behind it, in federal courts in Washington, D.C. and Maryland; a Congressional Research Service review dated March 26, 2026 reported no ruling in either case.

problem_example.headline: New rule removes firing procedures for policy jobs
problem_example.text: In February 2026, the Office of Personnel Management finalized a rule creating Schedule Policy/Career, which drops the usual legal steps required to fire career employees in policy-influencing jobs. The President can move positions into it by executive order. OPM says the jobs stay career posts and the rule bars political loyalty tests.

source.title: OPM Finalizes Schedule Policy/Career Rule to Strengthen Accountability

fix_example.headline: Pendleton Act makes merit the rule for federal jobs
fix_example.text: In January 1883, after the assassination of President James Garfield, President Chester Arthur signed the Pendleton Act. It required federal jobs to be filled on merit and made it unlawful to fire or demote covered workers for political reasons. At first it covered 10% of the government's 132,000 employees.
fix_example.result: Coverage widened over the decades, and the National Archives says the law now applies to most of the 2.9 million federal positions.

source.title: Pendleton Act (1883)

X05.title: Domestic troop deployments test the limits on military power
X05.summary: In 2025 the President federalized National Guard troops for deployments in Los Angeles, Portland and Chicago. In December 2025 the Supreme Court left a block on the Illinois deployment in place, reading the law to require a showing that the regular military cannot execute the laws.
X05.mechanism: National Guard federalizations in 2025 tested the legal limits on using troops for domestic law enforcement.
X05.evidence_note: Documented. In Trump v. Illinois (December 23, 2025), acting on its emergency docket by a 6 to 3 vote, the Supreme Court left in place a block on federalizing the Guard in Illinois. It read 'regular forces' in the statute as the regular military, so the President must first show that the military itself cannot execute the laws. The ruling is preliminary.
X05.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Clarifying the Insurrection Act and the Posse Comitatus Act has been proposed. Trump v. Illinois shows that courts can enforce the existing statute at the preliminary stage.
X05.response: Congress would clarify the Insurrection Act and the Posse Comitatus Act and require public findings and reporting before troops are used for domestic law enforcement.
X05.tradeoff: Clearer limits can slow the response to a real emergency.
X05.success_measure: Domestic deployments made with stated findings and reported to Congress.

aimed_reforms.why: Bounds delegated emergency authority, including powers used to deploy troops at home.

status.text: On December 23, 2025, in Trump v. Illinois, the Supreme Court refused on its emergency docket to lift a lower-court order blocking the deployment of federalized National Guard troops in Illinois. The majority read 'regular forces' in the federal statute (10 U.S.C. 12406) as likely meaning the regular U.S. military, so the President would first need legal authority to execute the laws with the military and be unable to do so; the government had not identified that authority. Justices Alito, Thomas and Gorsuch dissented. The order is preliminary.

problem_example.headline: Supreme Court left a block on Guard troops in Illinois
problem_example.text: In early October 2025, President Trump announced National Guard deployments to the Chicago area, and about 300 troops were sent. Illinois and Chicago sued. On December 23, 2025, the Supreme Court refused to lift a lower court order barring the deployment, finding at this preliminary stage that the government had not identified authority allowing the military to execute the laws in Illinois.

source.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump's effort to deploy National Guard in Illinois

fix_example.headline: Congress narrowed a 2006 expansion of troop powers
fix_example.text: In 2006, Congress amended the Insurrection Act to let the President use the armed forces during a natural disaster or terrorist attack. In 2008, Congress rewrote the section again, removing the disaster and terrorism language and returning it to suppressing insurrections and domestic violence in a state.
fix_example.result: The 2008 rewrite undid the 2006 expansion, though it also dropped a 2006 requirement to notify Congress when that authority was used.

source.title: 10 U.S. Code 253, Interference with State and Federal law (amendment notes)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School

X06.title: An attempted removal tests Federal Reserve independence
X06.summary: In 2025 the President tried to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook. In June 2026 the Supreme Court, at the stay stage, upheld for-cause protection for Fed governors and required notice and a hearing.
X06.mechanism: An attempted removal of a Federal Reserve governor tested for-cause protection, which the Supreme Court upheld at the stay stage.
X06.evidence_note: Documented. In Trump v. Cook (June 29, 2026), the Supreme Court upheld for-cause removal protection for a Federal Reserve governor at the stay stage and required notice and a hearing. The ruling is interim.
X06.remedy_note: Plausible. Writing cause, notice and a hearing into statute follows the Court's reasoning. Alesina and Summers (1993) found across countries that central-bank independence goes with lower inflation; the evidence is cross-sectional.
X06.response: Congress would write cause, notice and a hearing for removing Federal Reserve governors into statute.
X06.tradeoff: Protecting governors from removal limits the President's control over a body that sets interest rates for the whole economy.
X06.success_measure: Removals of governors made with stated reasons and a hearing.

aimed_reforms.why: Includes a codified Federal Reserve exception among its structural protections.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, the dispute over removing Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook has been decided only at the stay stage: on June 29, 2026 the Supreme Court, 5 to 4, denied the government's request to let her removal take effect while the case continues. Congress has not written cause, notice and a hearing for Fed governors into law.

problem_example.headline: A president tried to fire a Fed governor for cause
problem_example.text: In August 2025, after a federal housing official accused Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook of mortgage fraud, President Trump said he was firing her for cause. Cook sued, and a lower court kept her in office. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court refused to lift that order and held that removal for cause requires notice and a hearing.

source.title: Trump v. Cook, No. 25A312
source.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States

X07.title: State-level rules can weaken democratic accountability
X07.summary: Some state legislatures have drawn maps that protect supermajorities, taken over local boards and overridden city rules on labor and housing. These state choices decide how much accountability voters have, whatever happens in Washington.
X07.mechanism: Gerrymanders that protect legislative supermajorities, state takeovers of local boards and preemption of local rules erode democratic quality in some states.
X07.evidence_note: Well supported. Grumbach's Laboratories Against Democracy (2022) builds a state democracy index and documents declines in some states, including supermajority gerrymanders and preemption of city labor and housing rules. Georgia's 2021 SB 202 authorizes the state to take over county election administration. The Congressional Research Service has documented the mid-decade congressional redraws of 2025 and 2026.
X07.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Enforceable state districting criteria and limits on preemption are proposals. Grumbach's index measures the decline and does not test remedies.
X07.response: State legislatures, state courts and voters by initiative would adopt enforceable districting criteria, limits on preemption and independent state election boards.
X07.tradeoff: A state that adopts neutral maps on its own can lose seats to states that do not, which invites retaliatory redraws.
X07.success_measure: Partisan bias in state maps, preemption laws enacted, and takeovers of local boards.

aimed_reforms.why: Independent commissions take map-drawing away from the supermajority the map would protect.
Sets a floor of lawful certification and protected officials that independent state election boards would carry out.

status.text: These measures are proposals at the national level. Some states have pieces of them: in Utah, a state judge ruled on November 10, 2025 that the legislature's congressional map violated the districting standards voters adopted in Proposition 4, and adopted a replacement map.

problem_example.headline: Utah lawmakers replaced a voter-approved redistricting reform
problem_example.text: In November 2018, Utah voters passed Proposition 4, creating an independent redistricting commission and barring maps that unduly favor a party. In 2020 the legislature repealed and replaced it, and in 2021 lawmakers adopted their own congressional map, splitting Salt Lake County four ways. In July 2024 the Utah Supreme Court held that such voter reforms are protected from unfettered legislative repeal.

source.title: League of Women Voters of Utah v. Utah State Legislature, 2024 UT 21

fix_example.headline: New York's top court struck a partisan congressional map
fix_example.text: In 2014, New York voters amended their constitution to create an independent redistricting commission and ban partisan gerrymandering. When the Democratic-controlled legislature passed its own congressional map in 2022, the Court of Appeals struck it down on April 27, finding it was drawn with impermissible partisan purpose. The court ordered a trial court working with a special master to adopt new maps.
fix_example.result: The legislature's map, which a lower court found would yield 22 Democratic-majority districts out of 26, was set aside in favor of court-adopted maps for 2022.

source.title: Matter of Harkenrider v Hochul, 2022 NY Slip Op 02833, 38 NY3d 494
source.publisher: New York Court of Appeals (New York State Law Reporting Bureau)

X08.title: Typical pay has grown far more slowly than productivity
X08.summary: Since 1979 output per hour has grown much faster than the pay of typical workers, and workers' share of business income has fallen. Part of the measured gap comes from how pay and prices are measured, and pay still rises when productivity does.
X08.mechanism: Net productivity and typical worker pay grew together until the 1970s and then diverged, and the labor share of income fell. About a third of the measured gap comes from measurement choices. Research finds that productivity growth still passes through to pay, and the rest of the gap comes from rising inequality in how pay is distributed.
X08.evidence_note: Documented. The Economic Policy Institute's series shows net productivity up 93.2% and typical pay up 33.7% from late 1979 to early 2026; the size of the gap depends on which price index and which measure of compensation are used. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' labor share for the nonfarm business sector fell from about 63% in 2000 to the mid-50s. Stansbury and Summers (2017) found that productivity growth still passes through to pay, and traced the gap mainly to rising inequality in pay.
X08.remedy_note: Plausible. Each part of the proposed bundle, bargaining reform, wage floors and enforcement funding, has its own evidence, and Farber, Herbst, Kuziemko and Naidu link union density to inequality. No study evaluates the bundle's effect on the gap.
X08.response: Congress, the states and the National Labor Relations Board would reform bargaining law, set indexed minimum-wage floors and fund enforcement.
X08.tradeoff: Wage floors carry employment risk above about 60% of the local median wage, and stronger bargaining remedies raise employers' costs.
X08.success_measure: Wages at the 10th percentile, the labor share of income, and the employment rate.

aimed_reforms.why: Bargaining reform is one part of this record's response.
Sector-wide standards raise pay across an industry, another route to the bargaining part of the response.
An indexed minimum wage is the wage-floor part of the response.

status.text: Measured, with reforms proposed. The Economic Policy Institute, a progressive think tank, reports that from late 1979 to mid-2026 net productivity rose 93.7% while a typical worker's hourly compensation rose 32.7% (updated September 14, 2026). Part of the gap depends on measurement choices, such as the price index used and whether pay is measured for the typical worker or the average; one study (Stansbury and Summers, 2017) finds that faster productivity growth still goes with faster pay growth. Proposed responses include bargaining reform, higher wage floors and more enforcement funding.

problem_example.headline: Productivity has outpaced typical pay since 1979
problem_example.text: The Economic Policy Institute, a labor-oriented research group, calculates that U.S. net productivity rose 93.7% from 1979 to mid-2026, while average hourly compensation for production and nonsupervisory workers, about 80% of the workforce, rose 32.7%. Economists Anna Stansbury and Lawrence Summers found that productivity growth still lifts pay, but that other forces have held typical compensation back.

source.title: The Productivity-Pay Gap (updated Sept. 14, 2026)

X09.title: Partisan identity weakens punishment of one's own side
X09.summary: For many Americans, party has become a social identity tied to dislike of the other side. In experiments, voters penalized an undemocratic candidate from their own party, yet only about 3.5% were willing to switch their vote over it.
X09.mechanism: Party has become a social identity, and partisans punish norm-breaking by their own side only weakly: few are willing to switch their vote over it.
X09.evidence_note: Well supported. In Graham and Svolik's 2020 experiments, a candidate's undemocratic position cost an average of 11.7 points in vote share, while only about 3.5% of respondents were willing to defect from their own party's candidate over it in realistic matchups. Abramowitz and Webster (2016) document the rise since the 1990s of negative partisanship, voting against the other party more than for one's own. Mason's Uncivil Agreement (2018) gives an identity-based account of polarization.
X09.remedy_note: Plausible. Messages stressing a shared American identity reduced partisan animosity in a 2023 megastudy. Effects of electoral rules on polarization are contested: Woon (2018) finds that the effects of primaries depend on conditions, and opening primaries is no proven general remedy.
X09.response: States, civic organizations and researchers would adopt electoral rules that reward building coalitions, support institutions that bring people of different parties together and use common-identity messages tested in the 2023 megastudy.
X09.tradeoff: Effects of cross-party contact and messaging fade quickly, within about two weeks in the megastudy.
X09.success_measure: Cross-party membership, and measured animosity among members.

aimed_reforms.why: Cross-partisan membership and civic service are the institutions this record proposes.
Ranked ballots reward candidates who seek second choices from other camps.
Fusion voting lets parties form coalitions behind one candidate.

status.text: Graham and Svolik (American Political Science Review, 2020), using a national candidate-choice experiment and Montana's 2017 special House election, found that only a small fraction of American voters put democratic principles ahead of party and policy when they vote, and that this willingness shrinks as partisanship and polarization grow.

problem_example.headline: Only 3.5% would vote against their side to punish undemocratic conduct
problem_example.text: In 2020, Yale political scientist Milan Svolik and coauthor Matthew Graham reported a nationally representative survey experiment in which Americans chose between hypothetical state legislative candidates. When candidates held their party's usual positions, only 3.5% of respondents would vote against their partisan interests to punish undemocratic conduct. Svolik said voters, regardless of party affiliation, are willing to forgive such behavior.

source.title: Most U.S. Voters Value Party Over Democracy

X10.title: Recent antitrust cases produced mixed results
X10.summary: Courts found Google liable in search and ad tech and ordered conduct remedies without a breakup, and the FTC lost its case against Meta. A coalition of states won a jury verdict against Live Nation, and the Justice Department settled with RealPage.
X10.mechanism: The 2025 to 2026 antitrust record is mixed: liability findings against Google in search and ad tech with no divestitures, an FTC loss against Meta, a state win against Live Nation and a Justice Department settlement with RealPage. A court finding alone does not show that competition has improved.
X10.evidence_note: Documented. A federal court held in August 2024 that Google unlawfully maintained search monopolies; its December 5, 2025 final judgment requires data sharing and limits exclusive deals, without divestiture. Another federal court found in April 2025 that Google unlawfully tied its ad server to its exchange; remedies ordered on September 2, 2026 regulate conduct. On November 18, 2025, a federal court ruled for Meta in the FTC's case, and the FTC appealed. The New York Attorney General announced a jury verdict for a coalition of 33 states against Live Nation in April 2026, and NPR reported a Justice Department settlement with RealPage in November 2025.
X10.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Sector-specific rules for platforms have not been enacted. Structural remedies held in reserve for when conduct remedies fail have not been tested since the AT&T breakup.
X10.response: Congress, the antitrust agencies and the courts would adopt sector rules for platforms, hospitals, agriculture and ticketing, and use structural remedies where conduct remedies fail.
X10.tradeoff: Some mergers and integrated businesses create efficiencies, and winning a case differs from changing prices or wages in the market.
X10.success_measure: Prices after mergers and remedies, and concentration in local labor markets.

aimed_reforms.why: Covers the merger and structural remedies this record holds in reserve.
Applies sector-specific rules, the approach this record proposes for several industries.

status.text: Mixed results as of October 15, 2026, with several cases still open. Federal courts found Google liable in the Justice Department's search case (2024) and ad tech case (April 2025) and in both cases imposed conduct rules and denied requests to break up the business: the search judgment of December 5, 2025 is on appeal, and the ad tech remedies announced in September 2026 set six years of behavioral requirements with a monitor. A federal judge ruled for Meta in the FTC's monopolization case on November 18, 2025. A jury found for the states against Live Nation and Ticketmaster on April 15, 2026, with post-trial motions and remedies pending. The court entered the Justice Department's settlement with RealPage on May 19, 2026, and the states' own claims continue.

problem_example.headline: Google kept Chrome after losing its search case
problem_example.text: In September 2025, a year after ruling that Google illegally kept its search monopoly, Judge Amit Mehta declined to make Google sell its Chrome browser. He barred exclusive default deals but still let Google pay phone makers to preload its search engine.
problem_example.where: Federal (U.S. District Court, District of Columbia)

source.title: In a major antitrust ruling, a judge lets Google keep Chrome but levies other penalties

fix_example.headline: States won a jury verdict against Live Nation
fix_example.text: In April 2026, a jury found that Ticketmaster unlawfully maintains a monopoly over ticketing at major concert venues and that fans were overcharged, after a five-week trial brought by New York and 33 other states. The Justice Department had settled with Live Nation during the trial, and the states rejected that deal and kept litigating.
fix_example.result: Remedies and penalties will be set at a separate bench trial, so there is no measured result yet.

source.title: Attorney General James and Coalition of States Win Trial Against Live Nation and Ticketmaster
source.publisher: Office of the New York Attorney General

X11.title: Party organizations still steer who gets nominated
X11.summary: Party committees shape who runs and who survives a primary through endorsements, money and pressure on candidates to step aside. A June 2026 Supreme Court ruling lets parties coordinate unlimited spending with their candidates.
X11.mechanism: Party organizations shape who can win a nomination by steering endorsements, money and candidate entry. The 2026 ruling ending limits on coordinated party spending, and the spread of state bans on ranked-choice voting, add to that influence relative to primary reforms driven by voters.
X11.jurisdiction: United States (federal); Alaska; 19 states with RCV bans
X11.evidence_note: Well supported. On June 30, 2026, in NRSC v. FEC, the Supreme Court ruled that federal limits on spending parties coordinate with their candidates violate the First Amendment, overruling its earlier precedent. In Alaska's 2024 top-four primary, Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom finished third with about 20% and withdrew, with Republican consultants citing the risk of two Republicans splitting the vote against one Democrat; it is a single case. The Party Decides (Cohen and colleagues, 2008) argues that party insiders effectively pick presidential nominees through endorsements before voters engage, a thesis contested since 2016 and limited to presidential races. Nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting by statute as of March 2026.
X11.remedy_note: Plausible. Top-four primaries and ranked-choice voting reduce party pressure on who enters a race without removing it, as the 2024 Dahlstrom withdrawal shows. The claim that parties decide nominations is contested after 2016 and fits presidential nominations best.
X11.response: States and Congress would consider fusion voting and public funding directed to parties, require parties to publish their dues schedules, and treat party rules as part of the rules that govern elections.
X11.tradeoff: Fusion voting and party-centered funding can strengthen party leaders.
X11.success_measure: Minor-party ballot lines that win votes, and how long coalitions last.

aimed_reforms.why: Fusion voting and party-centered funding give organized coalitions a route that party committees do not control alone.

status.text: Proposed. One option, fusion voting, is legal and in regular use in New York and Connecticut. Massachusetts Question 3 (November 3, 2026) would let parties endorse candidates in a single all-candidate primary and print those endorsements on the ballot.

problem_example.headline: Alaska's lieutenant governor quit a House race after the primary
problem_example.text: Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, a Republican, finished third with about 20% in Alaska's 2024 top-four primary for the U.S. House, enough to advance, then withdrew. Many local Republican groups had endorsed Nick Begich, and a political consultant said two Republicans running against one Democrat would be a tough path.

source.title: Lt. Gov. Dahlstrom quits U.S. House race after finishing behind Peltola and Begich in the primary

X12.title: The 2025 tax law and rising interest narrow future budget choices
X12.summary: The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the July 2025 tax and spending law adds $3.4 trillion to deficits over ten years, before interest costs. Debt held by the public is projected to rise from 101% of GDP in 2026 to 120% in 2036.
X12.mechanism: The July 2025 reconciliation law adds about $3.4 trillion to ten-year deficits before interest, on top of a baseline in which debt held by the public rises from 101% of GDP in 2026 to 120% in 2036. Rising interest costs leave Congress less room to bargain over other spending.
X12.evidence_note: Documented. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that Public Law 119-21 increases deficits by $3.4 trillion over 2025 to 2034, with revenues down $4.5 trillion and direct spending down $1.1 trillion, excluding debt service and economic feedback. CBO's February 2026 outlook projects a deficit of $1.9 trillion (5.8% of GDP) in 2026 rising to $3.1 trillion (6.7%) in 2036, with rising net interest driving much of the increase.
X12.remedy_note: Documented. CBO's separate scoring adds debt-service costs to the $3.4 trillion estimate and shows that making the law's temporary tax provisions permanent would add further to the debt path. No enacted fiscal rule binds the trajectory.
X12.response: Congress would state the budget cost and the source of financing for every reform profile that spends or raises money, including revenue from IRS enforcement and capital taxation.
X12.tradeoff: Requiring every proposal to show its financing can hold back investments whose returns arrive slowly or fall outside a ten-year budget window.
X12.success_measure: Proposals published with a cost and a financing source, and net interest as a share of GDP.

aimed_reforms.why: Collecting tax already owed is one financing source this record names.

status.text: CBO estimates that the July 2025 tax and spending law (Public Law 119-21) adds $3.4 trillion to deficits over 2025 to 2034, not counting added interest costs. CBO's February 2026 baseline projects a $1.9 trillion deficit in 2026 and debt held by the public rising from 101% of GDP in 2026 to 120% in 2036.

problem_example.headline: 2025 tax law adds $3.4 trillion to deficits
problem_example.text: The Congressional Budget Office estimated in July 2025 that the tax and spending law enacted that month, Public Law 119-21, adds $3.4 trillion to deficits from 2025 to 2034. Revenues fall by $4.5 trillion over that period, while direct spending falls by $1.1 trillion.

source.title: Estimated Budgetary Effects of Public Law 119-21, Relative to CBO's January 2025 Baseline

fix_example.headline: Congress's pay-as-you-go rule ran from 1990 to 2002
fix_example.text: The Budget Enforcement Act of 1990 applied a pay-as-you-go process to new tax and entitlement laws. In December 2002, Congress set the remaining balances on its scorecard to zero, ending the process. A 2010 law revived the rule to enforce budget neutrality on new tax and entitlement laws, while excluding costs labeled emergencies.
fix_example.result: The 1990 rule ran until Congress zeroed out its scorecard in 2002, and the CRS report does not measure its effect on deficits.

source.title: The Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010: Summary and Legislative History (R41157)

X13.title: Feed ranking changes exposure; measured effects on hostility are small about the other party
X13.summary: Randomized studies show that changing how a feed is ranked changes what people see, and can nudge policy attitudes slightly. Large experiments found no change in hostility toward the other party over weeks or months; targeted changes to hostile posts moved it a little.
X13.mechanism: Engagement-ranked feeds measurably shift what users see and can move policy attitudes by about a tenth of a standard deviation. Large randomized studies found no effect of feed design on hostility toward the other party over weeks to months.
X13.jurisdiction: United States (platform experiments on X, Facebook, Instagram)
X13.evidence_note: Well supported. In a randomized trial of 4,965 U.S. X users from July to September 2023 (Gauthier and colleagues, Nature, 2026), switching from a chronological to an algorithmic feed raised an index of conservative policy and political views by 0.12 standard deviations, with no significant effect on hostility toward the other party; switching the algorithm off produced no attitude change. During the 2020 election, moving Facebook and Instagram users to chronological feeds changed exposure and time on the platform and left polarization and political knowledge unchanged over three months (Guess and colleagues, Science, 2023). Among 23,377 U.S. Facebook users, cutting content from like-minded sources by about a third produced no measurable change on eight preregistered attitude measures (Nyhan and colleagues, Nature, 2023). One platform's 2023 algorithm may not generalize to others.
X13.remedy_note: Well supported for the null results. Chronological feeds and reduced exposure to like-minded sources produced no measurable change in polarization in the 2020 studies. A ten-day 2024 experiment with 1,256 X users that reranked hostile and antidemocratic posts moved feelings toward the other party by about 2 points on a 100-point scale, in either direction. The pattern points to changes in specific content as a stronger lever than overall ranking rules.
X13.response: Congress, the Federal Trade Commission, the states and platforms would make feed choice the default, keep archives of political ads with sponsor labels, and evaluate effects before adopting new regulation.
X13.tradeoff: Researcher data access carries privacy risk, and most users keep the default feed even when offered a choice.
X13.success_measure: Share of users choosing a non-default feed, studies published with platform data, and measured exposure to hostile content.

aimed_reforms.why: Feed choice and researcher data access are the response this record proposes, and the experiments here are the kind of evidence it would produce.

status.text: Proposed: feed choice by default, public ad archives with sponsor labels, and evaluation of effects before regulation.

problem_example.headline: Cutting like-minded Facebook posts left attitudes unchanged
problem_example.text: During the 2020 U.S. election, researchers cut the content 23,377 Facebook users saw from like-minded sources by about a third for three months. The users saw more posts from other viewpoints and less uncivil language. The study found no measurable change on eight attitude measures, including hostility toward the other party.

source.title: Like-minded sources on Facebook are prevalent but not polarizing

fix_example.headline: Reranking hostile X posts nudges partisan feelings
fix_example.text: During the 2024 presidential campaign, researchers used an AI model to rerank the X feeds of 1,256 volunteers for ten days, reducing or increasing their exposure to posts with partisan animosity and antidemocratic attitudes. Changing exposure to those posts moved feelings toward the other party by about two points on a 100-point scale.
fix_example.result: Reducing or increasing exposure to hostile posts shifted feelings toward the other party by about two points within ten days.

source.title: Reranking partisan animosity in algorithmic social media feeds alters affective polarization (preprint: arXiv 2411.14652)
source.publisher: Piccardi, Saveski, Jia, Hancock, Tsai and Bernstein; Science (2025)

X14.title: Court rulings and White House orders move agency decisions to the President and the courts
X14.summary: Since 2024 the Supreme Court has ended judicial deference to agencies' reading of statutes and allowed the President to remove FTC commissioners at will, and a 2025 executive order put independent agencies' rules under White House review. Regulatory choices once left to agency experts now run through the presidency and the courts.
X14.mechanism: Between June 2024 and June 2026, the Supreme Court ended deference to agencies' interpretations of statutes and ended for-cause removal protection for multi-member regulators, and Executive Order 14215 placed independent agencies' rules under White House review and legal control. Together these shift regulatory policy from agency expertise toward presidential and judicial control.
X14.evidence_note: Documented. In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (June 28, 2024), the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that courts must interpret statutes independently and may not defer to an agency's reading because a statute is ambiguous, overruling Chevron. Executive Order 14215 (February 18, 2025) requires independent regulatory agencies to send significant rules to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs and to treat the President's and Attorney General's legal interpretations as controlling, with an exception for Federal Reserve monetary policy. In Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026), the Court ruled 6 to 3 that the FTC's protection against removal without cause violates the separation of powers, expressly overruling Humphrey's Executor and setting the Federal Reserve apart.
X14.remedy_note: Documented. The Slaughter ruling treats the Federal Reserve as a possible exception. The Congressional Research Service identifies the tools Congress keeps: reclaiming delegated powers, procedural requirements, quorum rules and supermajority voting. No legislative response has been enacted.
X14.response: Congress and the courts would build agency independence through process and structure: notice, public reasons, records, staggered bipartisan seats, agency authority to litigate and judicial review. Congress would also write the Federal Reserve's protection into statute, following Trump v. Cook.
X14.tradeoff: Independence built from structure and procedure gives agencies less insulation than protected terms did, and its durability depends on how courts apply Slaughter.
X14.success_measure: Removals accompanied by stated reasons, and days each agency holds a quorum.

aimed_reforms.why: Designs agency independence from the legal tools that remain after Slaughter.

status.text: Proposed. These options protect independence through process and structure, such as notice, written reasons, records and staggered bipartisan seats, because on June 29, 2026 the Supreme Court held in Trump v. Slaughter (6 to 3) that the President may remove Federal Trade Commission members at will, overruling Humphrey's Executor.

problem_example.headline: Supreme Court ends deference to agency legal readings
problem_example.text: Atlantic herring fishing businesses sued over a federal rule that made them pay for onboard observers, estimated at up to $710 a day. In June 2024, in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, the Supreme Court used their case to overrule the Chevron doctrine, ruling that courts may not defer to an agency's reading of a law simply because the law is ambiguous.

source.title: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, No. 22-451 (opinion text)
source.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)

X15.title: State supreme courts decide whether maps and voter-approved reforms take effect
X15.summary: In 2026 the supreme courts of Missouri, Virginia and Utah decided whether new congressional maps and voter-approved changes would take effect. Spending on state supreme court elections reached a record $157 million in 2023 and 2024.
X15.mechanism: State supreme courts now decide whether mid-decade congressional maps and voter-approved reforms take effect, as Missouri, Virginia and Utah show, while spending on those courts' own elections reached a record $157 million in 2023 and 2024.
X15.jurisdiction: Missouri; Virginia; Utah; 35 states with supreme court elections
X15.evidence_note: Documented. Missouri's Supreme Court upheld the 2025 mid-decade map 4 to 3 on March 24, 2026, then unanimously suspended it on September 3 until voters decide Proposition A on November 3, 2026. On September 10 the U.S. Supreme Court, with no public dissent, stayed a federal order that would have forced use of the new map, so Missouri votes in 2026 under its 2022 map. On May 8, 2026, the Supreme Court of Virginia ruled 4 to 3 that a redistricting amendment voters approved on April 21 was invalid because the legislature's first passage came after voting had begun in the 2025 House of Delegates elections. Utah's Supreme Court held in 2024 that the initiative power is constitutionally protected, and a trial judge imposed a court-selected map for 2026. The Brennan Center, an advocacy organization, counted $157.3 million spent on state supreme court elections in 2023 and 2024 across 79 seats in 35 states, a record, with interest groups outspending candidates for the first time.
X15.remedy_note: Documented. A voter referendum suspended Missouri's 2025 map until voters decide Proposition A on November 3, 2026, and Utah's initiative rights led to a court-selected map for 2026. The Brennan Center recommends ending contested supreme court elections or tightening disclosure of spending on them. The U.S. Supreme Court's September 2026 orders left Missouri's state ruling in place.
X15.response: State legislatures and voters would require disclosure of spending in judicial elections and consider merit selection of justices followed by retention elections. State courts would be treated as a check on maps.
X15.tradeoff: Merit selection moves the choice of justices further from voters, and disclosure rules raise privacy concerns for small donors.
X15.success_measure: Share of judicial-election spending with an identified source.

aimed_reforms.why: Disclosure of original funders applies to spending in state supreme court elections.

status.text: Proposed. State supreme courts decided several districting disputes in 2026. The Missouri Supreme Court upheld the legislature's mid-decade map 4 to 3 on March 24, 2026, then on September 3, 2026 held it suspended until voters decide Proposition A. The Supreme Court of Virginia struck down a voter-approved redistricting amendment on May 8, 2026. The Colorado Supreme Court ruled on June 29, 2026 that mid-decade redistricting is unconstitutional there.

problem_example.headline: Virginia's top court voided a voter-approved map amendment
problem_example.text: On April 21, 2026, Virginia voters narrowly approved a Democratic-backed amendment allowing congressional districts to be redrawn mid-decade. On May 8, the Supreme Court of Virginia struck it down 4 to 3, ruling that lawmakers first passed it after voting had begun in the 2025 House of Delegates elections. The current maps stay in place for 2026.

source.title: Supreme Court of Virginia strikes down redistricting amendment, keeps current maps in place

fix_example.headline: Arizona voters kept retention elections for judges
fix_example.text: Arizona voters decide whether to keep appointed supreme court justices in retention elections. In 2024, 78% of them rejected an amendment to end those votes. The Brennan Center reports that retention races have drawn less spending than contested elections, though an Oklahoma justice lost one in 2024 after $3.6 million in group spending.
fix_example.result: Arizona kept its appointment-plus-retention system, which the Brennan Center finds draws less money than contested races, while warning that retention fights are getting costlier.

source.title: The Politics of Judicial Elections 2023-24

X16.title: Incarceration and voting restrictions pull voters out of hard-hit communities
X16.summary: About 1.25 million people are in prison and about 660,000 in jail, and an estimated 4 million adults cannot vote because of a felony conviction. Strict ID and address rules, like North Dakota's, can add barriers for tribal voters.
X16.mechanism: Incarceration and felony disenfranchisement remove voters from the communities with the most incarceration and reduce their civic participation. Strict ID and address rules, such as North Dakota's, add barriers for tribal voters.
X16.evidence_note: Well supported. The Bureau of Justice Statistics counted 1,254,200 people in state and federal prisons at the end of 2023 and 657,500 in local jails at midyear 2024; end-of-2024 prison counts are not yet published. The Sentencing Project, an advocacy group, estimates from a model that 4 million people were barred from voting by felony convictions in 2024, about 72% of them living in the community. Using panel surveys, a 2010 study in the American Political Science Review found that contact with the criminal justice system carries a lasting penalty on voting and trust, after controlling for criminal history and income. In Brakebill v. Jaeger (July 31, 2019), the Eighth Circuit let North Dakota's street-address requirement stand while noting that about 4,998 Native Americans lacked qualifying ID.
X16.remedy_note: Mixed. Restoring voting rights on release is a documented fix, as is North Dakota's 2020 consent decree, which lets tribal voters without street addresses mark their homes on a map at the polls and requires the state to accept tribal IDs. Evidence that restoration raises turnout substantially is mixed.
X16.response: States would restore voting rights on release and adopt map-based address verification and recognition of tribal IDs, as in North Dakota's 2020 consent decree.
X16.tradeoff: Restoration rules vary by state and can confuse people about their eligibility, and evidence that restoration raises turnout by much is mixed.
X16.success_measure: Registrations by people whose rights were restored, and eligibility errors at the polls.

status.text: Proposed: restoring voting rights on release from prison, verifying addresses with maps, and recognizing tribal IDs, as North Dakota's April 24, 2020 consent decree does for tribal voters.

problem_example.headline: North Dakota's ID rule left thousands without valid IDs
problem_example.text: North Dakota required voters to show identification listing a current residential street address.
