A federal district court found that 4,998 otherwise eligible Native Americans, along with 64,618 non-Native voters, lacked qualifying ID. In July 2019, the Eighth Circuit voted 2 to 1 to vacate a statewide injunction against parts of the law.

source.title: Brakebill v. Jaeger, 932 F.3d 671 (8th Cir. 2019), No. 18-1725
source.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit (via Justia)

fix_example.headline: North Dakota settled to accept tribal IDs and map addresses
fix_example.text: In 2020, North Dakota's secretary of state settled lawsuits brought by the Spirit Lake Nation and Standing Rock Sioux Tribe. According to the Native American Rights Fund, which represented them, the state agreed to accept tribal IDs and let voters without a street address mark their home on a map at the polls. The agreement was set to take effect for the June 9 primary.
fix_example.result: NARF says the court-enforceable agreement covers two tribes with more than 7,000 voting-age residents; the source does not measure turnout effects.

source.title: North Dakota Voter ID Law (Brakebill v. Jaeger) case page

X17.title: Immigration shapes the labor supply, and enforcement shapes workers' security
X17.summary: After 2030 immigration is projected to be the only source of U.S. population growth, and lower immigration since 2025 means a smaller working-age population. Research finds small average effects of immigration on native-born workers' wages.
X17.mechanism: Immigration is projected to be the only source of U.S. population growth after 2030, and unauthorized immigrants made up about 5.6% of the 2023 workforce. The 2025 to 2026 enforcement surge tightens labor supply, while research finds small effects of immigration on native workers' wages.
X17.evidence_note: Well supported. The Congressional Budget Office's January 2026 outlook projects that births fall short of deaths from 2030, leaving immigration as the only source of population growth. Its September 2025 update put net immigration 1.6 million lower in 2025 and 960,000 lower in 2026 than earlier projected, leaving 2.1 million fewer people aged 25 to 54 in 2035. The Pew Research Center estimated 14 million unauthorized immigrants in July 2023; about 9.7 million of them were working, 5.6% of the U.S. workforce. A House Homeland Security Committee release citing Customs and Border Protection reports 237,538 southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2025, the lowest since 1970, and a secondary analysis of ICE data found 70,766 people in detention on January 24, 2026, the highest on public record.
X17.remedy_note: Well supported. The National Academies (2016) found that immigration's long-run effect on native wages is small, with any negative effects falling mainly on earlier immigrants and native workers without a high school diploma. Card (2009) found that immigration explains about 5% of the rise in U.S. wage inequality from 1980 to 2000. No reform profile addresses this record.
X17.response: No response is proposed. The record keeps visible the channel from labor supply to workers' bargaining power and household security, and states the model's limits on immigration status. Congress and the Department of Homeland Security set immigration and enforcement policy.
X17.tradeoff: Choices about immigration levels and enforcement weigh labor supply against other public goals that evidence on wages alone cannot settle.
X17.success_measure: No success measure is set because no reform is proposed. Indicators to watch are net immigration, the prime-age population and the wages of workers without a high school diploma.

status.text: Context record with no reform attached. It traces how immigration changes labor supply and how enforcement changes workers' exposure to detention. Its figures run from 2023 (workforce share of unauthorized immigrants) to January 2026 (immigration detention).

problem_example.headline: CBO sees net immigration falling to 410,000 in 2025
problem_example.text: The Congressional Budget Office estimated in January 2026 that net immigration, which declined after 2023, was 410,000 people in 2025. A September 2025 update projected 2.1 million fewer people aged 25 to 54 in 2035 than CBO had expected, citing administrative actions taken since January 20, 2025, as the largest factor. Without immigration, CBO says, the U.S. population would begin to shrink in 2030.

source.title: The Demographic Outlook: 2026 to 2056

X18.title: Where a case is filed can decide which judge hears it
X18.summary: Parties can file in federal divisions with one judge and know in advance who will hear their case. A 2025 Supreme Court ruling limited the nationwide orders such judges could issue, and challengers shifted to class actions.
X18.mechanism: Litigants file in single-judge divisions to choose their judge, and until June 2025 could get nationwide relief from that judge. The 2024 random-assignment policy was adopted unevenly. After Trump v. CASA limited universal injunctions, plaintiffs turned to class actions and to vacatur of rules under the Administrative Procedure Act.
X18.jurisdiction: United States (federal courts); Northern District of Texas
X18.evidence_note: Documented. The Judicial Conference's March 12, 2024 policy calls for district-wide random assignment of civil cases seeking to bar or require state or federal action; it is guidance, and the Northern District of Texas declined to change its process. Brookings documents that Amarillo civil cases went to Judge Kacsmaryk, the division's only resident judge, 95% of the time from July 2019 and all the time from September 2022. In Trump v. CASA (June 27, 2025), the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that universal injunctions likely exceed federal courts' equitable authority, leaving class actions and vacatur under the Administrative Procedure Act available. The Congressional Research Service counts 34 cases with nationwide injunctions before CASA and 16 after.
X18.remedy_note: Documented. Random assignment reduced the concentration of patent cases before one judge in Waco, where it was adopted. After CASA, plaintiffs turned to class actions within hours. A binding rule or statute would be needed for a uniform effect.
X18.response: The federal judiciary by binding rule, or Congress by statute, would require random assignment for cases seeking statewide or nationwide relief.
X18.tradeoff: Rural residents' access to court and legitimate specialized case management need protection.
X18.success_measure: Rate of predictable assignments, and exceptions found in audits.

status.text: The Congressional Research Service (report R49022, July 7, 2026) counted 34 cases in which federal courts issued nationwide injunctions against the second Trump administration between January 20, 2025 and June 27, 2025, the day the Supreme Court decided Trump v. CASA, and 16 more cases from June 28, 2025 to June 27, 2026, for 50 in all.

problem_example.headline: Nearly every Amarillo case went to one judge
problem_example.text: After Matthew Kacsmaryk joined the federal bench in Amarillo, Texas, in 2019, a court order sent him every criminal case and 95% of civil cases filed there, and from September 2022, all cases. In November 2022, anti-abortion physicians sued the FDA there over the abortion pill mifepristone, and Kacsmaryk applied his 2023 order nationwide. The Supreme Court later dismissed the case for lack of standing.

source.title: Effort to curb judge-shopping at the federal courts explained

fix_example.headline: Random assignment cut one Waco judge's patent docket
fix_example.text: After senators of both parties complained about patent suits clustering before the single judge in Waco, Texas, the Western District of Texas moved to spread incoming patent cases among a dozen judges at random. The Brennan Center reports that the share of patent cases assigned to the Waco judge then plummeted.
fix_example.result: The Waco judge's share of new patent cases fell sharply once assignment was random, though the source gives no figures.

glossary.definition: Whether children grow up to have higher income than their parents had at a similar age, after adjusting for inflation.
Hostility toward people in the other political party. Studies measure it separately from disagreement over policy.
Two measures that move together without an established causal path. The Atlas keeps associations in the register and never draws them on a map.

A connection showing that one body holds legal power over something: it appoints, appropriates, preempts, enforces or sets a rate. It says who decides, without saying which way the decision goes, so it has no sign and never closes a loop.
A feedback loop whose response pushes back against the first change. How well it works depends on whether each corrective step can act.
Building that can go ahead when it meets published rules, without a separate discretionary approval for that project.
A connection stating that a change in one variable changes another in a stated direction, other things held equal. It carries a sign, a delay and an evidence grade.
A Senate vote to end debate. For most legislation it takes 60 votes, which is how the filibuster blocks bills that have majority support.
A judgment of which way an outcome could move if stated requirements hold. It gives no numerical size and no forecast.

The short label on a claim or response saying what kind of evidence supports it: documented, well-supported, plausible, contested, hypothesis or not yet tested. The same scale grades connections on the map.
A claimed relationship between two variables. Its record explains the mechanism, gives the evidence grade and states the delay. Connection IDs begin with L, LE, LT, LX or T.
A temporary law that keeps agencies funded at existing levels when Congress has not passed regular appropriations, which prevents a shutdown.
Evidence that challenges a claim, narrows its scope or supports another explanation.
An estimate of what would have happened without the change being studied, used as the comparison for measuring an effect.
The time between a change and its effect. Codes: S, under 2 years; M, 2 to 10 years; L, over 10 years.
A list of 24 times American government did something hard at scale, each with its measured result, who enacted it and the qualification that travels with the result.

A system in which people can choose and replace leaders through meaningful elections, with equal political standing, civil liberties and enforceable limits on power. Measures of democracy combine these elements in different ways.
A variable calculated from others, such as how often the primary decides the winner. Drawn as a box with a thin border.
A lens showing how the same rule or connection reaches a group differently, through a named mechanism. Groups stay outside the variables, because a group cannot rise or fall as a quantity in a loop.

The confidence label for a fact or event on the public record: a statute, a court ruling or an official statistic. It establishes the event; it says nothing about the size of an effect unless the record does.
How well a change survives a new legislature, a new administration, a court challenge or a loss of funding.

A code showing the expected direction and rough size of a reform's effect on an outcome family: +L large positive, +M moderate positive, +S small positive, 0 no expected effect, -S small negative, -M moderate negative, ? direction uncertain.
The credible chance that an official will lose office. It can change behavior before any election removes anyone.
An ordinary paper a reader already handles, such as a rent renewal, a pay stub, a primary ballot, a bill or a notice, used as a starting point into the map.
A judgment of whether a route to change is open under present political and legal conditions. The Atlas rates it high, medium, low or very low for 2026 to 2030.
A chain of causes that returns to its starting variable. Reinforcing loops amplify change and balancing loops counteract it; either kind can produce good or harmful results.
An amount arriving or leaving over a period, such as annual income or money spent per election cycle. Its time unit is part of the measure.
A rule letting one candidate appear on the ballot lines of more than one party. It is legal and in regular use in New York and Connecticut.
For each outcome indicator, the 2036 level below which conditions would be getting worse. It is a teaching benchmark and makes no forecast.
The confidence label for a proposed relationship that needs stronger evidence. Diagrams draw it as a dotted line, and it never serves as the only support for a claim.
A President's withholding of money Congress has appropriated. The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 makes it unlawful unless Congress approves a rescission.
Money and resources received over a period. A figure should say whether it is for a household or a person, whether it is before or after taxes and benefits, and how it adjusts for inflation.

A dated measurement used to track a variable, with a defined population and source. An indicator can capture its variable imperfectly; survey trust, for example, only partly tracks trust earned through performance.
A connection along which content, data or attention moves, such as news coverage, feeds or disclosure. Its sign gives the causal effect on the target.
An official inside a federal agency who audits and investigates it. The law requires 30 days' notice to Congress and a specific reason before the President removes one.

One of 193 records beneath the map, with IDs such as I017 or X01. Each describes a documented problem, case or policy, names its mechanism, gives an evidence grade, status and sources, and links to a variable or connection where it can.
The place or governing body to which a rule, study or claim applies.
The part of income from production paid to workers as compensation. Its exact scope depends on the statistical series.
A place in a system where a change has wide effects. The Atlas ranks seven for teaching, using Donella Meadows' ordering from changing a number (low reach) to changing a system's goals (high reach).
A complete path of connections that returns to the starting variable. If any closing step is only a hypothesis, the whole loop stays uncertain.
The ability to profitably worsen prices or terms because customers, workers or suppliers lack good alternatives. National concentration alone does not measure it.
The steps through which one change produces another.
Redrawing election districts between the once-a-decade redraws that follow each census.
A connection along which dollars move, such as contributions, advertising revenue, taxes, transfers or prices. Its sign gives the causal effect of that movement on the target.

A way of sorting in which every item fits in one category only and the categories together cover everything within a stated boundary. Each issue has one main category, while its causes and effects can cross many.
The connected variables tend to move in opposite directions, with the model's other conditions held steady.

One of four groups of results used to judge reforms: democratic quality, government efficacy, economic performance, and income and wealth equality. The families use different units and are never added together.

A force that affects the model but whose own causes lie outside its boundary, such as technology, population patterns, trade, foreign interference and major shocks. Drawn as a rounded pill outside the clusters.
A connection where one quantity is held inside another or holds claims on it, such as stock holdings inside household wealth. Its sign says how a change in the part moves the whole.

A guided answer to one everyday question, such as why rent went up. It gives a short answer, the main mechanisms, narrower questions, the offices that decide, possible responses and the evidence behind each claim.
The confidence label for a coherent mechanism with some supporting evidence, where the studies are weak or few.
The confidence label for a relationship on which credible studies disagree. Both sides are shown with the connection.
The connected variables tend to move in the same direction, with the model's other conditions held steady. A positive sign does not mean a benefit.
The Voting Rights Act requirement that places with a history of discrimination get federal approval before changing voting rules. It stopped operating after Shelby County v. Holder (2013).
A higher level of government limiting what a lower level may do on a subject, such as a state barring cities from adopting ranked-choice voting.
Evidence that the condition or mechanism a reform addresses exists. It is graded separately from remedy evidence.
The minimum number of members a body needs to take certain actions. An agency can exist while lacking the quorum it needs to act.
A method in which voters rank candidates; if no one wins a majority of first choices, the last-place candidate is eliminated and those ballots move to their next choice until someone wins.
A federal budget procedure that lets qualifying tax and spending legislation pass the Senate by simple majority. Its rules limit what it can carry, and most rule changes fall outside it.
An observed pattern over time that the model is meant to explain, such as the rise in the top 1% share of wealth.

One of 50 entries, R-01 to R-50, describing a proposed change: the connections it aims at, the routes it can travel, what it depends on, separate evidence about the problem and the remedy, expected directions for each outcome family, and how it could fail.
A feedback loop whose returning effect amplifies the first change. Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.
A relationship that was reviewed against the evidence and left off the map, kept on record with the reason, such as the claim that feed ranking alone raises hostility toward the other party.
How strongly a person's place in the income distribution depends on family background. Everyone cannot rise in relative rank at the same time.
Evidence that an intervention changes the condition it targets, with attention to where and how it was carried out.
A dated list of 64 rule changes that altered who officials answer to, coded toward voters, away from voters, voters kept existing rules, mixed or pending.

A path a reform can travel through government or civil society, such as a city ordinance, a state statute, a ballot measure, a federal statute, executive action, a court ruling or a constitutional amendment. The Atlas uses eleven routes.
A seat where one party or candidate has a large expected advantage. The model counts seats won by more than ten points; check each source's definition before comparing counts.
An electoral loss, or a retirement under threat of defeat, that removes an official. The model separates this event from the earlier risk of losing.
A set of stated assumptions with the direction each outcome family would take if they hold. Scenarios are conditional directions, never forecasts or odds.

The dated state of the research behind the Atlas, most recently October 15, 2026. Facts that were checked carry their own check date; inclusion in the snapshot alone does not mean a fact was rechecked on that date.
A citable item with its publisher, date, link, study design and limitations.

The list of every source the Atlas cites. Each entry has an ID (a letter, S, N, Q, W or K, followed by numbers), title, publisher, date and link, with notes on the study design, its limits and how it was read.
Government's lawful ability to gather information, decide, carry out decisions, enforce rules and learn. Capacity and accountability need to be designed together.
An amount built up over time, such as wealth, debt, local news outlets or safe seats. It changes only through what flows in and out.
For each outcome indicator, the 2036 level that would mark a clear improvement. It is a teaching benchmark and makes no forecast.
A Census Bureau poverty measure that counts taxes, tax credits and benefits such as food aid, and subtracts costs such as medical expenses, so it can show how much a program reduces poverty.
Primaries in which every candidate appears on one ballot and the top two (or four) finishers advance to the general election, whatever their party.
One of five groups of pathways built around a part of everyday life: cost of living; health and care; work and financial security; public services where you live; and voice, power and information.
A quantity or condition in the model that can rise or fall. Its definition states what a higher or lower value means.
Confidence that follows shown competence, honesty and accountability, as distinct from unconditional trust in whoever holds office.
Assets minus debts at a point in time. A rise in an asset's value that has not been sold is different from cash income or taxable income.
The confidence label for a relationship on which several credible studies, designed to rule out other explanations, agree about direction. Each study's setting and limits still apply.

mixups.prompt: A district where the incumbent could lose but never does: is that pressure, sanction, both or neither?
mixups.answer: Pressure without sanction. Risk of losing office can be present while incumbents defeated stays at zero; the accountability loop needs both.
mixups.wrong: Treating any competitive-looking seat as accountable.

mixups.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain how a zoning meeting can change rents across a city.
mixups.answer: Owners whose equity rises with scarcity attend and block new homes; fewer homes keep rents high.
mixups.wrong: Rents rise only because landlords are greedy, or only because of interest rates.

mixups.prompt: Does housing scarcity raise the top 1% share of wealth?
mixups.answer: Not in the atlas. Scarcity widens the owner-renter gap; when house prices outrun stocks the top 1% share tends to fall.
mixups.wrong: Equating every wealth gap with the top 1%.

mixups.prompt: The 43-day shutdown happened. What part of the trust-through-service loop does that prove?
mixups.answer: That service failed (an event on quality of public services). It does not show that the failure lowered trust, or that trust lowered funding; those links carry their own grades.
mixups.wrong: A vivid case proves a whole loop.

mixups.prompt: Where does a rule allowing homes by right enter the atlas?
mixups.answer: At the link “Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing”, where owners with equity resist new homes, and at housing scarcity.

mixups.prompt: Name one reform a state can adopt without Congress, and one that needs sixty Senate votes today.
mixups.answer: Examples: on-cycle local elections (state statute); proportional House districts (federal statute).

mixups.prompt: A line labelled auth, with no plus or minus sign, connects Congress to public investment. What does it mean?
mixups.answer: Authority: Congress has the power to decide; the line does not say which way it will.

mixups.prompt: Why does the atlas not give each reform a single score?
mixups.answer: The four outcome families use different units, some reforms help one and cost another, and the evidence differs in quality.
mixups.wrong: More plus signs means a better reform.

mixups.prompt: What did the largest feed experiments find about polarization?
mixups.answer: Changing the feed changed what people saw a great deal and their partisan hostility little or not at all.

mixups.prompt: Household income rose last year. Does that mean household wealth rose too?
mixups.answer: Not necessarily. Income is a flow; wealth is a stock that also moves with asset prices and debts.

mixups.prompt: The same house-price rise: who gains most, a renter under 35 or an owner over 55?
mixups.answer: The owner; ownership and equity differ sharply by age.

mixups.prompt: Pick one reform profile. Which office decides it, and how could you reach that office?
mixups.answer: It depends on the route. The route board on this page lists who acts on each route for every profile.
mixups.wrong: No one decides; it just happens.

mixups.prompt: Name one thing that decides how a productivity gain is split between pay and profit.
mixups.answer: Bargaining power, which the rules for organizing shape. Productivity growth raises what can be paid; it does not settle who gets it.
mixups.wrong: Pay tracks productivity automatically, or pay never responds to it.

mixups.prompt: Which office sets your electric rates?
mixups.answer: For an investor-owned utility, the state public utility commission. For public power or a co-op, a city council or co-op board. In PJM states the grid operator's capacity auction, overseen by federal regulators, also feeds into bills.
mixups.wrong: The power company sets its own prices, or Washington sets them.

numbers.qualification: From a University of Maryland Program for Public Consultation survey of 2,625 registered voters (May 2023). The House passed a ban 232 to 198 on July 22, 2026. On September 30, 2026 the Senate fell short of the 60 votes needed to take it up, 53 to 47.

numbers.caption: of eligible voters cast the 2026 primary ballots that, by Unite America's count, effectively decided 88% of House seats (383 of 435)
numbers.qualification: Unite America, an advocacy group, built the count from Cook Political Report ratings (published September 16, 2026) and defines 'effectively decided' itself. Its 2024 figures (87% of seats, about 7%) used the voting-age population, so the two years are not directly comparable.

feasibility_scale.high: The route is open, and the reform has been adopted somewhere through it since 2020.
feasibility_scale.medium: The route is open in some places, and a credible campaign could carry the reform through it by 2030.
feasibility_scale.low: The route exists, but it needs a coalition that does not exist now.
feasibility_scale.very low: It needs a supermajority, a constitutional change or a reversal of court doctrine.

omissions.item: LGBTQ+ people as a distribution overlay
omissions.why: No mechanism in this model yet has a measured path specific to LGBTQ+ people backed by current, checked data.
omissions.would_add: A sourced mechanism, for example in benefits, employment law or ballot access, with current data.

omissions.why: No checked mechanism within the model's scope links a modeled rule to a religious group's outcomes.
omissions.would_add: Evidence linking a modeled rule to a religious group's outcomes.

omissions.why: Veterans appear in the Atlas in civic roles, such as poll workers; no overlay yet traces a veteran-specific mechanism with current data.
omissions.would_add: A mechanism such as Veterans Health Administration capacity tied to D5: Quality of public services, with current data.

omissions.item: Intersectional groups (for example, Black women with disabilities)
omissions.why: Samples in the sources used are too small to report reliable figures for these groups.
omissions.would_add: Administrative data with enough people in each group.

omissions.item: Policing, fines and fees, and physical safety
omissions.why: Most of the mechanisms sit in local and state criminal law, outside this model's boundary.
omissions.would_add: A separate layer with its own boundary statement.

omissions.item: Representation for the territories and the District of Columbia
omissions.why: Covered in the constitutional options (R-50: Assess constitutional representation changes and the popular-vote compact) and in issue records; not modeled as a variable.
omissions.would_add: A representation variable covering residents who live outside the states.

omissions.item: School finance, environmental health and the quality of the health system
omissions.why: Each would need its own layer; the model touches them only through EC9: Cost of essentials and D5: Quality of public services.
omissions.would_add: Variables for each layer, with outcome data.

omissions.item: Local effects of Louisiana v. Callais beyond congressional maps
omissions.would_add: State and local map data from after 2026.

omissions.why: D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions measures how durable control is, whichever party holds it, so the model's structure applies to either party.
omissions.would_add: No addition planned; the model is built to apply to either party.
